Pārājikuddeso		[sound:Bi_PJ_1.mp3]	21	At one time the Buddha was staying at Verañjā at the foot of Naḷeru’s Nimba tree with a large sangha of five hundred monks.<br><br>A brahmin in Verañjā was told:<br><br>“Sir, the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan, who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Verañjā at the foot of Naleru’s Nimba tree with a large sangha of five hundred monks.<br><br>That good Gotama has a fine reputation:<br><br>‘He is a Buddha, perfected and fully awakened, complete in insight and conduct, happy, knower of the world, supreme leader of trainable people, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, a Buddha.<br><br>With his own insight he has seen this world with its gods, its lords of death, and its supreme beings, this society with its monastics and brahmins, its gods and humans, and he makes it known to others.<br><br>He has a Teaching that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. It has a true goal and is well articulated. He sets out a perfectly complete and pure spiritual life.’<br><br>It’s good to see such perfected ones.”<br><br>That brahmin then went to the Buddha, exchanged pleasantries with him, sat down, and said,<br><br>“I’ve heard, good Gotama,<br><br>that you don’t bow down to old brahmins, stand up for them, or offer them a seat.<br><br>I’ve now seen that this is indeed the case.<br><br>This isn’t right.”<br><br>“Brahmin, in the world with its gods, lords of death, and supreme beings, in this society with its monastics and brahmins, its gods and humans, I don’t see anyone I should bow down to, rise up for, or offer a seat.<br><br>If I did, their head would explode.”<br><br>“Good Gotama lacks taste.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I lack taste.<br><br>For I’ve abandoned the taste for forms, sounds, smells, flavors, and touches. I’ve cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, eradicated it, and made it incapable of reappearing in the future.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama has no enjoyment.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I have no enjoyment.<br><br>For I’ve abandoned the enjoyment of forms, sounds, smells, flavors, and touches. I’ve cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, eradicated it, and made it incapable of reappearing in the future.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama teaches inaction.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I teach inaction.<br><br>For I teach the non-doing of misconduct by body, speech, and mind.<br><br>I teach the non-doing of the various kinds of bad, unwholesome actions.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama is an annihilationist.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I’m an annihilationist.<br><br>For I teach the annihilation of sensual desire, ill will, and confusion.<br><br>I teach the annihilation of the various kinds of bad, unwholesome qualities.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama is disgusting.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I’m disgusting.<br><br>For I am disgusted by misconduct by body, speech, and mind.<br><br>I am disgusted by the various kinds of bad, unwholesome qualities.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama is an exterminator.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I’m an exterminator.<br><br>For I teach the extermination of sensual desire, ill will, and confusion.<br><br>I teach the extermination of the various kinds of bad, unwholesome qualities.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama is austere.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I’m austere.<br><br>For I say that bad, unwholesome qualities—misconduct by body, speech, and mind—are to be disciplined.<br><br>One who has abandoned them, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, eradicated them, and made them incapable of reappearing in the future—such a one I call austere.<br><br>Now I’ve abandoned the bad, unwholesome qualities that are to be disciplined. I’ve cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, eradicated them, and made them incapable of reappearing in the future.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.”<br><br>“Good Gotama is withdrawn.”<br><br>“There’s a way you could rightly say that I’m withdrawn.<br><br>For one who has withdrawn from any future conception in a womb, any rebirth in a future life, who has cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, eradicated it, and made it incapable of reappearing in the future—such a one I call withdrawn.<br><br>Now I’ve withdrawn from any future conception in a womb, any rebirth in a future life. I’ve cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, eradicated it, and made it incapable of reappearing in the future.<br><br>But that’s not what you had in mind.<br><br>Suppose, brahmin, there was a hen with eight, ten, or twelve eggs,<br><br>which she had properly covered, warmed, and incubated.<br><br>The first chick that hatches safely—after piercing through the eggshell with its claw or its beak—is it to be called the eldest or the youngest?”<br><br>“It’s to be called the eldest,<br><br>for it’s the eldest among them.”<br><br>“Just so, in this deluded society, enveloped like an egg, I alone in the world have cracked the shell of delusion and reached the supreme full awakening.<br><br>I, brahmin, am the world’s eldest and best.<br><br>I was firmly energetic and had clarity of mindfulness; my body was tranquil and my mind stilled and unified.<br><br>Fully secluded from the five senses, secluded from unwholesome mental qualities, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has movement of the mind, as well as the joy and bliss of seclusion.<br><br>Through the stilling of the movement of the mind, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, as well as the joy and bliss of stillness.<br><br>Through the fading away of joy, I remained even-minded, mindful, and fully aware, experiencing bliss directly, and I entered and remained in the third absorption of which the noble ones declare:<br><br>‘You are even-minded, mindful, and abide in bliss.’<br><br>Through the abandoning of bliss and pain and the earlier ending of joy and aversion, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, which has neither pain nor bliss, but consists of purity of mindfulness and even-mindedness.<br><br>Then, with my mind stilled, purified, cleansed, flawless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and unshakable, I directed it to the knowledge that consists of recollecting past lives.<br><br>I recollected many past lives, that is,<br><br>one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of world dissolution, many eons of world evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution. And I knew:<br><br>‘There I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan.<br><br>Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere,<br><br>and there I had such a name, such a family, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan.<br><br>Passing away from there, I was reborn here.’<br><br>In this way I recollected many past lives with their characteristics and particulars.<br><br>This was the first true insight, which I attained in the first part of the night.<br><br>Delusion was dispelled and true insight arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose,<br><br>as happens to one who is heedful, energetic, and diligent.<br><br>This, brahmin, was my first breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.<br><br>Then, with my mind stilled, purified, cleansed, flawless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and unshakable, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and arising of beings.<br><br>With superhuman and purified clairvoyance, I saw beings passing away and getting reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, gone to good destinations and to bad destinations, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions:<br><br>‘These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who abused the noble ones, who had wrong views and acted accordingly,<br><br>at the breaking up of the body after death, have been reborn in a lower realm, a bad destination, a world of misery, hell.<br><br>But these beings who engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not abuse the noble ones, who held right view and acted accordingly,<br><br>at the breaking up of the body after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heaven world.’<br><br>In this way, with superhuman and purified clairvoyance, I saw beings passing away and getting reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, gone to good destinations and to bad destinations, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions.<br><br>This was the second true insight, which I  attained in the middle part of the night.<br><br>Delusion was dispelled and true insight arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose,<br><br>as happens to one who is heedful, energetic, and diligent.<br><br>This, brahmin, was my second breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.<br><br>Then, with my mind stilled, purified, cleansed, flawless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and unshakable, I directed it to the knowledge of the ending of the corruptions.<br><br>I knew according to reality: ‘This is suffering;’ ‘This is the origin of suffering;’ ‘This is the end of suffering;’ ‘This is the path leading to the end of suffering.’<br><br>I knew according to reality: ‘These are the corruptions;’ ‘This is the origin of the corruptions;’ ‘This is the end of the corruptions;’ ‘This is the path leading to the end of the corruptions.’<br><br>When I knew and saw this, my mind was freed from the corruption of worldly desire, from the corruption of desire to exist, and from the corruption of delusion.<br><br>When it was freed, I knew it was freed.<br><br>I understood that birth had come to an end, the spiritual life had been fulfilled, the job had been done, there was no further state of existence.<br><br>This was the third true insight, which I attained in the last part of the night.<br><br>Delusion was dispelled and true insight arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose,<br><br>as happens to one who is heedful, energetic, and diligent.<br><br>This, brahmin, was my third breaking out, like a chick from an eggshell.”<br><br>That brahmin then said to the Buddha,<br><br>“Good Gotama is the eldest! Good Gotama is the best!<br><br>Wonderful, good Gotama, wonderful!<br><br>Just as one might set upright what’s overturned, or reveal what’s hidden, or show the way to one who’s lost, or bring a lamp into the dark so that one with eyes might see what’s there—<br><br>just so has the Buddha made the Teaching clear in many ways.<br><br>Good Gotama, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Teaching, and the Sangha of monks.<br><br>Please accept me as a lay follower who’s gone for refuge for life.<br><br>And please consent to spend the rainy-season residence at Verañjā together with the Sangha of monks.”<br><br>The Buddha consented by keeping silent, and the brahmin understood.<br><br>He then got up from his seat, bowed down, circumambulated the Buddha with his right side toward him, and left.<br><br>At that time Verañjā was short of food and afflicted with hunger, with crops affected by whiteheads and turned to straw. It was not easy to get by on almsfood.<br><br>Just then some horse dealers from Uttarāpatha had entered the rainy-season residence at Verañjā with five hundred horses.<br><br>In the horse pen they prepared portion upon portion of steamed grain for the monks.<br><br>Then, after robing up in the morning, the monks took their bowls and robes and entered Verañjā for alms. Not getting anything, they went to the horse pen. They then brought back many portions of steamed grain to the monastery, where they pounded and ate them.<br><br>Venerable Ānanda crushed a portion on a stone, took it to the Buddha, and the Buddha ate it.<br><br>And the Buddha heard the sound of the mortar.<br><br>When Buddhas know what is going on, sometimes they ask and sometimes not.<br><br>They know the right time to ask and when not to ask.<br><br>Buddhas ask when it is beneficial, otherwise not,<br><br>for Buddhas are incapable of doing what is unbeneficial.<br><br>Buddhas question the monks for two reasons: to give a teaching or to lay down a training rule.<br><br>And so he said to Ānanda, “Ānanda, what’s this sound of a mortar?”<br><br>Ānanda told him what was happening.<br><br>“Well done, Ānanda.<br><br>You’re all superior people who have conquered the problems of famine. Later generations will despise even meat and rice.”<br><br>Then Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“At present, sir, Verañjā is short of food and afflicted with hunger, with crops affected by whiteheads and turned to straw.<br><br>It’s not easy to get by on almsfood.<br><br>But the undersurface of this great earth abounds with food, tasting just like pure honey.<br><br>Would it be good, sir, if I inverted the earth so that the monks may enjoy the nutrition in that ground fungus?”<br><br>“But what will you do, Moggallāna, with the creatures that live there?”<br><br>“I’ll transform one hand to be like the great earth and make those creatures go there.<br><br>I’ll then invert the earth with the other hand.”<br><br>“Let it be, Moggallāna, don’t invert the earth.<br><br>Those creatures might lose their minds.”<br><br>“In that case, sir, would it be good if the whole Sangha of monks could go to Uttarakuru for alms?”<br><br>“Let it be, Moggallāna, don’t pursue this.”<br><br>Soon afterwards, while reflecting in private, Venerable Sāriputta thought,<br><br>“Which Buddhas had a long-lasting spiritual life, and which not?”<br><br>In the evening, after coming out of seclusion, Sāriputta went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Just now, sir, while I was reflecting in private, I was wondering which Buddhas had a long-lasting spiritual life, and which not.”<br><br>“Sāriputta, the spiritual life established by the Buddhas Vipassī, Sikhī, and Vessabhū didn’t last long.<br><br>But the spiritual life established by the Buddhas Kakusandha, Konāgamana, and Kassapa did.”<br><br>“And why did the spiritual life established by the former three Buddhas not last long?”<br><br>“They made no effort to give detailed teachings to their disciples.<br><br>They gave few discourses in prose or in mixed prose and verse; few expositions, verses, heartfelt exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing accounts, and analyses.<br><br>Nor did they lay down training rules or recite a monastic code.<br><br>After the disappearance of those Buddhas and the disciples awakened under them, those who were the last disciples—of various names, families, and castes, who had gone forth from various households—allowed that spiritual life to disappear rapidly.<br><br>It’s like flowers on a wooden plank. If they’re not held together with a string, they’re scattered about, whirled about, and destroyed by the wind.<br><br>Why?<br><br>Because they’re not held together with a string.<br><br>Just so, after the disappearance of those Buddhas and the disciples awakened under them, those who were the last disciples allowed that spiritual life to disappear rapidly.<br><br>Instead they were untiring at instructing their disciples by reading their minds.<br><br>At one time, Sāriputta, the Buddha Vessabhū, the Perfected and the fully Awakened One, was staying in a certain frightening forest grove. He instructed a sangha of a thousand monks by reading their minds, saying,<br><br>‘Think like this, not like that;<br><br>pay attention like this, not like that;<br><br>abandon this and attain that.’<br><br>When they had been instructed by Buddha Vessabhū, their minds were freed from the corruptions through letting go.<br><br>But if anyone with sensual desire entered that frightening forest grove, they usually had goosebumps all over.<br><br>This is why the spiritual life established by those Buddhas did not last long.”<br><br>“Why then did the spiritual life established by the latter three Buddhas last long?”<br><br>“The Buddhas Kakusandha, Konāgamana, and Kassapa were untiring in giving detailed teachings to their disciples.<br><br>They gave many discourses in prose and in mixed prose and verse; many expositions, verses, heartfelt exclamations, quotations, birth stories, amazing accounts, and analyses.<br><br>And they laid down training rules and recited a monastic code.<br><br>After the disappearance of those Buddhas and the disciples awakened under them, those who were the last disciples—of various names, families, and castes, who had gone forth from various households—made that spiritual life last for a long time.<br><br>It’s like flowers on a wooden plank. If they’re held together with a string, they’re not scattered about, whirled about, or destroyed by the wind.<br><br>Why?<br><br>Because they are held together with a string.<br><br>Just so, after the disappearance of those Buddhas and the disciples awakened under them, those who were the last disciples made that spiritual life last for a long time.<br><br>This is why the spiritual life established by those Buddhas lasted long.”<br><br>Sāriputta then got up from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, raised his joined palms, and said,<br><br>“This is the time, venerable sir,<br><br>for laying down training rules and reciting a monastic code, so that this spiritual life may last for a long time.”<br><br>“Hold on, Sāriputta.<br><br>The Buddha knows the appropriate time for this.<br><br>The Teacher doesn’t lay down training rules or recite a monastic code until the causes of corruption appear in the Sangha.<br><br>And they don’t appear until the Sangha has attained long standing,<br><br>great size,<br><br>an abundance of the best material support,<br><br>or great learning.<br><br>When the causes of corruption appear for any of these reasons, then the Teacher lays down training rules for his disciples and recites a monastic code in order to counteract these causes.<br><br>Sāriputta, the Sangha of monks is free from cancer and danger, stainless, pure, and established in the essence.<br><br>Even the least developed of these five hundred monks is a streamenterer. They will not be reborn in the lower world, but are fixed in destiny and bound for awakening.”<br><br>Then the Buddha said to Ānanda, “Ānanda, it’s the custom for Buddhas not to go wandering the country without taking leave of those who invited them to spend the rainy-season residence.<br><br>Let’s go to the brahmin of Verañjā and take leave.”<br><br>“Yes, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha robed up, took his bowl and robe and, with Ānanda as his attendant, went to that brahmin’s house where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>The brahmin approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>And the Buddha said, “Brahmin, we’ve completed the rains residence according to your invitation, and now we take leave of you.<br><br>We wish to depart to wander the country.”<br><br>“It’s true, good Gotama, that you’ve completed the rains residence according to my invitation, but I haven’t given anything.<br><br>That’s not good.<br><br>It’s not because I didn’t want to, but because household life is so busy.<br><br>Would you and the Sangha of monks please accept a meal from me tomorrow?”<br><br>The Buddha consented by keeping silent.<br><br>Then, after instructing, inspiring, and gladdening that brahmin with a teaching, the Buddha got up from his seat and left.<br><br>The following morning the brahmin prepared various kinds of fine foods in his own house and then had the Buddha informed that the meal was ready.<br><br>The Buddha robed up, took his bowl and robe and, together with the Sangha of monks, he went to that brahmin’s house where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>And that brahmin personally served and satisfied the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha with various kinds of fine foods. When the Buddha had finished his meal, the brahmin gave him a set of three robes and to each monk two pieces of cloth.<br><br>The Buddha instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a teaching, and then got up from his seat and left.<br><br>After remaining in Verañjā for as long as he liked, the Buddha traveled to Payāgapatiṭṭhāna via Soreyya, Saṅkassa, and Kaṇṇakujja. There he crossed the river Ganges and continued on to Benares.<br><br>After remaining at Benares for as long as he liked, he set out wandering toward Vesālī.<br><br>When he eventually arrived,<br><br>he stayed in the house with the peaked roof in the Great Wood.<br><br>The section for recitation on Verañjā is finished.<br><br>At that time Sudinna, the son of a wealthy merchant, lived in a village called Kalanda not far from Vesālī.<br><br>On one occasion Sudinna went to Vesālī on some business together with a number of friends.<br><br>Just then the Buddha was seated giving a teaching, surrounded by a large gathering of people.<br><br>When Sudinna saw this, he thought, “Why don’t I listen to the Teaching?”<br><br>He then approached that gathering and sat down.<br><br>As he was sitting there, he thought,<br><br>“The way I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, it’s not easy for one who lives at home to lead the spiritual life perfectly complete and pure as a polished conch shell.<br><br>Why don’t I cut off my hair and beard, put on the ocher robes, and go forth into homelessness?”<br><br>When those people had been instructed, inspired, and gladdened by the Buddha, they got up from their seats, bowed down, circumambulated him with their right sides toward him, and left.<br><br>Sudinna then approached the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and told him what he had thought, adding,<br><br>“Sir, please give me the going forth.”<br><br>“But, Sudinna, do you have your parents’ permission?”<br><br>“No.”<br><br>“Buddhas don’t give the going forth to anyone who hasn’t gotten their parents’ permission.”<br><br>“I’ll do whatever is necessary, sir, to get my parents’ permission.”<br><br>After finishing his business in Vesālī, Sudinna returned to Kalanda. He then went to his parents and said,<br><br>“Mom and dad, the way I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, it’s not easy for one who lives at home to lead the spiritual life perfectly complete and pure.<br><br>I want to cut off my hair and beard, put on the ocher robes, and go forth into homelessness.<br><br>Please give me permission to go forth.”<br><br>“But, Sudinna, you’re our only child, and we love you dearly. You live in comfort and we care for you. You don’t have any suffering.<br><br>Even if you died we wouldn’t want to lose you.<br><br>So how can we allow you to go forth into homelessness while you’re still living?”<br><br>Sudinna asked his parents a second<br><br>and a third time,<br><br>but got the same reply.<br><br>He then lay down on the bare ground and said,<br><br>“I’ll either die right here or go forth!”<br><br>And he did not eat at the next seven meals.<br><br>His parents repeated what they had said, adding,<br><br>“Get up, Sudinna, eat, drink, and enjoy yourself!<br><br>Enjoy the pleasures of the world and do acts of merit.<br><br>We won’t allow you to go forth.”<br><br>But Sudinna did not respond.<br><br>His parents said the same thing a second<br><br>and a third time,<br><br>but Sudinna remained silent.<br><br>Then Sudinna’s friends went to him and repeated three times what his parents had said.<br><br>When Sudinna still did not respond, Sudinna’s friends went to his parents and said,<br><br>“Sudinna says he’ll either die right there on the bare ground or go forth.<br><br>If you don’t allow him to go forth, he’ll die there.<br><br>But if you allow him to go forth, you’ll see him again afterwards.<br><br>And if he doesn’t enjoy the going forth, what alternative will he have but to come back here?<br><br>So please allow him to go forth.”<br><br>“Alright, then.”<br><br>And Sudinna’s friends said to him,<br><br>“Get up, Sudinna, your parents have given you permission to go forth.”<br><br>When Sudinna heard this, he was excited and joyful, stroking his limbs with his hands as he got up.<br><br>After spending a few days to regain his strength, he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Sir, I’ve gotten my parents’ permission to go forth.<br><br>Please give me the going forth.”<br><br>He then received the going forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Buddha.<br><br>Not long afterwards he practiced these kinds of ascetic practices: he stayed in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and went on continuous almsround.<br><br>And he lived supported by a certain Vajjian village.<br><br>Soon afterwards, the Vajjians were short of food and afflicted with hunger, with crops affected by whiteheads and turned to straw. It was not easy to get by on almsfood.<br><br>Sudinna considered this and thought,<br><br>“I have many wealthy relatives in Vesālī.<br><br>Why don’t I get them to support me?<br><br>My relatives will be able to make offerings and merit, the monks will get material support, and I’ll have no trouble getting almsfood.”<br><br>He then put his dwelling in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out for Vesālī.<br><br>When he eventually arrived, he stayed in the house with the peaked roof in the Great Wood.<br><br>His relatives heard that he had arrived in Vesālī, and they presented him with an offering of sixty servings of food.<br><br>Sudinna gave the sixty servings to the monks. He then took his bowl and robe and went to the village of Kalanda for alms.<br><br>As he was going on continuous almsround, he came to his own father’s house.<br><br>Just then a female slave of Sudinna’s relatives was about to throw away the previous evening’s porridge.<br><br>Sudinna said to her,<br><br>“If that’s to be thrown away, sister, put it here in my almsbowl.”<br><br>As she was putting the porridge into his bowl, she recognized his hands, feet, and voice.<br><br>She then went to his mother and said,<br><br>“Please be aware, ma’am,<br><br>that master Sudinna is back.”<br><br>“Gosh, if you’re telling the truth, you’re a free woman!”<br><br>As Sudinna was eating the previous evening’s porridge at the base of a certain wall,<br><br>his father was coming home from work.<br><br>When he saw him sitting there, he went up to him and said,<br><br>“But, Sudinna, isn’t there … What! You’re eating old porridge!<br><br>Why don’t you come to your own house?”<br><br>“We went to your house, householder.<br><br>That’s where we received this porridge.”<br><br>Sudinna’s father took him by the arm and said, “Come, let’s go home.”<br><br>Sudinna went to his father’s house and sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>His father said to him, “Please eat, Sudinna.”<br><br>“There’s no need. I’m done for today.”<br><br>“Then come back for the meal tomorrow.”<br><br>Sudinna consented by keeping silent, and he got up from his seat and left.<br><br>The next morning Sudinna’s mother had the floor smeared with fresh cow-dung. She then piled up two heaps, one with money, the other with gold.<br><br>The heaps were so large that a man standing on one side could not see a man standing on the other.<br><br>She hid the heaps behind screens, prepared a seat between them, and surrounded it all with a curtain. And she said to Sudinna’s ex-wife,<br><br>“Now please adorn yourself in the way our son Sudinna found you especially attractive.”<br><br>“Yes, ma’am.”<br><br>Then, after robing up, Venerable Sudinna took his bowl and robe and went to his father’s house where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>His father went up to him, uncovered the heaps, and said,<br><br>“This dowry, dear Sudinna, is the fortune from your mother. It’s yours. Another is the fortune from your father and another the fortune from your ancestors.<br><br>Please return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.”<br><br>“I can’t, father. I’m enjoying the spiritual life.”<br><br>Sudinna’s father repeated his request and Sudinna replied as before.<br><br>When Sudinna’s father repeated his request a third time, Sudinna said,<br><br>“If you wouldn’t get offended, I could tell you what to do.”<br><br>“Let’s hear it.”<br><br>“Well then, make some large hempen sacks, put all the money and gold inside, take it all away in carts, and dump it in the middle of the Ganges.<br><br>And why?<br><br>Because that way you will avoid the danger, fear, and terror that it will otherwise cause you, as well as the trouble with protecting it.”<br><br>His father became upset, thinking, “How can our son Sudinna say such things?”<br><br>He then said to Sudinna’s ex-wife,<br><br>“Well then, since you were so dear to him, perhaps our son Sudinna will listen to you?”<br><br>Sudinna’s ex-wife took hold of his feet and said,<br><br>“What are these nymphs like, sir, for which you practice the spiritual life?”<br><br>“Sister, I don’t practice the spiritual life for the sake of nymphs.”<br><br>His ex-wife thought, “Sudinna is now calling me ‘sister’,” and she fainted right there.<br><br>Sudinna said to his father,<br><br>“If there’s food to be given, householder, give it,<br><br>but don’t annoy me.”<br><br>“Eat, Sudinna,” he said.<br><br>And Sudinna’s mother and father personally served and satisfied him with various kinds of fine foods.<br><br>When Sudinna had finished his meal, his mother said to him:<br><br>“Sudinna dear, our family is rich.<br><br>Please return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.”<br><br>“Mother, I can’t. I’m enjoying the spiritual life.”<br><br>His mother repeated her request a second time, but got the same reply.<br><br>She then said,<br><br>“Our family is wealthy, Sudinna.<br><br>Please give us an offspring,<br><br>so that the Licchavīs don’t take over our heirless property.”<br><br>“Yes, mother, I can do that.”<br><br>“But where are you staying?”<br><br>“In the Great Wood.”<br><br>And he got up from his seat and left.<br><br>Sudinna’s mother then said to his ex-wife,<br><br>“Well then, as soon as you reach your fertile period, please tell me.”<br><br>“Yes, ma’am.”<br><br>Not long afterwards Sudinna’s ex-wife reached her fertile period,<br><br>and she reported it to Sudinna’s mother.<br><br>“Now, please adorn yourself in the way that our son Sudinna found you especially attractive.”<br><br>“Yes.”<br><br>Then Sudinna’s mother, together with his ex-wife, went to Sudinna in the Great Wood, and she said to him:<br><br>“Our family, dear Sudinna, is rich.<br><br>Please return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.”<br><br>“Mother, I can’t.<br><br>I’m enjoying the spiritual life.”<br><br>His mother repeated her request a second time, but got the same reply.<br><br>She then said this:<br><br>“Well then, please give us an offspring.<br><br>We don’t want the Licchavīs to take over our heirless property.”<br><br>“Alright, mother.”<br><br>He then took his ex-wife by the arm, disappeared into the Great Wood and—there being no training rule and he seeing no danger—had sexual intercourse with her three times.<br><br>As a result she conceived.<br><br>And the earth gods cried out:<br><br>“Sirs, the Sangha of monks has been free from cancer and danger.<br><br>But Sudinna of Kalanda has produced a cancer and endangered it.”<br><br>Hearing the earth gods, the gods of the four great kings cried out …<br><br>the gods of the Thirty-three …<br><br>the Yāma gods …<br><br>the contented gods …<br><br>the gods who delight in creation …<br><br>the gods who control the creation of others …<br><br>the gods of the realm of the supreme beings cried out:<br><br>“Sirs, the Sangha of monks has been free from cancer and danger.<br><br>But Sudinna of Kalanda has produced a cancer and endangered it.”<br><br>Thus in that moment, in that instance, the news spread as far as the world of the supreme beings.<br><br>In the meantime, the pregnancy of Sudinna’s ex-wife developed, and she eventually gave birth to a son.<br><br>Sudinna’s friends called him Offspring,<br><br>while calling Sudinna’s ex-wife Offspring’s mother,<br><br>and Venerable Sudinna Offspring’s father.<br><br>After some time, they both went forth into homelessness and realized perfection.<br><br>But Sudinna was anxious and remorseful, thinking,<br><br>“This is truly bad for me,<br><br>that after going forth on such a well-proclaimed spiritual path, I wasn’t able to practice the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life to the end.”<br><br>And because of his anxiety and remorse, he became thin, haggard, and pale, with veins protruding all over his body. He became sad, sluggish, miserable, and depressed, weighed down by remorse.<br><br>The monks who were Sudinna’s friends said to him:<br><br>“In the past, Sudinna, you had a good color, a bright face, clear skin, and sharp senses.<br><br>But look at you now.<br><br>Could it be that you are dissatisfied with the spiritual life?”<br><br>“I am not dissatisfied with the spiritual life,<br><br>but I’ve done something bad.<br><br>I’ve had sexual intercourse with my ex-wife.<br><br>I’m anxious and remorseful<br><br>because I wasn’t able to practice the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life to the end.”<br><br>“No wonder you’re anxious, Sudinna, no wonder you have remorse.<br><br>Hasn’t the Buddha given many teachings for the sake of dispassion, not for the sake of lust;<br><br>for the sake of freedom from bondage, not for the sake of bondage;<br><br>for the sake of non-grasping, not for the sake of grasping?<br><br>When the Buddha has taught in this way, how could you choose lust, bondage, and grasping?<br><br>Hasn’t the Buddha given many teachings for the fading away of lust,<br><br>for the clearing away of intoxication, for the removal of thirst, for the uprooting of attachment, for the cutting off of the round of rebirth, for the stopping of craving, for fading away, for ending, for extinguishment?<br><br>Hasn’t the Buddha in many ways taught the abandoning of worldly pleasures,<br><br>the full understanding of the perceptions of worldly pleasures,<br><br>the removal of thirst for worldly pleasures,<br><br>the elimination of thoughts of worldly "There is no offense:<br><br>if he does not know;<br><br>if he does not consent;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is deranged;<br><br>if he is overwhelmed by pain;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The section for recitation on covering is finished.<br><br>Summary verses of case studies<br><br>“The female monkey, and the Vajjians,<br><br>Householder, and a naked one, monastics of other religions;<br><br>The girl, and Uppalavaṇṇā,<br><br>Two others with characteristics.<br><br>Mother, daughter, and sister,<br><br>And wife, supple, with long;<br><br>Two on wounds, and a picture,<br><br>And a wooden doll.<br><br>Five with Sundara,<br><br>Five about charnel grounds, bones;<br><br>A female dragon, and a female spirit, and a female ghost,<br><br>A <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, impaired, should touch.<br><br>The sleeping Perfected One in Bhaddiya,<br><br>Four others in Sāvatthī;<br><br>Three in Vesālī, garlands,<br><br>The one from Bhārukaccha in his dream.<br><br>Supabbā, Saddhā, a nun,<br><br>A trainee nun, and a novice nun;<br><br>A sex worker, a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, a female householder,<br><br>Each other, gone forth in old age, a deer.”"	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṁ viharati naḷerupucimandamūle mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṁ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi.<br><br>Assosi kho verañjo brāhmaṇo—<br><br>“samaṇo khalu bho gotamo sakyaputto sakyakulā pabbajito verañjāyaṁ viharati naḷerupucimandamūle mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṁ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi.<br><br>Taṁ kho pana bhavantaṁ gotamaṁ evaṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato—<br><br>‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavā’,<br><br>so imaṁ lokaṁ sadevakaṁ samārakaṁ sabrahmakaṁ sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṁ pajaṁ sadevamanussaṁ sayaṁ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti,<br><br>so dhammaṁ deseti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ;
