unenclosed storehouse belonging to many clans and having many rooms: one must stay in the room where the robe is kept, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the room.<br><br><b>A watchtower</b><br><br>A watchtower belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept in the watchtower, one must stay within the watchtower.<br><br>A watchtower belonging to many clans and having many rooms: one must stay in the room where the robe is kept, or at the main entrance, or not go beyond arm’s reach of either.<br><br><b>A stilt house</b><br><br>A stilt house belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept in the stilt house, one must stay within the stilt house.<br><br>A stilt house belonging to many clans and having many rooms: one must stay in the room where the robe is kept, or at the main entrance, or not go beyond arm’s reach of either.<br><br><b>A boat</b><br><br>A boat belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept on the boat, one must stay on the boat.<br><br>A boat belonging to many clans and having many rooms: one must stay in the room where the robe is kept, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the room.<br><br><b>A caravan</b><br><br>A caravan belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept within the caravan, one must not go further than 80 meters in front of or behind the caravan, and no further than 11 meters from either side.<br><br>A caravan belonging to many clans: if the robe is kept within the caravan, one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the caravan.<br><br><b>A field</b><br><br>An enclosed field belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept within the field, one must stay within that field.<br><br>An unenclosed field belonging to one clan: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br>An enclosed field belonging to many clans: if the robe is kept within the field, one must stay at the entrance to the field, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the entrance or the robe.<br><br>An unenclosed field belonging to many clans: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br><b>A threshing floor</b><br><br>An enclosed threshing floor belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept on the threshing floor, one must stay on that threshing floor.<br><br>An unenclosed threshing floor belonging to one clan: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br>An enclosed threshing floor belonging to many clans: if the robe is kept on the threshing floor, one must stay at the entrance to the threshing floor, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the entrance or the robe.<br><br>An unenclosed threshing floor belonging to many clans: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br><b>A monastery</b><br><br>An enclosed monastery belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept within the monastery, one must stay within that monastery.<br><br>An unenclosed monastery belonging to one clan: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br>An enclosed monastery belonging to many clans: if the robe is kept within the monastery, one must stay at the entrance to the monastery, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the entrance or the robe.<br><br>An unenclosed monastery belonging to many clans: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br><b>A dwelling</b><br><br>An enclosed dwelling belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept within the dwelling, one must stay within that dwelling.<br><br>An unenclosed dwelling belonging to one clan: one must stay in the dwelling where the robe is kept, or not go beyond arm’s reach of that dwelling.<br><br>An enclosed dwelling belonging to many clans: one must stay in the dwelling where the robe is kept, or at the main entrance to the dwelling, or not go beyond arm’s reach of either.<br><br>An unenclosed dwelling belonging to many clans: one must stay in the dwelling where the robe is kept, or not go beyond arm’s reach of the dwelling.<br><br><b>The foot of a tree</b><br><br>At the foot of a tree belonging to one clan: if the robe is kept within the area of the midday shadow of the tree, one must stay within that area.<br><br>At the foot of a tree belonging to many clans: one must not go beyond arm’s reach of the robe.<br><br><b>In the open</b><br><br>Out-in-the-open with a single access: in an uninhabited area, in the wilderness, the area covered by a circle with 80 meters radius has a single access.<br><br>Whatever lies beyond that has many accesses.<br><br>If he has stayed apart and he perceives that he has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he has stayed apart, but he is unsure of it, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he has stayed apart, but he does not perceive that he has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been relinquished, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been given away, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been lost, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been destroyed, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been burned, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been stolen, but he perceives that it has, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he uses a robe that should be relinquished without first relinquishing it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he has not stayed apart, but he perceives that he has, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he has not stayed apart, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he has not stayed apart and he does not perceive that he has, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if before dawn it has been relinquished, given away, lost, destroyed, burned, stolen, or taken on trust;<br><br>if he has the permission of the monks;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on storehouses, the second, is finished. [sound:ABi_NP_14.mp3]	{-the “storehouse”} When a bhikkhunī has finished her robe-making and the frame is destroyed: If she dwells apart from (any of) her three robes even for one night — unless authorized by the bhikkhunīs—it is to be forfeited and confessed. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::2 Cīvara Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 16	Aññātakaviññattisikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī aññātakaṁ gahapatiṁ vā gahapatāniṁ vā cīvaraṁ viññāpeyya aññatra samayā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. <br>Tatthāyaṁ samayo acchinnacīvarā vā hoti bhikkhunī, naṭṭhacīvarā vā, ayaṁ tattha samayo.		Matches Bu NP 6	Uses 'bhikkhunī',&nbsp;acchinnacīvarā, naṭṭhacīvarā	If a nun asks an unrelated male or female householder for a robe, except on an appropriate occasion, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br>These are the appropriate occasions: her robes are stolen or her robes are lost.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Cīvaravaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_16.mp3]	151	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time Venerable Upananda the Sakyan was skilled at teaching.<br><br>On one occasion the son of a wealthy merchant went to Upananda, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>And Upananda instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a teaching.<br><br>Afterwards that merchant’s son said to Upananda:<br><br>“Venerable, please tell me what you need.<br><br>I can give you robe-cloth, almsfood, a dwelling, and medicinal supplies.”<br><br>“If you wish to give me something, give me one of your wrap garments.”<br><br>“It’s shameful, venerable, for a gentleman to walk around in only one wrap.<br><br>Please wait until I get back home.<br><br>I’ll send you this wrap or a better one.”<br><br>A second time<br><br>and a third time Upananda said<br><br>the same thing to that merchant’s son,<br><br>and he got the same reply.<br><br>He then said, “What’s the point of inviting me if you don’t want to give?”<br><br>Being pressured by Upananda, that merchant’s son gave him one of his wraps and left.<br><br>People asked him why he was walking around in only one wrap,<br><br>and he told them what had happened.<br><br>People complained and criticized him,<br><br>“These Sakyan monastics have great desires. They’re not content.<br><br>Even to make them an appropriate offer isn’t easy.<br><br>How could they take his wrap when the merchant’s son was making an appropriate offer?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda ask the merchant’s son for a robe?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned Upananda:<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>“Is he a relative of yours?”<br><br>“No.”<br><br>“Foolish man, people who are unrelated don’t know what’s appropriate and inappropriate, what’s good and bad, in dealing with each other.<br><br>And still you did this.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk asks an unrelated male or female householder for a robe, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of monks who were traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī were robbed by bandits.<br><br>Knowing that the Buddha had laid down this training rule and being afraid of wrongdoing, they did not ask for robes.<br><br>As a consequence, they walked naked to Sāvatthī, where they bowed down to the monks.<br><br>The monks there said, “These Ājīvaka ascetics are good people, as they bow down to the monks.”<br><br>“We’re not Ājīvakas! We’re monks!”<br><br>The monks asked Venerable Upāli to examine them.<br><br>When the naked monks told him what had happened, Upāli said to the monks, “They are monks. Please give them robes.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can monks go naked?<br><br>Shouldn’t they have covered up with grass and leaves?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, if a monk’s robes are stolen or lost, I allow him to ask an unrelated householder for robes.<br><br>At the first monastery where he arrives, if the Sangha has a communal robe, a bedspread, a floor cover, or a mattress cover, he should take that and put it on, thinking, ‘When I get a robe, I’ll return it.’<br><br>If there’s none of these things, he should cover up with grass and leaves before going on. He should not go on while naked.<br><br>If he does, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Unrelated:<br><br>anyone who is not a descendant of one’s male ancestors going back eight generations, either on the mother’s side or on the father’s side.<br><br>A male householder:<br><br>any man who lives at home.<br><br>A female householder:<br><br>any woman who lives at home.<br><br>A robe:<br><br>one of the six kinds of robe-cloth, but not smaller than what can be assigned to another.<br><br>Except on an appropriate occasion:<br><br>unless it is an appropriate occasion.<br><br>His robes are stolen:<br><br>a monk’s robe is taken by kings, bandits, scoundrels, or whoever.<br><br>His robes are lost:<br><br>a monk’s robe is burned by fire, carried away by flooding, eaten by rats or termites, or worn through use.<br><br>If he asks, except on an appropriate occasion, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets the robe-cloth, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The robe-cloth should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a related, but the monk is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the person is related and the monk perceives them as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is an appropriate occasion;<br><br>if he asks relatives;<br><br>if he asks those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if he asks for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on asking non-relations, the sixth, is finished. [sound:ABi_NP_16.mp3]	{-asking a non-relative} Should any bhikkhunī ask for robe-cloth from a man or woman householder unrelated to her, except at the proper occasion, it is to be forfeited and confessed. Here the proper occasion is this: The bhikkhunī’s robe has been stolen or destroyed. This is the proper occasion in this case. [6]

Tato ce uttari cetāpeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun carries out an exchange to get a heavy cloak, it is to be worth at most four kaṁsa coins. If she gets one in exchange that is worth more than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Cīvaravaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_11.mp3]	142	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nun Thullanandā was a learned reciter, and she was confident and skilled at giving teachings.<br><br>On one occasion when the weather was cold, King Pasenadi of Kosala put on an expensive woolen cloak and went to Thullanandā. He bowed and sat down.<br><br>And Thullanandā instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a teaching.<br><br>He then said,<br><br>“Venerable, please say what you need.”<br><br>“Great king, if you wish to give me something, then give me this woolen cloak.”<br><br>The king gave her his cloak. He then got up from his seat, bowed down, circumambulated her with his right side toward her, and left.<br><br>People complained and criticized her,<br><br>“These nuns have great desires; they are not content.<br><br>How can they ask the king for his woolen cloak?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā ask the king for his woolen cloak?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā asked for this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā ask the king for his woolen cloak?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A heavy cloak:<br><br>whatever cloak is used in cold weather.<br><br>Carries out an exchange to get:<br><br>asks for.<br><br>It is to be worth at most four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins:<br><br>it may be worth sixteen <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i> coins.<br><br>If she gets one in exchange that is worth more than that:<br><br>if she asks for one worth more than that, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she gets it, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>It should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual nun.<br><br>“And, monks, it’s to be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bi-vb-np1/en/brahmali#2.1.21"">Bi Np 1:2.1.21</a>–Bi Np 1:2.1.43, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, this heavy cloak worth more than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, which I got in exchange, is to be relinquished. I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is worth more than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, and she perceives it as such, and she gets it in exchange, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is worth more than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, but she is unsure of it, and she gets it in exchange, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is worth more than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, but she perceives it as being worth less, and she gets it in exchange, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is worth less than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, but she perceives it as being worth more, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is worth less than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is worth less than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins, and she perceives it as such, there is no offense."	"There is no offense:<br><br>if she carries out an exchange for one worth at most four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins;<br><br>if she carries out an exchange for one worth less than four <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kaṁsa</i> coins;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she gets one in exchange that has little value from someone who wants to exchange one of great value;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eleventh training rule is finished."	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena thullanandā bhikkhunī bahussutā hoti bhāṇikā visāradā paṭṭā dhammiṁ kathaṁ [sound:ABi_NP_11.mp3]	{-heavy cloth} When a bhikkhunī is asking for a heavy cloth, one worth four bronzes at most may be asked for. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::2 Cīvara Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 17	Tatuttarisikkhāpadaṁ	Tañce aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā bahūhi cīvarehi abhihaṭṭhuṁ pavāreyya, santaruttaraparamaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā tato cīvaraṁ sāditabbaṁ. <br>Tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu NP 7	Uses 'tāya bhikkhuniyā'. Uses 'uttari' instead of 'uttariṃ'.	If an unrelated male or female householder invites that nun to take many robes, she should accept at most one sarong and one upper robe.<br>If she accepts more than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Cīvaravaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_17.mp3]	154	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six said to the monks whose robes had been stolen,<br><br>“The Buddha has allowed<br><br>a monk whose robes have been stolen or lost to ask an unrelated householder for a robe.<br><br>You should ask for a robe.”<br><br>“It’s not necessary. We’ve already gotten robes.”<br><br>“We’ll ask for you.”<br><br>“Do as you please.”<br><br>The monks from the group of six then went to householders and said,<br><br>“Monks have arrived whose robes have been stolen.<br><br>Please give them robes.”<br><br>And they asked for many robes.<br><br>Soon afterwards in the public meeting hall a certain man said to another,<br><br>“Sir, monks have arrived whose robes have been stolen.<br><br>I’ve given them robes.”<br><br>The other replied, “So have I.”<br><br>And another said the same.<br><br>They complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics ask for many robes without moderation?<br><br>Are they going to trade in cloth or set up shop?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six ask for many robes without moderation?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>That monk:<br><br>the monk whose robes have been stolen.<br><br>Unrelated:<br><br>anyone who is not a descendant of one’s male ancestors going back eight generations, either on the mother’s side or on the father’s side.<br><br>A male householder:<br><br>any man who lives at home.<br><br>A female householder:<br><br>any woman who lives at home.<br><br>Many robes:<br><br>a lot of robes.<br><br>Invites to take:<br><br>saying, “Take as many as you like.”<br><br>He should accept at most one sarong and one upper robe:<br><br>if three robes are lost, he should accept two; if two robes are lost, he should accept one; if one robe is lost, he should not accept any.<br><br>If he accepts more than that:<br><br>if he asks for more than that, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets the robe, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The robe should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-vb-np1#3.2.5"">Bu NP 1:3.2.5</a>–3.2.29, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, this robe, which I received after asking an unrelated householder for too many, is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this robe back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the person is unrelated and the monk perceives them as such, and he asks them for too many robes, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If the person is unrelated, but the monk is unsure of it, and he asks them for too many robes, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If the person is unrelated, but the monk perceives them as related, and he asks them for too many robes, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If the person is related, but the monk perceives them as unrelated, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the person is related, but the monk is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the person is related and the monk perceives them as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if he takes too much, but with the intention of returning the remainder;<br><br>if they give, saying, “The remainder is for you;”<br><br>if they give, but not because his robes were stolen;<br><br>if they give, but not because his robes were lost;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on more than that, the seventh, is finished. [sound:ABi_NP_17.mp3]	{-accepting more than that} If that unrelated man or woman householder presents the bhikkhunī with many robes (pieces of robe-cloth), she is to accept at most (enough for) an upper and an under robe. If she accepts more than that, it is to be forfeited and confessed. [7]	
Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::2 Cīvara Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 11-20		11. Garupāvuraṇaṁ pana bhikkhuniyā cetāpentiyā catukkaṁsaparamaṁ cetāpetabbaṁ. Tato ce uttari cetāpeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>12. Lahupāvuraṇaṁ pana bhikkhuniyā cetāpentiyā aḍḍhateyyakaṁsaparamaṁ cetāpetabbaṁ. Tato ce uttari cetāpeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>13. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine dasāhaparamaṁ atirekacīvaraṁ dhāretabbaṁ. <br>Taṁ atikkāmentiyā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>14. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine ekarattampi ce bhikkhunī ticīvarena vippavaseyya, aññatra bhikkhunisammutiyā nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>15. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine bhikkhuniyā paneva akālacīvaraṁ uppajjeyya, ākaṅkhamānāya bhikkhuniyā taṁ paṭiggahetabbaṁ, paṭiggahetvā khippameva kāretabbaṁ, no cassa pāripūri, māsaparamaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā taṁ cīvaraṁ nikkhipitabbaṁ ūnassa pāripūriyā satiyā paccāsāya. Tato ce uttari nikkhipeyya satiyāpi paccāsāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>16. Yā pana bhikkhunī aññātakaṁ gahapatiṁ vā gahapatāniṁ vā cīvaraṁ viññāpeyya aññatra samayā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. <br>Tatthāyaṁ samayo acchinnacīvarā vā hoti bhikkhunī, naṭṭhacīvarā vā, ayaṁ tattha samayo.<br><br>17. Tañce aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā bahūhi cīvarehi abhihaṭṭhuṁ pavāreyya, santaruttaraparamaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā tato cīvaraṁ sāditabbaṁ. <br>Tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>18. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa aññātakassa gahapatissa vā gahapatāniyā vā cīvaracetāpannaṁ upakkhaṭaṁ hoti: “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarena acchādessāmī”ti. Tatra cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya: “sādhu vata, maṁ āyasmā iminā cīvaracetāpannena evarūpaṁ vā evarūpaṁ vā cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā acchādehī”ti kalyāṇakamyataṁ upādāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>19. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa ubhinnaṁ aññātakānaṁ gahapatīnaṁ vā gahapatānīnaṁ vā paccekacīvaracetāpannāni upakkhaṭāni honti: “imehi mayaṁ paccekacīvaracetāpannehi paccekacīvarāni cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarehi acchādessāmā”ti. Tatra cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya: “sādhu vata maṁ āyasmanto imehi paccekacīvaracetāpannehi evarūpaṁ vā evarūpaṁ vā cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā acchādetha ubhova santā ekenā”ti kalyāṇakamyataṁ upādāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>20. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa rājā vā rājabhoggo vā brāhmaṇo vā gahapatiko vā dūtena cīvaracetāpannaṁ pahiṇeyya: “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarena acchādehī”ti. So ce dūto taṁ bhikkhuniṁ upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ vadeyya: “idaṁ kho, ayye, ayyaṁ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṁ ābhataṁ, paṭiggaṇhātu āyyā cīvaracetāpanna”nti. Tāya bhikkhuniyā so dūto evamassa vacanīyo: “na kho mayaṁ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma kālena kappiya”nti. So ce dūto taṁ bhikkhuniṁ evaṁ vadeyya: “atthi panāyyāya, kāci veyyāvaccakarā”ti, cīvaratthikāya, bhikkhuniyo, bhikkhuniyā veyyāvaccakarā&nbsp;niddisitabbā&nbsp;ārāmikā&nbsp;vā upāsikā&nbsp;vā: “esā&nbsp;kho, āvuso, bhikkhunīnaṁ veyyāvaccakarā”ti. So ce dūto taṁ veyyāvaccakaraṁ saññāpetvā taṁ bhikkhuniṁ upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ vadeyya: “yaṁ kho, ayye, ayyā veyyāvaccakaraṁ niddisi, saññattā sā&nbsp;mayā, upasaṅkamatāyyā kālena, cīvarena taṁ acchādessatī”ti. Cīvaratthikāya, bhikkhuniyo, bhikkhuniyā veyyāvaccakarā&nbsp;upasaṅkamitvā dvattikkhattuṁ codetabbā&nbsp;sāretabbā: “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti, dvattikkhattuṁ codayamānā sārayamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṁ kusalaṁ, no ce abhinipphādeyya, catukkhattuṁ pañcakkhattuṁ chakkhattuparamaṁ tuṇhībhūtāya uddissa ṭhātabbaṁ, catukkhattuṁ pañcakkhattuṁ chakkhattuparamaṁ tuṇhībhūtā uddissa tiṭṭhamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṁ kusalaṁ. Tato ce uttari vāyamamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. No ce abhinipphādeyya, yatassā cīvaracetāpannaṁ ābhataṁ, tattha sāmaṁ vā gantabbaṁ, dūto vā pāhetabbo: “yaṁ kho tumhe āyasmanto bhikkhuniṁ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṁ pahiṇittha, na taṁ tassā bhikkhuniyā kiñci atthaṁ anubhoti, yuñjantāyasmanto sakaṁ, mā vo sakaṁ vinassā”ti, ayaṁ tattha sāmīci. <br><br>Cīvaravaggo dutiyo.	11. Lahupāvuraṇaṁ pana bhikkhuniyā cetāpentiyā aḍḍhateyyakaṁsaparamaṁ cetāpetabbaṁ. Tato ce uttari cetāpeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>13. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine dasāhaparamaṁ atirekacīvaraṁ dhāretabbaṁ. <br>Taṁ atikkāmentiyā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>14. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine ekarattampi ce bhikkhunī ticīvarena vippavaseyya, aññatra bhikkhunisammutiyā nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>15. Niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṁ bhikkhuniyā ubbhatasmiṁ kathine bhikkhuniyā paneva akālacīvaraṁ uppajjeyya, ākaṅkhamānāya bhikkhuniyā paṭiggahetabbaṁ, paṭiggahetvā khippameva kāretabbaṁ, no cassa pāripūri, māsaparamaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā taṁ cīvaraṁ nikkhipitabbaṁ ūnassa pāripūriyā satiyā paccāsāya. Tato ce uttari nikkhipeyya satiyāpi paccāsāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>16. Yā pana bhikkhunī aññātakaṁ gahapatiṁ vā gahapatāniṁ vā cīvaraṁ viññāpeyya aññatra samayā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. <br>Tatthāyaṁ samayo acchinnacīvarā vā hoti bhikkhunī, naṭṭhacīvarā vā, ayaṁ tattha samayo.<br><br>17. Tañce aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā bahūhi cīvarehi abhihaṭṭhuṁ pavāreyya, santaruttaraparamaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā tato cīvaraṁ sāditabbaṁ. <br>Tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>18. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa aññātakassa gahapatissa vā gahapatāniyā vā cīvaracetāpannaṁ upakkhaṭaṁ hoti: “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarena acchādessāmī”ti. Tatra cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya: “sādhu vata, maṁ āyasmā iminā cīvaracetāpannena evarūpaṁ vā evarūpaṁ vā cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā acchādehī”ti kalyāṇakamyataṁ upādāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>19. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa ubhinnaṁ aññātakānaṁ gahapatīnaṁ vā gahapatānīnaṁ vā paccekacīvaracetāpannāni upakkhaṭāni honti: “imehi mayaṁ paccekacīvaracetāpannehi paccekacīvarāni cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarehi acchādessāmā”ti. Tatra cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya: “sādhu vata maṁ āyasmanto imehi paccekacīvaracetāpannehi evarūpaṁ vā evarūpaṁ vā cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā acchādetha ubhova santā ekenā”ti kalyāṇakamyataṁ upādāya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>20. Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa rājā vā rājabhoggo vā brāhmaṇo vā gahapatiko vā dūtena cīvaracetāpannaṁ pahiṇeyya: “iminā cīvaracetāpannena cīvaraṁ cetāpetvā itthannāmaṁ bhikkhuniṁ cīvarena acchādehī”ti. So ce dūto taṁ bhikkhuniṁ upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ vadeyya: “idaṁ kho, ayye, ayyaṁ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṁ ābhataṁ, paṭiggaṇhātāyyā cīvaracetāpanna”nti. Tāya bhikkhuniyā so dūto evamassa vacanīyo: “na kho mayaṁ, āvuso, cīvaracetāpannaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma, cīvarañca kho mayaṁ paṭiggaṇhāma kālena kappiya”nti. So ce dūto taṁ bhikkhuniṁ evaṁ vadeyya: “atthi panāyyāya, koci veyyāvaccakaro”ti, cīvaratthikāya, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā veyyāvaccakaro niddisitabbo ārāmiko vā upāsako vā: “eso kho, āvuso, bhikkhunīnaṁ veyyāvaccakaro”ti. So ce dūto taṁ veyyāvaccakaraṁ saññāpetvā taṁ bhikkhuniṁ upasaṅkamitvā evaṁ vadeyya: “yaṁ kho, ayye, ayyā veyyāvaccakaraṁ niddisi, saññatto so mayā, upasaṅkamatāyyā kālena, cīvarena taṁ acchādessatī”ti. Cīvaratthikāya, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā veyyāvaccakaro upasaṅkamitvā dvattikkhattuṁ codetabbo sāretabbo: “attho me, āvuso, cīvarenā”ti, dvattikkhattuṁ codayamānā sārayamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṁ kusalaṁ, no ce abhinipphādeyya, catukkhattuṁ pañcakkhattuṁ chakkhattuparamaṁ tuṇhībhūtāya uddissa ṭhātabbaṁ, catukkhattuṁ pañcakkhattuṁ chakkhattuparamaṁ tuṇhībhūtā uddissa tiṭṭhamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, iccetaṁ kusalaṁ. Tato ce uttari vāyamamānā taṁ cīvaraṁ abhinipphādeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. No ce abhinipphādeyya, yatassā cīvaracetāpannaṁ ābhataṁ, tattha sāmaṁ vā gantabbaṁ, dūto vā pāhetabbo: “yaṁ kho tumhe āyasmanto bhikkhuniṁ uddissa cīvaracetāpannaṁ pahiṇittha, na taṁ tassā bhikkhuniyā kiñci atthaṁ anubhoti, yuñjantāyasmanto sakaṁ, mā vo sakaṁ vinassā”ti, ayaṁ tattha sāmīci.<br><br>Cīvaravaggo dutiyo.			11. If a nun carries out an exchange to get a heavy cloak, it is to be worth at most four kaṁsa coins. If she gets one in exchange that is worth more than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>12. If a nun carries out an exchange to get a light cloak, it is to be worth at most two-and-a-half kaṁsa coins. If she gets one in exchange that is worth more than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>13. When her robe is finished and the robe season has ended, a nun should keep an extra robe for ten days at the most.<br>If she keeps it longer than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>14. When her robe is finished and the robe season has ended, if a nun stays apart from her three robes even for a single day, except if the nuns have agreed, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>15. When her robe is finished and the robe season has ended, if out-of-season robe-cloth is offered to a nun, she may receive it if she wishes. If she receives it, she should quickly make a robe. If there is not enough cloth, but she is expecting more, she should keep it at most one month to make up the lack. If she keeps it longer than that, then even if she expects more cloth, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>16. If a nun asks an unrelated male or female householder for a robe, except on an appropriate occasion, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br>These are the appropriate occasions: her robes are stolen or her robes are lost.<br><br>17. If an unrelated male or female householder invites that nun to take many robes, she should accept at most one sarong and one upper robe.<br>If she accepts more than that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>18. If a male or female householder has set aside a robe fund for an unrelated nun, thinking, ‘With this robe fund I will buy robe-cloth and give it to nun so-and-so;’ and if that nun, without first being invited, goes to them and specifies the kind of robe-cloth she wants, saying, ‘Please use this robe fund to buy such-and-such robe-cloth and then give it to me,’ and she does so because she wants something fine, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>19. If two male or female householders have set aside separate robe funds for an unrelated nun, thinking, ‘With these separate robe funds we’ll buy separate robe-cloths and give them to nun so-and-so;’ and if that nun, without first being invited, goes to them and specifies the kind of robe-cloth she wants, saying, ‘Please put these separate robe funds together to buy such-and-such robe-cloth and then give it to me,’ and she does so because she wants something fine, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>20. If a king, a king’s employee, a brahmin, or a householder sends a robe fund for a nun by messenger, saying, ‘Buy robe-cloth with this robe fund and give it to nun so-and-so,’ and the messenger goes to that nun and says, ‘Venerable, I have brought a robe fund for you. Please receive it,’ then that nun should reply, ‘We don’t receive robe funds, but we do receive allowable robe-cloth at the right time.’ If that messenger says, ‘Is there anyone who provides services for you?’ the nun, if she needs robe-cloth, should point out a monastery worker or a lay follower and say, ‘They provide services for the nuns.’ If the messenger instructs that service provider and then returns to the nun and says, ‘Venerable, I have instructed the service provider you pointed out. Please go to them at the right time and they’ll give you robe-cloth,’ then, if that nun needs robe-cloth, she should go to that service provider and prompt them and remind them two or three times, saying, ‘I need robe-cloth.’ If she then gets robe-cloth, all is well. If she does not get it, she should stand in silence for it at most six times. If she then gets robe-cloth, all is well. If she makes any further effort and then gets robe-cloth, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession. If she does not get robe-cloth, she should go to the owners of that robe fund, or send a message, saying, ‘That nun hasn’t received any benefit from the robe fund you sent for her. Please recover what’s yours, or it might perish.’ This is the proper procedure.<br><br>The second subchapter on robes.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Cīvaravaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_11-20.mp3]	181							[sound:ABi_NP_11-20.mp3]	11. {-heavy cloth} When a bhikkhunī is asking for a heavy cloth, one worth four bronzes at most may be asked for. If she asks for more than that, it is to be forfeited and confessed.<br><br>12. {-light cloth} When a bhikkhunī is asking for a light cloth, one worth two and a half bronzes at most may be asked for. If she asks for more than that, it is to be forfeited and confessed.<br><br>13. {-kaṭhina} When a bhikkhunī has finished her robe- making and the frame is destroyed (her kaṭhina privileges are in abeyance), she is to keep an extra robe- cloth ten days at most. Beyond that, it is to be forfeited and confessed. [1]<br><br>14. {-the “storehouse”} When a bhikkhunī has finished her robe-making and the frame is destroyed: If she dwells apart from (any of) her three robes even for one night — unless authorized by the bhikkhunīs—it is to be forfeited and confessed. [2]<br><br>15. {-out-of-season robe-cloth} When a bhikkhunī has finished her robe-making and the frame is destroyed: If out-of-season robe-cloth accrues to her, she may accept it if she so desires. Once she accepts it, she is to make it up immediately. If it should not be enough,&nbsp;she may lay it aside for a month at most if she has an expectation for filling the lack. Should she keep it beyond that, even when there is an expectation (for further cloth), it is to be forfeited and confessed. [3]<br><br>16. {-asking a non-relative} Should any bhikkhunī ask for robe-cloth from a man or woman householder unrelated to her, except at the proper occasion, it is to be forfeited and confessed. Here the proper occasion is this: The bhikkhunī’s robe has been stolen or destroyed. This is the proper occasion in this case. [6]<br><br>17. {-accepting more than that} If that unrelated man or woman householder presents the bhikkhunī with many robes (pieces of robe-cloth), she is to accept at most (enough for) an upper and an under robe. If she accepts more than that, it is to be forfeited and confessed. [7]<br><br>18. {-1st on setting up a robe fund} In case a man or woman householder prepares a robe fund for the sake of an unrelated bhikkhunī, thinking. “Having purchased a robe with this robe fund, I will supply the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with a robe”: If the bhikkhunī, not previously invited, approaching (the householder) should make a stipulation with regard to the robe, saying, “It would be good indeed, sir, if you supplied me (with a robe),” having purchased a robe of such-and-such a sort with this robe fund—out of a desire for something fine—it is to be forfeited and confessed. [8]<br><br>19. {-2nd on setting up a robe fund} In case two householders —men or women—prepare separate robe funds for the sake of a bhikkhunī unrelated to them, thinking, “Having purchased separate robes with these separate robe funds of ours, we will supply the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with robes”: If the bhikkhunī, not previously invited, approaching (them) should make a stipulation with regard to the robe, saying, “It would be good indeed, sirs, if you supplied me (with a robe), having purchased a robe of such-and-such a sort with these separate robe funds, the two (funds) together for one (robe),” out of desire for something fine, it is to be forfeited and confessed. [9]<br><br>20. {-the king} In case a king, a royal official, a brahmin or a householder sends a robe fund for a bhikkhunī via a messenger: “Purchase a robe with this robe fund and supply the bhikkhunī named so-and-so with a robe.” If the messenger approaches the bhikkhunī and says: “This robe fund is for the venerable. May the venerable accept this robe fund.” Then the bhikkhunī is to tell the messenger: “We do not accept robe funds, friend. We accept robes at the right time.” If the messenger says to the bhikkhunī: “Does the venerable have a steward?” Then, if the bhikkhunī desires a robe, she may indicate a steward, either a monastery attendant or a lay follower: “That, sir, is the bhikkhunīs’ steward.” If the messenger, having instructed the steward, goes to the bhikkhunī and says: “I have instructed the steward the venerable indicated. May the venerable go and she (the steward) will supply you with a robe in-season.” Then the bhikkhunī, desiring a robe and approaching the steward, may prompt and remind her 2 or 3 times: “I have need of a robe.” Should (the steward) produce the robe after being prompted and reminded 2 or 3 times, that is good. If she does not produce the robe, (the bhikkhunī) should stand in silence 4, 5, or 6 times at most for that purpose. Should (the steward) produce the robe after (the bhikkhunī) has stood in silence for the purpose 4, 5, or 6 times at most, that is good. If she should not produce the robe, but she produces the robe after (the bhikkhunī) has tried further, it is to be forfeited and confessed. If she should not produce (the robe), then the bhikkhunī herself should go to the place from which the robe fund was brought, or a messenger should be sent (to say), “The robe fund that you, Venerable sirs, sent for the sake of the bhikkhunī has given no benefit to the bhikkhunī at all. May you be united with what is yours. May what is yours not be lost.” This is the proper course here. [10]<br><br>Part Two: The Robe-cloth Chapter

Pācittiyā	Lasuṇavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_9.mp3]	215	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time a brahmin had a barley field next to the ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Feces:<br><br>excrement is what is meant.<br><br>Urine:<br><br>pee is what is meant.<br><br>Trash:<br><br>refuse is what is meant.<br><br>Food scraps:<br><br>food remnants or bones or used water.<br><br>Cultivated plants:<br><br>grain, vegetables, whatever cultivated plants people consider valuable or useful.<br><br>Disposes of:<br><br>if she disposes of it herself, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has it disposed of:<br><br>in asking another, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she only asks once, then even if the other disposes of such things many times, she commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If they are cultivated plants, and she perceives them as such, and she disposes of it or has it disposed of, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If they are cultivated plants, but she is unsure of it, and she disposes of it or has it disposed of, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If they are cultivated plants, but she perceives them as uncultivated, and she disposes of it or has it disposed of, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If they are uncultivated plants, but she perceives them as cultivated, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If they are uncultivated plants, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If they are uncultivated plants, and she perceives them as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she disposes of it after having looked;<br><br>if she disposes of it at the edge of the field;<br><br>if she disposes of it after asking and getting permission from the owners;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The ninth training rule is finished. Pācittiyā	Lasuṇavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_1.mp3]	207	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time a lay follower had invited the Sangha of nuns to ask for garlic:<br><br>“If any of the nuns need garlic, I’ll supply it.”<br><br>And he had told his field-keeper,<br><br>“If the nuns come, give two or three bulbs to each nun.”<br><br>On that occasion they were holding a celebration in Sāvatthī,<br><br>and the garlic was used up as soon as it arrived there.<br><br>Just then the nuns went to that lay follower and said,<br><br>“We need garlic.”<br><br>“Venerables, there isn’t any.<br><br>As soon as the garlic arrives, it’s used up.<br><br>Please go to the field.”<br><br>The nun Thullanandā went to the field, and not having any sense of moderation she took a large amount of garlic.<br><br>The field-keeper complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns not have any sense of moderation and take a large amount of garlic?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of that field-keeper,<br><br>and the nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā not have any sense of moderation and take a large amount of garlic?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her,<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā not have any sense of moderation and take a large amount of garlic?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>and after giving a teaching he addressed the monks:<br><br>“Once upon a time, monks, Thullanandā was the wife of a brahmin.<br><br>They had three daughters,<br><br>Nandā, Nandavatī, and Sundarīnandā.<br><br>When that brahmin eventually died, he was reborn as a goose,<br><br>whose feathers were all made of gold.<br><br>And he gave his former family members one feather at the time.<br><br>Thullanandā considered this. She then grabbed hold of that king of geese and plucked him.<br><br>But when his feathers regrew they were white.<br><br>At that time too, monks, Thullanandā lost her gold because she was too greedy.<br><br>Now she will lose her garlic.”<br><br>“One should be content with what one gets,<br><br>Because excessive greed is bad.<br><br>After grabbing hold of the king of geese,<br><br>The gold came to an end.”<br><br>Then, after rebuking the nun Thullanandā in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Garlic:<br><br>from Magadha is what is meant.<br><br>If she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is garlic and she perceives it as such, and she eats it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is garlic, but she is unsure of it, and she eats it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is garlic, but she does not perceive it as such, and she eats it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is not garlic, but she perceives it as such, and she eats it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not garlic, but she is unsure of it, and she eats it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not garlic and she does not perceive it as such, and she eats it, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is an onion;<br><br>if it is a shallot;<br><br>if it is chebulic myrobalan;<br><br>if it is a spring onion;<br><br>if it is cooked in a bean curry;<br><br>if it is cooked with meat;<br><br>if it is cooked with oil;<br><br>if it is in sweets;<br><br>if it is a special curry;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on garlic, the first, is finished. Udakasuddhikaṁ pana bhikkhuniyā ādiyamānāya dvaṅgulapabbaparamaṁ ādātabbaṁ. Taṁ atikkāmentiyā pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>6. Yā pana bhikkhunī āmakadhaññaṁ viññatvā vā viññāpetvā vā bhajjitvā vā bhajjāpetvā vā koṭṭetvā vā koṭṭāpetvā vā pacitvā vā pacāpetvā vā bhuñjeyya, pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>8. Yā pana bhikkhunī uccāraṁ vā passāvaṁ vā saṅkāraṁ vā vighāsaṁ vā tirokuṭṭe vā tiropākāre vā chaḍḍeyya vā chaḍḍāpeyya vā, pācittiyaṁ.<br><br>9. Yā pana bhikkhunī naccaṁ vā gītaṁ vā vāditaṁ vā dassanāya gaccheyya, pācittiyaṁ. <br><br>Lasuṇavaggo paṭhamo.				Venerables, these one hundred and sixty-six rules on confession come up for recitation.<br><br>1. If a nun eats garlic, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>2. If a nun removes hair from her private parts, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>3. If a nun slaps her genitals with the palm of her hand, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>4. If a nun uses a dildo, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>5. If a nun is cleaning herself with water, she may insert two finger joints at the most. If she goes further than that, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>6. If, when a monk is eating, a nun attends on him with drinking water or a fan, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>7. If a nun asks for or has someone else ask for raw grain, or she roasts it or has it roasted, or she pounds it or has it pounded, or she cooks it or has it cooked, and she then eats it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>8. If a nun disposes of feces or urine or trash or food scraps over a wall or over an encircling wall, or she has it disposed of in this way, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>9. If a nun disposes of feces or urine or trash or food scraps on cultivated plants, or she has it disposed of in this way, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>10. If a nun goes to see dancing or singing or music, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>The first subchapter on garlic.	Pācittiyā	Lasuṇavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_0-10.mp3]	217							[sound:ABi_PC_0-10.mp3]	Now, Venerables, these hundred and sixty-six matters entailing confession come up for recitation.<br><br>1. {The precept about -garlic} Should any bhikkhunī eat garlic, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.34.1]<br><br>2. {-hair on the body} Should any bhikkhunī have the hair in the tight places (armpits and pelvic areas) removed, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.27.4]<br><br>3. {-slapping} (Genital) slapping (even to the extent of consenting to a blow with a lotus-leaf) is to be confessed.<br><br>4. {-a dildo} (The insertion of) a dildo is to be confessed.<br><br>5. {-water ablution} When a bhikkhunī is giving herself an ablution, it is to be given only to the depth of two finger joints (and using no more than two fingers). Beyond that, it is to be confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Saṅghādisesa 1]<br><br>6. {-standing close} Should any bhikkhunī, when a bhikkhu is eating, attend on him with water or a fan, it is to be confessed.<br><br>7. {-raw grain} Should any bhikkhunī, having asked for raw grain or having had it asked for, having roasted it or having had it roasted, having pounded it or having had it pounded, having cooked it or having had it cooked, then eat it, it is to be confessed.<br><br>8. {-1st about tossing excrement} Should any bhikkhunī toss or get someone else to toss excrement or urine or trash or leftovers over a wall or a fence, it is to be confessed.<br><br>9. {-2nd about tossing excrement} Should any bhikkhunī toss or get someone else to toss excrement or urine or trash or leftovers on living crops, it is to be confessed.<br><br>10. {-singing and dancing} Should any bhikkhunī go to see dancing or singing or instrument-playing, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.2.6]<br><br>Part One: The Garlic Chapter

Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun stands or talks alone with a man in a concealed place, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Rattandhakāravaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_12.mp3]	219	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a male relative of a nun who was a pupil of Bhaddā Kāpilānī went from his own village to Sāvatthī on some business.<br><br>Then,<br><br>knowing that the Buddha had prohibited standing or talking alone with a man in the dark of the night without a lamp, she instead stood and talked alone with that man in a concealed place.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could a nun do such a thing?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that a nun did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could a nun do such a thing?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>In a concealed place:<br><br>it is concealed by a wall, a door, a screen, a cloth screen, a tree, a pillar, a grain container, or anything else.<br><br>A man:<br><br>a human male, not a male spirit, not a male ghost, not a male animal. He understands and is capable of standing together and talking.<br><br>With:<br><br>together.<br><br>Alone:<br><br>just the man and the nun.<br><br>Stands with:<br><br>if she stands within arm’s reach of the man, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Talks with:<br><br>if she stands talking within arm’s reach of the man, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she stands or talks outside of arm’s reach, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she stands or talks with a male spirit, a male ghost, a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, or a male animal in human form, she commits an offense of wrong conduct."	There is no offense:<br><br>if she has a companion who understands;<br><br>if she is not seeking privacy;<br><br>if she stands or talks thinking of something else;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The second training rule is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena bhaddāya kāpilāniyā antevāsiniyā bhikkhuniyā ñātako puriso gāmakā sāvatthiṁ agamāsi kenacideva karaṇīyena.<br><br>Atha kho sā bhikkhunī—<br><br>“bhagavatā paṭikkhittaṁ rattandhakāre appadīpe purisena saddhiṁ ekenekā santiṭṭhituṁ sallapitun”ti teneva purisena saddhiṁ paṭicchanne okāse ekenekā santiṭṭhatipi sallapatipi.<br><br>Yā tā bhikkhuniyo appicchā …pe… tā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma bhikkhunī paṭicchanne okāse purisena saddhiṁ ekenekā santiṭṭhissatipi sallapissatipī”ti …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira, bhikkhave, bhikkhunī paṭicchanne okāse purisena saddhiṁ ekenekā santiṭṭhatipi sallapatipī”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma, bhikkhave, bhikkhunī paṭicchanne okāse purisena saddhiṁ ekenekā santiṭṭhissatipi sallapissatipi.<br><br>Netaṁ, bhikkhave, appasannānaṁ vā pasādāya …pe…<br><br>evañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyo imaṁ sikkhāpadaṁ uddisantu—	Yā panāti<br><br>yā yādisā …pe…<br><br>bhikkhunīti<br><br>…pe… ayaṁ imasmiṁ atthe adhippetā bhikkhunīti.<br><br>Paṭicchanno nāma<br><br>okāso kuṭṭena vā kavāṭena vā kilañjena vā sāṇipākārena vā rukkhena vā thambhena vā kotthaḷiyā vā yena kenaci paṭicchanno hoti.<br><br>Puriso nāma<br><br>manussapuriso na yakkho na peto na tiracchānagato viññū paṭibalo santiṭṭhituṁ sallapituṁ.<br><br>Saddhinti<br><br>ekato.<br><br>Ekenekāti<br><br>puriso ceva hoti bhikkhunī ca.<br><br>Santiṭṭheyya vāti<br><br>purisassa hatthapāse tiṭṭhati, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Sallapeyya vāti<br><br>purisassa hatthapāse ṭhitā sallapati, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Hatthapāsaṁ vijahitvā santiṭṭhati vā sallapati vā, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Yakkhena vā petena vā paṇḍakena vā tiracchānagatamanussaviggahena vā saddhiṁ santiṭṭhati vā sallapati vā, āpatti dukkaṭassa.	Anāpatti—<br><br>yo koci viññū dutiyo hoti,<br><br>arahopekkhā,<br><br>aññavihitā santiṭṭhati vā sallapati vā,<br><br>ummattikāya,<br><br>ādikammikāyāti.<br><br>Dutiyasikkhāpadaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ. Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun visits families after the meal, and then sits down or lies down on a seat without asking permission of the owners, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Rattandhakāravaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_16.mp3]	225	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nun Thullanandā visited families after the meal, and she sat down and lay down on the seats without asking permission of the owners.<br><br>Because of Thullanandā, the people there had qualms,  neither sitting nor lying down.<br><br>They then complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā visit families after the meal, and then sit down and lie down on the seats without asking the owners for permission?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā act in this way?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā act in this way?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>After the meal:<br><br>when the middle of the day has passed, until sunset.<br><br>A family:<br><br>there are four kinds of families: the aristocratic family, the brahmin family, the merchant family, the worker family.<br><br>Visits:<br><br>goes there.<br><br>Without asking permission of the owners:<br><br>not having asked permission of a person in that family who is an owner and who has the authority to give.<br><br>A seat:<br><br>a place for sitting cross-legged is what is meant.<br><br>Sits down:<br><br>if she sits down on that seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Lies down:<br><br>if she lies down on that seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she has not asked permission, and she does not perceive that she has, and she sits down or lies down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she is unsure of it, and she sits down or lies down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she perceives that she has, and she sits down or lies down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is not a place for sitting cross-legged, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she does not perceive that she has, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, and she perceives that she has, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she sits down or lies down after asking permission;<br><br>if a dedicated seat is permanently ready for her;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The sixth training rule is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::02 Rattandhakāra Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 15	Anāpucchāpakkamanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī purebhattaṁ kulāni upasaṅkamitvā āsane nisīditvā sāmike anāpucchā pakkameyya, pācittiyaṁ. Pācittiyā	Rattandhakāravaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_15.mp3]	224	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time a certain nun was associating with a family from which she received a regular meal.<br><br>Then, after robing up one morning, she took her bowl and robe and went to that family where she sat down on a seat. and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Before the meal:<br><br>from dawn until midday.<br><br>A family:<br><br>there are four There is no offense:<br><br>if she departs after informing someone;<br><br>if the seat is not movable;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fifth training rule is finished. should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>The wrong time:<br><br>from sunset until dawn.<br><br>A family:<br><br>there are four kinds of families: the aristocratic family, the brahmin family, the merchant family, the worker family.<br><br>Visits:<br><br>goes there.<br><br>Without asking permission of the owners:<br><br>not having asked permission of a person in that family who is an owner and who has the authority to give.<br><br>Bedding:<br><br>even a spread of leaves.<br><br>Puts out:<br><br>she puts it out herself.<br><br>Has it put out:<br><br>she has someone else to put it out.<br><br>Sits down:<br><br>if she sits down on it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Lies down:<br><br>if she lies down on it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she has not asked permission, and she does not perceive that she has, and she sits down or lies down on bedding after putting it out or having it put out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she is unsure of it, and she sits down or lies down on bedding after putting it out or having it put out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she perceives that she has, and she sits down or lies down on bedding after putting it out or having it put out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she does not perceive that she has, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, and she perceives that she has, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she first asks permission, and then, after putting out bedding or having it put out, sits down or lies down on it;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The seventh training rule is finished. Pācittiyā	Rattandhakāravaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_14.mp3]	223	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nun Thullanandā stood and talked alone with men on streets, in cul-de-sacs, and at intersections, and she whispered in their ears and dismissed her companion nun.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How can Venerable Thullanandā do such things?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā does this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How can the nun Thullanandā do such things?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>A street:<br><br>a carriage road is what is meant.<br><br>A cul-de-sac:<br><br>one departs the same way one enters.<br><br>An intersection:<br><br>a crossroads is what is meant.<br><br>A man:<br><br>a human male, not a male spirit, not a male ghost, not a male animal. He understands and is capable of standing together and talking.<br><br>With:<br><br>together.<br><br>Alone:<br><br>just the man and the nun.<br><br>Stands with:<br><br>if she stands within arm’s reach of the man, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Talks with:<br><br>if she stands talking within arm’s reach of the man, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Whispers in his ear:<br><br>if she speaks into the ear of a man, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Dismisses her companion nun:<br><br>if, wanting to misbehave, she dismisses her companion nun, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the companion nun is in the process of going beyond the range of sight or the range of hearing, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the companion nun has gone beyond, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she stands or talks outside of arm’s reach, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she stands or talks with a male spirit, a male ghost, a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, or a male animal in human form, she commits an offense of wrong conduct."	There is no offense:<br><br>if she has a companion who understands;<br><br>if she is not seeking privacy;<br><br>if she stands or talks thinking of something else;<br><br>if she does not want to misbehave;<br><br>if she dismisses her companion nun when there is something to be done;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fourth training rule is finished. Pācittiyā	Naggavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_24.mp3]	236	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nuns stored one of their robes with this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion than five days, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is less than five days and she perceives it as less, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she wears or suns the five robes on the fifth day;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fourth training rule is finished. case.<br><br>A nun’s:<br><br>another nun’s.<br><br>Robe:<br><br>one of the six kinds of robes.<br><br>Unstitching:<br><br>she unstitches it herself.<br><br>Having it unstitched:<br><br>she has someone else unstitch it.<br><br>And there were no obstacles:<br><br>when there is no obstacle.<br><br>She neither sews:<br><br>she does not sew it herself.<br><br>Nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it:<br><br>she does not ask anyone else.<br><br>Except if it was no more than four or five days:<br><br>unless it was no more than four or five days.<br><br>If she thinks, “I’ll neither sew it nor make any effort to have someone else sew it,” then by the mere fact of abandoning her duty, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, and she perceives her as such, and she unstitches her robe or has it unstitched, and then neither sews it herself nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it, and there were no obstacles, then, except if it was no more than four or five days, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but she is unsure of it, and she unstitches her robe or has it unstitched, and then neither sews it herself nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it, and there were no obstacles, then, except if it was no more than four or five days, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but she does not perceive her as such, and she unstitches her robe or has it unstitched, and then neither sews it herself nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it, and there were no obstacles, then, except if it was no more than four or five days, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she unstitches another requisite or has it unstitched, and then neither sews it herself nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it, and there were no obstacles, then, except if it was no more than four or five days, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and she unstitches her robe or another requisite, or has it unstitched, and then neither sews it herself nor makes any effort to have someone else sew it, and there were no obstacles, then, except if it was no more than four or five days, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but she perceives her as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and she does not perceive her as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if there is an obstacle;<br><br>if she searches for someone to sew, but does not find anyone;<br><br>if she is doing it, but she takes longer than four or five days;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The third training rule is finished. [See Mv.VIII.28.1]<br><br>22. {-bathing cloth} When a bhikkhunī is making a bathing cloth, it is to be made to the standard measurement. Here the standard is this: four spans— using the Sugata span—in length, two spans in width. In excess of that, it is to be cut down and confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 91]<br><br>23. {-unsewing a robe} Should any bhikkhunī, having unsewn (another) bhikkhunī’s robe or having had it unsewn, and then later—when there are no obstructions—neither sew it nor make an effort to have it sewn within four or five days, it is to be confessed.<br><br>24. {-outer robe period} Should any bhikkhunī exceed her five-day outer robe period, it is to be confessed.<br><br>25. {-robe to be given back} Should any bhikkhunī wear a robe that should be given back (one that she has borrowed from another bhikkhunī without asking her permission), it is to be confessed.<br><br>26. {-robes of a group} Should any bhikkhunī put an obstruction in the way of a group’s receiving robe-cloth, it is to be confessed.<br><br>27. {-blocking} Should any bhikkhunī block a robe-cloth distribution that is in accordance with the rule, it is to be confessed.<br><br>28. {-giving robes} Should any bhikkhunī give a contemplative robe (a robe that has been marked so as to be allowable for a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī) to a householder, a male wanderer, or female wanderer, it is to be confessed.<br><br>29. {-letting the season pass} Should any bhikkhunī let the robe-season (the period for receiving kaṭhina donations) pass on the basis of a weak expectation for cloth, it is to be confessed.<br><br>30. {-removal of kaṭhina} Should any bhikkhunī block or prohibit the removal of the kaṭhina privileges in accordance with the rule, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Three: The Naked Chapter

Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun gives a dwelling place to a nun, and then, in anger, throws her out or has her thrown out, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Tuvaṭṭavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_35.mp3]	248	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time Bhaddā Kāpilānī had entered the rainy-season residence at Sāketa.<br><br>But because she was disturbed by a certain matter, she sent a message to the nun Thullanandā:<br><br>“If you would give me a dwelling place, I would come to Sāvatthī.”<br><br>Thullanandā replied,<br><br>“Please come; I’ll give you one.”<br><br>Bhaddā Kāpilānī then traveled from Sāketa to Sāvatthī,<br><br>and Thullanandā gave her a dwelling place.<br><br>At that time Thullanandā was a learned reciter, and she was confident and skilled at giving teachings.<br><br>Bhaddā Kāpilānī, too, was a learned reciter who was confident and skilled at giving teachings, and she was respected for her excellence.<br><br>Because of this, people visited Bhaddā Kāpilānī first and then Thullanandā.<br><br>Overcome by jealousy, Thullanandā thought,<br><br>“These ones, who are supposedly contented and have few desires, who are supposedly secluded and not socializing, are always persuading and convincing people.” And in anger she threw Bhaddā Kāpilānī out of that dwelling place.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā give a dwelling place to Venerable Bhaddā Kāpilānī and then throw her out in anger?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>To a nun:<br><br>to another nun.<br><br>A dwelling place:<br><br>one that has a door is what is meant.<br><br>Gives:<br><br>she gives it herself.<br><br>In anger:<br><br>discontent, having hatred, hostile.<br><br>Throws out:<br><br>if she takes hold of her in a room and throws her out to the entryway, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she takes hold of her in the entryway and throws her outside, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Even if she makes her go through many doors with a single effort, she commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has thrown out:<br><br>if she asks another, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she only asks once, then even if the other makes her go through many doors, she commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, and she perceives her as such, and she gives her a dwelling place, and she then throws her out in anger or has her thrown out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but she is unsure of it, and she gives her a dwelling place, and she then throws her out in anger or has her thrown out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but she does not perceive her as such, and she gives her a dwelling place, and she then throws her out in anger or has her thrown out, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she throws out one of her requisites, or she has it thrown out, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she throws her out or has her thrown out from a dwelling place without a door, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she throws out one of her requisites from a dwelling place without a door, or she has it thrown out, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she throws out one who is not fully ordained, or she has her thrown out, from a dwelling place with or without a door, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she throws out one of her requisites from that place, or she has it thrown out, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but she perceives her as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and she does not perceive her as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, one who is shameless;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, a requisite belonging to that person;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, one who is insane;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, a requisite belonging to that person;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, one who is quarrelsome and argumentative, and who creates legal issues in the Sangha;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, a requisite belonging to that person;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, a pupil or student who is not conducting herself properly;<br><br>if she throws out, or has thrown out, a requisite belonging to that person;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fifth training rule is finished. Pācittiyā	Tuvaṭṭavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_40.mp3]	256	At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary.<br><br>At that time the nuns were staying right there at Rājagaha for the rainy season, the winter, and the summer.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“The nuns are leaving the districts in darkness and obscurity.
