Kd1/Mv 1:37.12.2&nbsp;<br>He’s capable of five things in regard to a student: to train him in good conduct; to train him in the basics of the spiritual life; to train him in the Teaching; to train him in the Monastic Law; and to use the Teaching to make him give up wrong views. And he has ten or more years of seniority.<br><br>Kd18/Cv 8: 12.1.1-12.11.11<br>Discussion of the proper conduct toward a student		If a nun gives the full admission to a disciple, and then, for the next two years, neither guides her nor has her guided, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Gabbhinivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_68.mp3]	291	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nun Thullanandā gave the full admission to a disciple, but then, for the next two years, neither guided her nor had her guided.<br><br>They were ignorant and incompetent,<br><br>and they did not know what was allowable and what was not.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How can Venerable Thullanandā give the full admission to a disciple, and then neither guide her nor have her guided for two years?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā does this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How can the nun Thullanandā do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>A disciple:<br><br>a student is what is meant.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>Two years:<br><br>two twelve-month periods.<br><br>Neither guides her:<br><br>she does not herself guide her—through recitation, through questioning, through instruction, though teaching.<br><br>Nor has her guided:<br><br>she does not ask anyone else.<br><br>If she thinks, “I’ll neither guide her nor have her guided for two years,” then by the mere fact of abandoning her duty, she commits an offense entailing confession. Pācittiyā	Gabbhinivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_65.mp3]	288	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns were giving the full admission to married girls less married girl:<br><br>one who has gone to the place of a man is what is meant.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is less than twelve years old, but the nun perceives her as more, and she gives her the full admission, there is no offense.<br><br>If the girl is more than twelve years old, but the nun perceives her as less, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is more than twelve years old, but the nun is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is more than twelve years old, and the nun perceives her as more, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she gives the full admission to a girl less than twelve years old, but she perceives her as more;<br><br>if she gives the full admission to a girl more than twelve years old, and she perceives her as more;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fifth training rule is finished. Kd18/ Cv 8: 11.1.1-11.18.3&nbsp;Discussion of the proper conduct toward a preceptor		If a nun does not follow the mentor who gave her the full admission for two years, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Gabbhinivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_69.mp3]	292	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time nuns who had received the full admission did not follow their mentors for two years.<br><br>They were ignorant and incompetent,<br><br>and they did not know what was allowable and what was not.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can those nuns receive the full admission and then not follow their mentors for two years?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that nuns don’t do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can nuns not do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who gave her the full admission:<br><br>who gave her the full ordination.<br><br>The mentor:<br><br>the preceptor is what is meant.<br><br>Two years:<br><br>two twelve-month periods.<br><br>Does not follow:<br><br>does not herself attend on her.<br><br>If she thinks, “I won’t follow her for two years,” then by the mere fact of abandoning her duty, she commits an offense entailing confession.	There is no offense:<br><br>if the preceptor is ignorant or shameless;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The ninth training rule is finished. Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun is told, ‘Venerable, you’ve given enough full admissions for now,’ and she consents, saying, ‘Fine,’ but then criticizes it afterwards, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_76.mp3]	300	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nun Caṇḍakāḷī approached the Sangha of nuns and asked for approval to give the full admission.<br><br>The Sangha of nuns<br><br>decided that she should not,<br><br>and Caṇḍakāḷī consented.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Sangha of nuns gave approval to other nuns to give the full admission.<br><br>Caṇḍakāḷī complained and criticized it,<br><br>“So it seems I’m ignorant and shameless,<br><br>since the Sangha gives approval to other nuns, but not to me.”<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Caṇḍakāḷī<br><br>consent to not being approved to give the full admission, and then criticize it afterwards?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Caṇḍakāḷī did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Caṇḍakāḷī<br><br>do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>“Venerable, you’ve given enough full admissions for now”:<br><br>“Venerable, you’ve given enough full ordinations for now.”<br><br>If she consents, saying, “Fine,” but then criticizes it afterwards, she commits an offense entailing confession.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she criticizes one who regularly acts out of favoritism, ill will, confusion, or fear;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The sixth training rule is finished. She should then squat on her heels, raise her joined palms, and say:<br><br>‘Venerables, I, the unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, ask the Sangha for approval to be fully admitted.’<br><br>And she should ask a second<br><br>and a third time.<br><br>A competent and capable nun should then inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>This unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, is asking the Sangha for approval to be fully admitted.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should give approval for the unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, to be fully admitted.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>This unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, is asking the Sangha for approval to be fully admitted.<br><br>The Sangha gives approval for the unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, to be fully admitted.<br><br>Any nun who approves of giving approval for the unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, to be fully admitted should remain silent.<br><br>Any nun who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has given approval for the unmarried girl so-and-so, who is more than twenty years old and who has trained for two years in the six rules under Venerable so-and-so, to be fully admitted.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>Then, after rebuking those nuns in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is more than twenty years old:<br><br>who has reached twenty years of age.<br><br>An unmarried girl:<br><br>a novice nun is what is meant.<br><br>Two years:<br><br>two twelve-month periods.<br><br>Who has trained:<br><br>who has trained in the six rules.<br><br>Who has not been approved:<br><br>approval to be fully admitted has not been given though a legal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or she establishes a monastery zone, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After the motion, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After each of the first two announcements, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the last announcement is finished, the preceptor commits an offense entailing confession,<br><br>and the group and the teacher commit an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, and legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::08 Kumāribhūta Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 75	Paripuṇṇadvādasavassasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī paripuṇṇadvādasavassā saṅghena asammatā vuṭṭhāpeyya, pācittiyaṁ.		Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun who has twelve years of seniority gives the full admission without approval from the Sangha, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_75.mp3]	299	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time nuns who had twelve years of seniority were giving the full admission without being approved by the Sangha.<br><br>They were ignorant and incompetent,<br><br>and they did not know what was allowable and what was not.<br><br>And their students too were ignorant and incompetent,<br><br>and they too did not know what was allowable and what was not.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns who have twelve years of seniority give the full admission without being approved by the Sangha?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can nuns do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …”<br><br>After rebuking them …<br><br>he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, approval is required for a nun who has twelve years of seniority to give the full admission.<br><br>And the approval is to be given like this.<br><br>After approaching the Sangha of nuns, that nun who has twelve years of seniority should arrange her upper robe over one shoulder and pay respect at the feet of the senior nuns. She should then squat on her heels, raise her joined palms, and say:<br><br>‘Venerables, I, the nun so-and-so who has twelve years of seniority, ask the Sangha for approval to give the full admission.’<br><br>And she should ask a second<br><br>and a third time.<br><br>The Sangha should then decide whether that nun is competent and has a sense of conscience.<br><br>If she is ignorant and shameless, approval should not be given.<br><br>If she is ignorant but has a sense of conscience, approval should not be given.<br><br>If she is competent but shameless, approval should not be given.<br><br>If she is competent and has a sense of conscience, approval should be given.<br><br>And it is to be given like this.<br><br>A competent and capable nun should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, is asking the Sangha for approval to give the full admission.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should give approval to nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, to give the full admission.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, is asking the Sangha for approval to give the full admission.<br><br>The Sangha gives approval to nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, to give the full admission.<br><br>Any nun who approves of giving approval to nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, to give the full admission should remain silent.<br><br>Any nun who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has given approval to nun so-and-so, who has twelve years of seniority, to give the full admission.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>Then, after rebuking those nuns in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who has twelve years of seniority:<br><br>who has reached twelve years of seniority.<br><br>Without approval:<br><br>approval to give the full admission has not been given though a legal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or she establishes a monastery zone, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After the motion, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After each of the first two announcements, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the last announcement is finished, the preceptor commits an offense entailing confession,<br><br>and the group and the teacher commit an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but she perceives it as illegitimate, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but she perceives it as legitimate, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she has twelve years of seniority, has been approved by the Sangha, and then gives the full admission;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The fifth training rule is finished. If a nun gives the full admission to an unmarried woman who is less than twenty years old, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_71.mp3]	295	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nuns were giving the full admission to unmarried girls less than twenty years old.<br><br>They were unable to endure cold and heat; hunger and thirst; contact with horseflies, mosquitoes, wind, the burning sun, and creeping animals and insects; rude and unwelcome speech;<br><br>and they were unable to bear up with bodily feelings that are painful, severe, sharp, and destructive of life.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns give the full admission to unmarried girls less than twelve years old?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can nuns do this?<br><br>An unmarried girl less than twenty years old is unable to endure cold and heat; hunger and thirst; contact with horseflies, mosquitoes, wind, the burning sun, and creeping animals and insects; rude and unwelcome speech;<br><br>and she’s unable to bear up with bodily feelings that are painful, severe, sharp, and destructive of life.<br><br>But an unmarried girl who is twenty years old is able to endure these things.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is less than twenty years old:<br><br>who has not reached twenty years of age.<br><br>An unmarried girl:<br><br>a novice nun is what is meant.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or she establishes a monastery zone, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After the motion, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After each of the first two announcements, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the last announcement is finished, the preceptor commits an offense entailing confession,<br><br>and the group and the teacher commit an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the girl is less than twenty years old, and the nun perceives her as less, and she gives her the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the girl is less than twenty years old, but the nun is unsure of it, and she gives her the full admission, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is less than twenty years old, but the nun perceives her as more, and she gives her the full admission, there is no offense.<br><br>If the girl is more than twenty years old, but the nun perceives her as less, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is more than twenty years old, but the nun is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the girl is more than twenty years old, and the nun perceives her as more, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she gives the full admission to a girl less than twenty years old, but she perceives her as more;<br><br>if she gives the full admission to a girl more than twenty years old, and she perceives her as more;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The first training rule is finished. Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun gives the full admission to an unmarried woman who is more than twenty years old, but who has not trained for two years in the six rules, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_72.mp3]	296	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the nuns were giving the full admission to unmarried girls who were more than twenty years old, but who had not trained for two years in the six rules.<br><br>They were ignorant and incompetent,<br><br>and they did not know what was allowable and what was not.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns give the full admission to unmarried girls who are more than twenty years old, but who haven’t trained for two years in the six rules?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can nuns do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …”<br><br>After rebuking them …<br><br>he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, approval is required for an unmarried girl who is eighteen years old to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>And the approval is to be given like this.<br><br>After approaching the Sangha of nuns, that unmarried girl who is eighteen years old should arrange her upper robe over one shoulder and pay respect at the feet of the nuns. She should then squat on her heels, raise her joined palms, and say:<br><br>‘Venerables, I, so-and-so, an unmarried girl who is eighteen years old, am training under Venerable so-and-so. I ask the Sangha for approval to train for two years in the six rules.’<br><br>And she should ask a second<br><br>and a third time.<br><br>A competent and capable nun should then inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>This unmarried girl so-and-so, who is eighteen years old and training under Venerable so-and-so, is asking the Sangha for approval to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should give approval to the unmarried girl so-and-so who is eighteen years old to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, Venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>This unmarried girl so-and-so, who is eighteen years old and training under Venerable so-and-so, is asking the Sangha for approval to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>The Sangha gives approval to the unmarried girl so-and-so who is eighteen years old to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>Any nun who approves of giving approval to the unmarried girl so-and-so who is eighteen years old to train in the six rules for two years should remain silent.<br><br>Any nun who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has given approval to the unmarried girl so-and-so who is eighteen years old to train in the six rules for two years.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’<br><br>That unmarried girl who is eighteen years old should be told to say this:<br><br>‘I undertake to abstain from killing living beings for two years without transgression. …<br><br>I undertake to abstain from eating at the wrong time for two years without transgression.’”<br><br>Then, after rebuking those nuns in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is more than twenty years old:<br><br>who has reached twenty years of age.<br><br>An unmarried girl:<br><br>a novice nun is what is meant.<br><br>Two years:<br><br>two twelve-month periods.<br><br>Who has not trained:<br><br>the training has not been given to her, or the training has been given to her, but she has failed in it.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or she establishes a monastery zone, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After the motion, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After each of the first two announcements, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the last announcement is finished, the preceptor commits an offense entailing confession,<br><br>and the group and the teacher commit an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but she perceives it as illegitimate, and she gives the full admission, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but she perceives it as legitimate, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and she perceives it as such, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she gives the full admission to an unmarried girl who is more than twenty years old, and who has trained in the six rules for two years;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The second training rule is finished. Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_77.mp3]	303	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a trainee nun went to the nun Thullanandā and asked her for the full ordination.<br><br>Thullanandā told her,<br><br>“If you give me a robe, Venerable, I’ll give you the full admission.” But she neither gave her the full admission nor made any effort to have her fully admitted.<br><br>That trainee nun told the nuns what had happened.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā say that to a trainee nun<br><br>and then neither give her the full admission nor make any effort to have her fully admitted?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā act in this way?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>A trainee nun:<br><br>one who has trained for two years in the six rules.<br><br>If you give me a robe, Venerable, I’ll give you the full admission:<br><br>I’ll give you the full ordination.<br><br>Then, if there were no obstacles:<br><br>when there is no obstacle.<br><br>She neither gives her the full admission:<br><br>does not herself give her the full admission.<br><br>Nor makes any effort to have her fully admitted:<br><br>does not ask anyone else to give her the full ordination.<br><br>If she thinks, “I’ll neither give her the full admission nor make any effort to have her fully admitted,” then by the mere fact of abandoning her duty, she commits an offense entailing confession.	There is no offense:<br><br>if there is an obstacle;<br><br>if she searches for someone to give her the full ordination, but is unable to find anyone;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The seventh training rule is finished. Unique to Bhikkhunī		If, when a given consent has expired, a nun gives the full admission to a trainee nun, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Kumāribhūtavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_81.mp3]	307	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nun Thullanandā<br><br>had gathered a group of senior monks, intending to give the full admission to a trainee nun. But after seeing much fresh and cooked food, she dismissed the senior monks, saying,<br><br>“Venerables, I won’t give the full admission to the trainee nun just yet.” She then gathered Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodakatissaka, Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, and Samuddadatta, and gave the full admission to that trainee nun.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized her,<br><br>“How could Venerable Thullanandā give the full admission to a trainee nun when the given consent had expired?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked her …<br><br>“How could the nun Thullanandā do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>When a given consent has expired:<br><br>when the gathering has left.<br><br>A trainee nun:<br><br>one who has trained for two years in the six rules.<br><br>Gives the full admission:<br><br>gives the full ordination.<br><br>If, intending to give the full admission, she searches for a group, a teacher, a bowl, or a robe, or she establishes a monastery zone, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After the motion, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>After each of the first two announcements, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the last announcement is finished, the preceptor commits an offense entailing confession,<br><br>and the group and the teacher commit an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she gives her the full admission while the gathering has not yet left;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eleventh training rule is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena thullanandā bhikkhunī—<br><br>“sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpessāmī”ti there bhikkhū sannipātetvā pahūtaṁ khādanīyaṁ bhojanīyaṁ passitvā—<br><br>“na tāvāhaṁ, ayyā, sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpessāmī”ti there bhikkhū uyyojetvā devadattaṁ kokālikaṁ kaṭamodakatissakaṁ khaṇḍadeviyā puttaṁ samuddadattaṁ sannipātetvā sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpesi.<br><br>Yā tā bhikkhuniyo appicchā …pe… tā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma ayyā thullanandā pārivāsikachandadānena sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpessatī”ti …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira, bhikkhave, thullanandā bhikkhunī pārivāsikachandadānena sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpetī”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma, bhikkhave, thullanandā bhikkhunī pārivāsikachandadānena sikkhamānaṁ vuṭṭhāpessati.<br><br>Netaṁ, bhikkhave, appasannānaṁ vā pasādāya …pe…<br><br>evañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyo imaṁ sikkhāpadaṁ uddisantu—	Yā panāti<br><br>yā yādisā …pe…<br><br>bhikkhunīti<br><br>…pe… ayaṁ imasmiṁ atthe adhippetā bhikkhunīti.<br><br>Pārivāsikachandadānenāti<br><br>vuṭṭhitāya parisāya.<br><br>Sikkhamānā nāma<br><br>dve vassāni chasu dhammesu sikkhitasikkhā.<br><br>Vuṭṭhāpeyyāti<br><br>upasampādeyya.<br><br>“Vuṭṭhāpessāmī”ti gaṇaṁ vā ācariniṁ vā pattaṁ vā cīvaraṁ vā pariyesati, sīmaṁ vā sammannati, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Ñattiyā dukkaṭaṁ.<br><br>Dvīhi kammavācāhi dukkaṭā.<br><br>Kammavācāpariyosāne upajjhāyāya āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Gaṇassa ca ācariniyā ca āpatti dukkaṭassa. The Buddha then had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to use a sunshade and sandals.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without a sunshade and sandals.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without a sunshade and sandals.<br><br>A sunshade:<br><br>there are three kinds of sunshades: the white sunshade, the reed sunshade, the leaf sunshade. They are bound at the rim and bound at the ribs.<br><br>Uses:<br><br>if she uses them even once, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she uses a sunshade and sandals, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she uses a sunshade and sandals, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she uses a sunshade and sandals, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she uses a sunshade, but not sandals, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she uses sandals, but not a sunshade, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense. Unique to Bhikkhunī		If a nun sits down on a seat in front of a monk without asking permission, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Chattupāhanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_94.mp3]	321	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>nuns sat down on seats in front of a monk without asking permission.<br><br>The monks complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns sit down on seats in front of a monk without asking permission?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can nuns do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>In front of a monk:<br><br>in front of one who is fully ordained.<br><br>Without asking permission:<br><br>without getting permission.<br><br>Sits down on a seat:<br><br>even if she sits down on the ground, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she has not asked permission, and she does not perceive that she has, and she sits down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she is unsure of it, and she sits down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has not asked permission, but she perceives that she has, and she sits down on a seat, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she does not perceive that she has, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she has asked permission, and she perceives that she has, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she sits down on the seat after asking permission;<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eleventh training rule is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::10 Musāvāda Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 104	Bhūtārocanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī anupasampannāya uttarimanussadhammaṁ āroceyya, bhūtasmiṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 8	Uses 'bhikkhunī', 'anupasampannāya' (feminine).	If a nun truthfully tells a person who is not fully ordained of a superhuman quality, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_104.mp3]	332	At one time when the Buddha was staying in the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood near Vesālī,<br><br>a number of monks who were friends had entered the rainy-season residence on the banks of the river Vaggumudā.<br><br>At that time Vajjī was short of food and afflicted with hunger, with crops affected by whiteheads and turned to straw. It was not easy to get by on almsfood.<br><br>The monks considered the difficult circumstances, and they thought, “How can we live together in peace and harmony, have a comfortable rains, and get almsfood without trouble?”<br><br>Some said, “We could work for the householders, and they’ll support us in return.”<br><br>Others said, “There’s no need to work for the householders.<br><br>Let’s instead take messages for them, and they’ll support us in return.”<br><br>Still others said, “There’s no need to do work or take messages for them.<br><br>Let’s instead talk up one another’s superhuman qualities to the householders:<br><br>‘That monk has the first absorption, that monk the second absorption, that monk the third, that monk the fourth; that monk is a stream-enterer, that monk a once-returner, that a non-returner, that a perfected one; that monk has the three true insights, and that the six direct knowledges.’<br><br>Then they’ll support us.<br><br>In this way we’ll have a comfortable rains, live together in peace and harmony, and get almsfood without trouble.<br><br>This is the way to go.”<br><br>Then those monks did just that.<br><br>And the people there thought, “We’re so fortunate that such monks have come to us for the rainy-season residence. Such virtuous and good monks have never before entered the rains residence with us.”<br><br>And they gave such food and drink to those monks that they did not even eat and drink themselves, or give to their parents, to their wives and children, to their slaves, servants, and workers, to their friends and companions, or to their relatives.<br><br>Soon those monks had a good color, bright faces, clear skin, and sharp senses.<br><br>Now it was the custom for monks who had completed the rainy-season residence to go and visit the Buddha.<br><br>And so, when the three months were over and they had completed the rains residence, those monks put their dwellings in order, took their bowls and robes, and set out for Vesālī.<br><br>When they eventually arrived, they went to the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood.<br><br>There they approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>At that time the monks who had completed the rains residence in that region were thin, haggard and pale, with veins protruding all over their bodies.<br><br>Yet the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā had a good color, bright faces, clear skin, and  sharp senses.<br><br>Since it is the custom for Buddhas to greet newly-arrived monks,<br><br>the Buddha said to them,<br><br>“I hope you’re keeping well, monks, I hope you’re getting by?<br><br>I hope you had a comfortable and harmonious rains, and doing what is unbeneficial.<br><br>Buddhas question the monks for two reasons: to give a teaching or to lay down a training rule.<br><br>And the Buddha said to those monks, “In what way, monks, did attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I master … I’ve realized the first absorption and the second absorption,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a …<br><br>and the desireless stillness … I’m attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I master … I’ve realized the first absorption and the desireless stillness,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the first absorption and the noble eightfold path … I’m attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I obtain … I master … I’ve realized the first absorption and perfection,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I realized the first absorption and I’ve given up confusion,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the first confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the second absorption and the third absorption …<br><br>the second absorption and the fourth absorption … I’m attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I master … I’ve realized the second absorption and the fourth absorption,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the second absorption and the emptiness release … and my mind is free from the hindrance of confusion,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the second absorption and the first absorption … I’m attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I master … I’ve realized the second absorption and the first absorption,” he commits an offense entailing confession. …<br><br>The basis in brief is finished.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “My mind is free from the hindrance of confusion and I attained the first absorption … I’m attaining … I’ve attained … I obtain … I master … My mind is free from the hindrance of confusion and I’ve realized the first absorption,” he commits an offense entailing confession. …<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “My mind is free from the hindrance of confusion and my mind is free from the hindrance of ill will,” he commits an offense entailing confession. …<br><br><b>Combination of all attainments</b><br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk says to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the first absorption and the second absorption and the third absorption and the fourth absorption and the emptiness release and the signless release and the desireless release and the emptiness stillness and the signless stillness and the desireless stillness and the emptiness attainment and the signless attainment and the desireless attainment and the three true insights and the four applications of mindfulness and the four right efforts and the four foundations for supernormal power and the five spiritual faculties and the five spiritual powers and the seven factors of awakening and the noble eightfold path and the fruit of stream entry and the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning and perfection …<br><br>and I’ve given up sensual desire, renounced it, let it go, abandoned it, relinquished it, forsaken it, thrown it aside; and I’ve given up ill will, renounced it, let it go, abandoned it, relinquished it, forsaken it, thrown it aside; and I’ve given up confusion, renounced it, let it go, abandoned it, relinquished it, forsaken it, thrown it aside; and my mind is free from the hindrance of sensual desire; and my mind is free from the hindrance of ill will; and my mind is free from the hindrance of confusion,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Meaning to say one thing, but saying something else</b><br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk means to say to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the first absorption,” but actually says, “I attained the second absorption,” then, if the listener understands, he commits an offense entailing confession; if the listener does not understand, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>if a monk means to say to a person who is not fully ordained, “I attained the first absorption,” but actually says, “I attained the third absorption …<br><br>the fourth There is no offense:<br><br>if he truthfully tells one who is fully ordained;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on telling truthfully, the eighth, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā vesāliyaṁ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṁ.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena sambahulā sandiṭṭhā sambhattā bhikkhū vaggumudāya nadiyā tīre vassaṁ upagacchiṁsu.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena vajjī dubbhikkhā hoti—dvīhitikā setaṭṭhikā salākāvuttā, na sukarā uñchena paggahena yāpetuṁ.<br><br>Atha kho tesaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ etadahosi—“etarahi kho vajjī dubbhikkhā—dvīhitikā setaṭṭhikā salākāvuttā, na sukarā uñchena paggahena yāpetuṁ. Kena nu kho mayaṁ upāyena samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā phāsukaṁ vassaṁ vaseyyāma, na ca piṇḍakena kilameyyāmā”ti?<br><br>Ekacce evamāhaṁsu—“handa mayaṁ, āvuso, gihīnaṁ kammantaṁ adhiṭṭhema. Evaṁ te amhākaṁ dātuṁ maññissanti.<br><br>Ekacce evamāhaṁsu—“alaṁ, āvuso, kiṁ gihīnaṁ kammantaṁ adhiṭṭhitena?<br><br>Handa mayaṁ, āvuso, gihīnaṁ dūteyyaṁ harāma. Evaṁ te amhākaṁ dātuṁ maññissanti.<br><br>Ekacce evamāhaṁsu—“alaṁ, āvuso; kiṁ gihīnaṁ kammantaṁ adhiṭṭhitena. Kiṁ gihīnaṁ dūteyyaṁ haṭena.<br><br>Handa mayaṁ, āvuso, gihīnaṁ aññamaññassa uttarimanussadhammassa vaṇṇaṁ bhāsissāma—<br><br>‘asuko bhikkhu paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, asuko bhikkhu dutiyassa jhānassa lābhī, asuko bhikkhu tatiyassa jhānassa lābhī, asuko bhikkhu catutthassa jhānassa lābhī, asuko bhikkhu sotāpanno, asuko bhikkhu sakadāgāmī, asuko bhikkhu anāgāmī, asuko bhikkhu arahā, asuko bhikkhu tevijjo, asuko bhikkhu chaḷabhiñño’ti.<br><br>Evaṁ te amhākaṁ dātuṁ maññissanti.<br><br>Evaṁ mayaṁ samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā phāsukaṁ vassaṁ vasissāma, na ca piṇḍakena kilamissāmā”ti.<br><br>“Eso yeva kho, āvuso, seyyo, yo amhākaṁ gihīnaṁ aññamaññassa uttarimanussadhammassa vaṇṇo bhāsito”ti.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū gihīnaṁ aññamaññassa uttarimanussadhammassa vaṇṇaṁ bhāsiṁsu—<br><br>Atha kho te manussā—“lābhā vata no, suladdhaṁ vata no, yesaṁ no evarūpā bhikkhū vassaṁ upagatā, na vata no ito pubbe evarūpā bhikkhū vassaṁ upagatā, yathayime bhikkhū sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā”ti.<br><br>Te na tādisāni bhojanāni attanā bhuñjanti, mātāpitūnaṁ denti puttadārassa denti dāsakammakaraporisassa denti mittāmaccānaṁ denti ñātisālohitānaṁ denti yādisāni bhikkhūnaṁ denti.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū vaṇṇavā ahesuṁ pīṇindriyā pasannamukhavaṇṇā vippasannachavivaṇṇā.<br><br>Āciṇṇaṁ kho panetaṁ vassaṁvuṭṭhānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ bhagavantaṁ dassanāya upasaṅkamituṁ.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū vassaṁvuṭṭhā temāsaccayena senāsanaṁ saṁsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena vesālī tena pakkamiṁsu.<br><br>Anupubbena yena vesālī mahāvanaṁ kūṭāgārasālā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu;<br><br>upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena disāsu vassaṁvuṭṭhā bhikkhū kisā honti lūkhā dubbaṇṇā uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātā dhamanisanthatagattā.<br><br>Vaggumudātīriyā pana bhikkhū vaṇṇavā honti pīṇindriyā pasannamukhavaṇṇā vippasannachavivaṇṇā.<br><br>Āciṇṇaṁ kho panetaṁ buddhānaṁ bhagavantānaṁ āgantukehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ paṭisammodituṁ.<br><br>Atha kho bhagavā vaggumudātīriye bhikkhū etadavoca—<br><br>“kacci, bhikkhave, khamanīyaṁ, kacci yāpanīyaṁ,<br><br>kacci samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā phāsukaṁ vassaṁ vasittha, na ca piṇḍakena kilamitthā”ti?<br><br>“Khamanīyaṁ, bhagavā, yāpanīyaṁ, bhagavā.<br><br>Samaggā ca mayaṁ, bhante, sammodamānā avivadamānā phāsukaṁ vassaṁ vasimhā, na ca piṇḍakena kilamimhā”ti.<br><br>Jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchanti, jānantāpi na pucchanti.<br><br>Kālaṁ viditvā pucchanti, kālaṁ viditvā na pucchanti.<br><br>Atthasañhitaṁ tathāgatā pucchanti, no anatthasañhitaṁ.<br><br>Anatthasañhite setughāto tathāgatānaṁ.<br><br>Dvīhākārehi buddhā bhagavanto bhikkhū paṭipucchanti—“dhammaṁ vā desessāma, sāvakānaṁ vā sikkhāpadaṁ paññapessāmā”ti.<br><br>Atha kho bhagavā vaggumudātīriye bhikkhū etadavoca—“yathā kathaṁ pana tumhe, bhikkhave, samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā phāsukaṁ vassaṁ vasittha, na ca piṇḍakena kilamitthā”ti?<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū bhagavato etamatthaṁ ārocesuṁ.<br><br>“Kacci pana vo, bhikkhave, bhūtan”ti?<br><br>“Bhūtaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma tumhe, bhikkhave, udarassa kāraṇā nāma.<br><br>Uttarimanussadhammo nāma<br><br>jhānaṁ, vimokkho, samādhi, samāpatti, ñāṇadassanaṁ, maggabhāvanā, phalasacchikiriyā, kilesappahānaṁ, vinīvaraṇatā cittassa, suññāgāre Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_106.mp3]	334	At one time the Buddha was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.<br><br>At that time the monks of Āḷavī were doing building work, and they dug the earth and had it dug.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics dig the earth and have it dug?<br><br>They are hurting one-sensed life.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can those monks at Āḷavī dig the earth and have it dug?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>People regard the earth as conscious.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>The earth:<br><br>there are two kinds of earth: productive earth and unproductive earth.<br><br>Productive earth:<br><br>pure soil, pure clay, with few stones, with few pebbles, with few potsherds, with little gravel, with little sand; Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_102.mp3]	330	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Anuruddha was walking through the Kosalan country on his way to Sāvatthī, when one evening he arrived at a certain village.<br><br>Just then a woman in that village had prepared her guesthouse.<br><br>Anuruddha went to that woman and said, “If it’s not inconvenient for you, I’d like to stay in your guesthouse for one night.”<br><br>“Please stay, venerable.”<br><br>Other travelers also went to that woman and said, “Ma’am, if it’s not troublesome for you, we’d like to stay in your guesthouse for one night.”<br><br>“Sirs, a monastic is already staying there. If he agrees, you may stay.”<br><br>Those travelers then approached Anuruddha and said, “If you don’t mind, venerable, we’d like to stay one night in the guesthouse.”<br><br>“No problem.”<br><br>Now as soon as that woman had seen Anuruddha, she had fallen in love with him.<br><br>She now went to him and said, “Sir, you won’t be comfortable surrounded by these people.<br><br>Why don’t I prepare a bed for you in the main house?”<br><br>Anuruddha consented by remaining silent.<br><br>After preparing a bed in the main house, she put on jewelery and perfume, and she went to Anuruddha and said,<br><br>“You’re attractive, sir, and so am I.<br><br>Why don’t you take me as your wife?”<br><br>But Anuruddha remained silent.<br><br>She said the same thing a second time, but again got no response.<br><br>And a third time she said,<br><br>“You’re attractive, sir, and so am I.<br><br>Why don’t you take me and all this property?”<br><br>Once again Anuruddha remained silent.<br><br>She then threw off her wrap, and she walked back and forth, stood, sat down, and lay down in front of him.<br><br>But Anuruddha controlled his senses and neither looked at nor spoke to her.<br><br>Then that woman said, “It’s astonishing and amazing.<br><br>Many people pay a hundred or a thousand coins to be with me.<br><br>But this monastic doesn’t want me and all this property, even when I beg him!”<br><br>After dressing, she bowed down with her head at Anuruddha’s feet and said,<br><br>“Sir, I’ve made a mistake. I’ve been foolish, confused, and unskillful.<br><br>Please forgive me so that I may restrain myself in the future.”<br><br>“You have certainly made a mistake. You’ve been foolish, confused, and unskillful.<br><br>But since you acknowledge your mistake and make proper amends, I forgive you.<br><br>For this is called growth in the training of the noble ones: acknowledging a mistake, making proper amends, and undertaking restraint for the future.”<br><br>The following morning that woman personally served and satisfied Anuruddha with various kinds of fine foods. When he had finished his meal, she bowed and sat down to one side.<br><br>And Anuruddha instructed, inspired, and gladdened her with a teaching.<br><br>She then said to him,<br><br>“Wonderful, sir, wonderful!<br><br>Just as one might set upright what’s overturned, or reveal what’s hidden, or show the way to one who’s lost, or bring a lamp into the darkness so that one with eyes might see what is there—<br><br>just so has the Buddha made the Teaching clear in many ways.<br><br>I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Teaching, and the Sangha of monks.<br><br>Please accept me as a lay follower who’s gone for refuge for life.”<br><br>Soon afterwards, after arriving at Sāvatthī, Anuruddha told the monks what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How can Venerable Anuruddha lie down in the same sleeping place as a woman?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. even a girl born on that very day, let alone an older one.<br><br>Same:<br><br>together.<br><br>Sleeping place:<br><br>fully roofed, fully walled; mostly roofed, mostly walled.<br><br>Lies down in the same sleeping place:<br><br>when the sun has set—<br><br>if the monk lies down when the woman is already lying down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if the woman lies down when the monk is already lying down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if they both lie down together, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>every time they get up and then lie down again, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a woman, and he perceives her as such, and he lies down in the same sleeping place as her, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a woman, but he is unsure of it, and he lies down in the same sleeping place as her, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a woman, but he does not perceive her as such, and he lies down in the same sleeping place as her, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is half-roofed and half-walled, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he lies down in the same sleeping place as a female spirit, a female ghost, a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, or a female animal, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, and he does not perceive them as such, there is no offense." Matches Bu PC 3	Uses 'bhikkhunipesuññe' instead of 'bhikkhu-pesuññe'.	If a nun engages in malicious talebearing between nuns, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_99.mp3]	327	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were engaged in malicious talebearing between monks who were arguing.<br><br>After hearing something on one side they reported it to the other side, and vice versa, in order to create division between them.<br><br>In this way they started new quarrels and made existing quarrels worse.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six engage in malicious talebearing between monks who are arguing?<br><br>How can they report to one side what they have heard on the other side, and vice versa, in order to create division,<br><br>and in this way start new quarrels and make existing quarrels worse?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned those monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Malicious talebearing:<br><br>there is malicious talebearing in two ways: for one wanting to endear himself and for one aiming at division.<br><br>One engages in malicious talebearing in ten ways: about caste, about name, about family, about occupation, about profession, about illnesses, about physical traits, about defilements, about offenses, and by name-calling.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br><b>Permutations part 1</b><br><br><b>Definitions</b><br><br>Caste:<br><br>there are two kinds of castes: low castes and high castes.<br><br>Low castes:<br><br>outcasts, bamboo workers, hunters, carriage makers, waste removers—these are called “low castes”.<br><br>High castes:<br><br>aristocrats and brahmins—these are called “high castes”.<br><br>(To be expanded as in previous rule.)<br><br>Name-calling:<br><br>there are two kinds of name-calling: low name-calling and high name-calling.<br><br>Low name-calling:<br><br>“You’re a camel,” “You’re a ram,” “You’re an ox,” “You’re a donkey,” “You’re an animal,” “You’re bound for hell,” “You’re not going to a good destination,” “You can only expect a bad destination,” or adding disparaging endings to someone’s name, or calling someone words for the male and female genitals—this is called “low name-calling”.<br><br>High name-calling:<br><br>“You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination”—this is called “high name-calling”.<br><br><b>Exposition</b><br><br><b>Direct abuse</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s an outcast,’ ‘He’s a bamboo worker,’ ‘He’s a hunter,’ ‘He’s a carriage maker,’ ‘He’s a waste remover,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s an aristocrat,’ ‘He’s a brahmin,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s an Avakaṇṇaka,’ ‘He’s a Javakaṇṇaka,’ ‘He’s a Dhaniṭṭhaka,’ ‘He’s a Saviṭṭhaka,’ ‘He’s a Kulavaḍḍhaka,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a Buddharakkhita,’ ‘He’s a Dhammarakkhita,’ ‘He’s a Sangharakkhita,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a Kosiya,’ ‘He’s a Bhāradvāja,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a Gotama,’ ‘He’s a Moggallāna,’ ‘He’s a Kaccāna,’ ‘He’s a Vāsiṭṭha,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a carpenter,’ ‘He’s a waste remover,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a farmer,’ ‘He’s a trader,’ ‘He’s a cattle keeper,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a reed worker,’ ‘He’s a potter,’ ‘He’s a weaver,’ ‘He’s a leather worker,’ ‘He’s a hairdresser,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s an arithmetician,’ ‘He’s an accountant,’ ‘He’s a clerk,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a leper,’ ‘He has abscesses,’ ‘He has mild leprosy,’ ‘He has tuberculosis,’ ‘He’s an epileptic,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a diabetic,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s too tall,’ ‘He’s too short,’ ‘He’s too dark,’ ‘He’s too fair,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s not too tall,’ ‘He’s not too short,’ ‘He’s not too dark,’ ‘He’s not too fair,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s full of sensual desire,’ ‘He’s full of ill will,’ ‘He’s full of confusion,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s without sensual desire,’ ‘He’s without ill will,’ ‘He’s without confusion,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He has committed an offense entailing expulsion,’ ‘He has committed an offense entailing suspension,’ ‘He has committed a serious offense,’ ‘He has committed an offense entailing confession,’ ‘He has committed an offense entailing acknowledgment,’ ‘He has committed an offense of wrong conduct,’ ‘He has committed an offense of wrong speech,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a stream-enterer,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s a camel,’ ‘He’s a ram,’ ‘He’s an ox,’ ‘He’s a donkey,’ ‘He’s an animal,’ ‘He’s bound for hell,’ ‘He’s not going to a good destination,’ ‘He can only expect a bad destination,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says this about you, ‘He’s wise,’ ‘He’s competent,’ ‘He’s intelligent,’ ‘He’s learned,’ ‘He’s an expounder of the Teaching,’ ‘He’s not going to a bad destination,’ ‘He can only expect a good destination,’” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Indirect abuse</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘There are outcasts right here,’ ‘There are bamboo workers right here,’ ‘There are hunters right here,’ ‘There are carriage makers right here,’ ‘There are waste removers right here,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘There are aristocrats right here,’ ‘There are brahmins right here,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct. …<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘There are wise ones right here,’ ‘There are competent ones right here,’ ‘There are intelligent ones right here,’ ‘There are learned ones right here,’ ‘There are expounders of the Teaching right here,’ ‘There are those not going to a bad destination right here,’ ‘There are those who can only expect a good destination right here,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘Perhaps these are outcasts,’ ‘Perhaps these are bamboo workers,’ ‘Perhaps these are hunters,’ ‘Perhaps these are carriage makers,’ ‘Perhaps these are waste removers,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct. …<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘Perhaps these are wise ones,’ ‘Perhaps these are competent ones,’ ‘Perhaps these are intelligent ones,’ ‘Perhaps these are learned ones,’ ‘Perhaps these are expounders of the Teaching,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘We’re not outcasts,’ ‘We’re not bamboo workers,’ ‘We’re not hunters,’ ‘We’re not carriage makers,’ ‘We’re not waste removers,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct. …<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing by saying to yet another who is fully ordained, “So-and-so says, ‘We’re not wise ones,’ ‘We’re not competent ones,’ ‘We’re not intelligent ones,’ ‘We’re not learned ones,’ ‘We’re not expounders of the Teaching,’ ‘We’re not going to a bad destination,’ ‘We can only expect a good destination,’ and he’s not speaking about someone else, he’s speaking about you,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations part 2</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing to yet another who is fully ordained, then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from another who is fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing to one who is not fully ordained, then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from one who is not fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing to another who is fully ordained, then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, after hearing it from one who is not fully ordained, engages in malicious talebearing to another who is not fully ordained, then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he does not want to endear himself<br><br>and he is not aiming at division;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on malicious talebearing, the third, is finished. Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_101.mp3]	329	At one time the Buddha was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.<br><br>At that time the lay followers were coming to the monastery to listen to the Teaching.<br><br>When the instruction was over, the senior monks went to their own dwellings,<br><br>but the newly ordained monks lay down right there in the assembly hall together with the lay followers—absentminded, heedless, naked, muttering, and snoring.<br><br>The lay followers complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the venerables lie down absentminded, heedless, naked, muttering, and snoring?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those lay followers,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can monks lie down in the same sleeping place as people who are not fully ordained?”<br><br>After rebuking those newly ordained monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that monks did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How could those foolish men do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk lies down in the same sleeping place as a person who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>After staying at Āḷavī for as long as he wanted, the Buddha set out wandering toward Kosambī.<br><br>When he eventually arrived, he stayed at the Badarikā Monastery.<br><br>Just then the monks there said to Venerable throat.<br><br>Rāhula, too, cleared his throat.<br><br>“Who’s there?”<br><br>“It’s me, sir, Rāhula.”<br><br>“Why are you sitting here, Rāhula?”<br><br>Rāhula told the Buddha what had three nights.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination There is no offense:<br><br>if he stays together with them for two or three nights;<br><br>if he stays together with them for less than two or three nights;<br><br>if, after staying together for two nights, he leaves before dawn on the third night and then stays together again;<br><br>if it is fully roofed, but not walled;<br><br>if it is fully walled, but not roofed;<br><br>if it is mostly not roofed;<br><br>if it is mostly not walled;<br><br>if the monk sits when the person who is not fully ordained is lying down;<br><br>if the person who is not fully ordained sits when the monk is lying down;<br><br>if they both sit;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on the same sleeping place, the fifth, is finished. offense entailing confession.<br><br>Except in the presence of a man who understands:<br><br>unless a man who understands is present.<br><br>A man who understands:<br><br>one who is capable of discerning bad speech and good speech, what is indecent and what is decent.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a woman, and he perceives her as such, and he teaches her more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man who understands, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a woman, but he is unsure of it, and he teaches her more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man who understands, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a woman, but he does not perceive her as such, and he teaches her more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man who understands, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he teaches more than five or six sentences to a female spirit, a female ghost, a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">paṇḍaka</i>, or a female animal in the form of a woman, except in the presence of a man who understands, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a woman, and he does not perceive them as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if a man who understands is present;<br><br>if he teaches five or six sentences;<br><br>if he teaches fewer than five or six sentences;<br><br>if he gets up, sits down again, and then teaches;<br><br>if the woman gets up and sits down again, and he then teaches her;<br><br>if he teaches another woman;<br><br>if he asks a question;<br><br>if he is asked a question and then speaks;<br><br>if he is speaking for the benefit of someone else and a woman listens in;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on teaching, the seventh, is finished.
