Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_105.mp3]	333	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Upananda the Sakyan was quarreling with the monks from the group of six.<br><br>He then committed an offense of intentional emission of semen. He asked the Sangha for probation for that offense,<br><br>which he received.<br><br>Just then an association in Sāvatthī was offering a meal to the Sangha.<br><br>Because Upananda was on probation, he sat on the last seat in the dining hall.<br><br>The monks from the group of six then told those lay followers,<br><br>“This Venerable Upananda, the esteemed associate of your families, eats the food given in faith with the same hand he uses to masturbate.<br><br>After committing an offense of intentional emission of semen, he asked the Sangha for probation for that offense,<br><br>which he received.<br><br>And because he’s on probation, he now sits on the last seat.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six tell a person who’s not fully ordained about a monk’s grave offense?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A monk’s:<br><br>another monk’s.<br><br>A grave offense:<br><br>the four offenses entailing expulsion and the thirteen entailing suspension.<br><br>A person who is not fully ordained:<br><br>anyone except a fully ordained monk or a fully ordained nun.<br><br>Tells:<br><br>tells a woman or a man, a lay person or a monastic.<br><br>Except if the monks have agreed:<br><br>unless the monks have agreed.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br><b>Permutations part 1</b><br><br><b>Summary</b><br><br>There is agreement of the monks with a limit on offenses, but not on families.<br><br>There is agreement of the monks with a limit on families, but not on offenses. There is agreement of the monks with a limit both on offenses and on families. There is agreement of the monks with neither a limit on offenses nor on families.<br><br><b>Definitions</b><br><br>With a limit on offenses:<br><br>offenses are specified: “These particular offenses can be told about.”<br><br>With limit on families:<br><br>families are specified: “These particular families can be told.”<br><br>With a limit both on offenses and on families:<br><br>both offenses and families are specified: “These particular offenses can be told about, and these particular families can be told.”<br><br>With neither a limit on offenses nor on families:<br><br>neither offenses nor families are specified in this way.<br><br><b>Exposition</b><br><br>When there is a limit on offenses, if he tells about other offenses than those that are specified, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is a limit on families, if he tells other families than those that are specified, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is a limit both on offenses and on families, if he tells about other offenses than those that are specified or he tells other families than those that are specified, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is neither a limit on offenses nor on families, there is no offense.<br><br><b>Permutations part 2</b><br><br>If the offense is grave, and he perceives it as such, and he tells a person who is not fully ordained, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the offense is grave, but he is unsure of it, and he tells a person who is not fully ordained, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the offense is grave, but he perceives it as minor, and he tells a person who is not fully ordained, then, except if the monks have agreed, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he tells about a minor offense, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he tells about the misconduct of a person who is not fully ordained, whether grave or minor, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the offense is minor, but he perceives it as grave, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the offense is minor, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the offense is minor, and he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he tells about the action that was the basis for the offense, but not the class of offense;<br><br>if he tells about the class of offense, but not the action that was the basis for the offense;<br><br>if the monks have agreed;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on telling about what is grave, the ninth, is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::10 Musāvāda Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 98	Omasavādasikkhāpadaṁ	Omasavāde pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 2	100% Identical.	If a nun speaks abusively, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_98.mp3]	326	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were arguing with and speaking abusively to the good monks.<br><br>They reviled and insulted them about their caste, name, family, occupation, profession, illnesses, physical traits, defilements, and offenses, and by calling them names.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six argue with and abuse good monks?<br><br>How can they revile and insult them about these things?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you’re doing this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …”<br><br>After rebuking them …<br><br>he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Once upon a time, monks, there was a brahmin in Takkasilā who had an ox called Nandivisāla.<br><br>On one occasion the ox said to that brahmin,<br><br>‘Go, brahmin, and bet a thousand coins with the wealthy merchant that your ox will pull one hundred carts tied together.’<br><br>And that brahmin did just that.<br><br>Then, after tying one hundred carts together and yoking Nandivisāla to them, he said,<br><br>‘Go, you fraud! Pull, you liar!’<br><br>But Nandivisāla didn’t budge.<br><br>Then that brahmin became depressed because he had lost a thousand coins.<br><br>Nandivisāla said to him,<br><br>‘Why are you depressed?’<br><br>‘Because I lost one thousand coins because of you.’<br><br>‘But why did you disgrace me by calling me a fraud when I’m not?<br><br>Now go, brahmin, and make the same bet with that merchant, but increase the stakes to two thousand coins.<br><br>Just don’t disgrace me by calling me a fraud.’<br><br>Once again that brahmin did just that.<br><br>Then, after tying one hundred carts together and yoking Nandivisāla to them, he said,<br><br>‘Go, good ox! Pull, good ox!’<br><br>And Nandivisāla pulled those one hundred carts.<br><br>‘One should say what’s pleasant,<br><br>Never what’s unpleasant.<br><br>Because of his pleasant speech,<br><br>Heavy loads were pulled,<br><br>And he obtained wealth;<br><br>And he was delighted with that.’<br><br>Even at that time, monks, reviling and insulting was unpleasant to me.<br><br>How then could reviling and insulting be pleasant now?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	Speaks abusively:<br><br>he speaks abusively in ten ways: about caste, about name, about family, about occupation, about profession, about illnesses, about physical traits, about defilements, about offenses, and by name-calling.<br><br>Caste:<br><br>there are two kinds of castes: low castes and high castes.<br><br>Low castes:<br><br>outcasts, bamboo workers, hunters, carriage makers, waste removers—these are called “low castes”.<br><br>High castes:<br><br>aristocrats and brahmins—these are called “high castes”.<br><br>Name:<br><br>there are two kinds of names: low names and high names.<br><br>Low names:<br><br>Avakaṇṇaka, Javakaṇṇaka, Dhaniṭṭhaka, Saviṭṭhaka, Kulavaḍḍhaka, or names, in whatever countries, that are despised, looked down upon, scorned, treated with contempt, disregarded—these are called “low names”.<br><br>High names:<br><br>those connected with the Buddha, connected with the Teaching, or connected with the Sangha, or names, in whatever countries, that are highly regarded, highly thought of, respected, valued, esteemed—these are called “high names”.<br><br>Family:<br><br>there are two kinds of families: low families and high families.<br><br>Low families:<br><br>the Kosiya family, the Bhāradvāja family, or families, in whatever countries, that are despised, looked down upon, scorned, treated with contempt, disregarded—these are called “low families”.<br><br>High families:<br><br>the Gotama family, the Moggallāna family, the Kaccāna family, the Vāsiṭṭha family, or families, in whatever countries, that are highly regarded, highly thought of, respected, valued, esteemed—these are called “high families”.<br><br>Occupation:<br><br>there are two kinds of occupations: low occupations and high occupations.<br><br>Low occupations:<br><br>carpentry, waste removing, or occupations, in whatever countries, that are despised, looked down upon, scorned, treated with contempt, disregarded—these are called “low occupations”.<br><br>High occupations:<br><br>farming, trade, cattle keeping, or occupations, in whatever countries, that are highly regarded, highly thought of, respected, valued, esteemed—these are called “high occupations”.<br><br>Profession:<br><br>there are two kinds of professions: low professions and high professions.<br><br>Low professions:<br><br>reed work, pottery, weaving, leather work, barbering, or professions, in whatever countries, that are despised, looked down upon, scorned, treated with contempt, disregarded—these are called “low professions”.<br><br>High professions:<br><br>arithmetic, accounting, writing, or professions, in whatever countries, that are highly regarded, highly thought of, respected, valued, esteemed—these are called “high professions”.<br><br>Illnesses:<br><br>all are low, but there is the illness of diabetes which is high.<br><br>Physical traits:<br><br>there are two kinds of physical traits: low physical traits and high physical traits.<br><br>Low physical traits:<br><br>too tall, too short, too dark, too fair—these are called “low physical traits”.<br><br>High physical traits:<br><br>not too tall, not too short, not too dark, not too fair—these are called “high physical traits”.<br><br>Defilements:<br><br>all are low.<br><br>Offenses:<br><br>all are low, but there is the attainment of streamentry which is high.<br><br>Name-calling:<br><br>there are two kinds of name-calling: low name-calling and high name-calling.<br><br>Low name-calling:<br><br>“You’re a camel,” “You’re a ram,” “You’re an ox,” “You’re a donkey,” “You’re an animal,” “You’re bound for hell,” “You’re not going to a good destination,” “You can only expect a bad destination,” or adding disparaging endings to someone’s name, or calling someone words for the male or female genitals—this is called “low name-calling”.<br><br>High name-calling:<br><br>“You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination”—this is called “high name-calling”.<br><br><b>Exposition</b><br><br><b>Abuse about caste</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—an outcast, a bamboo worker, a hunter, a carriage maker, a waste remover—saying, “You’re an outcast,” “You’re a bamboo worker,” “You’re a hunter,” “You’re a carriage maker,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—an aristocrat, a brahmin—saying, “You’re an outcast,” “You’re a bamboo worker,” “You’re a hunter,” “You’re a carriage maker,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—an outcast, a bamboo worker, a hunter, a carriage maker, a waste remover—saying, “You’re an aristocrat,” “You’re a brahmin,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—an aristocrat, a brahmin—saying, “You’re an aristocrat,” “You’re a brahmin,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about name</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—an Avakaṇṇaka, a Javakaṇṇaka, a Dhaniṭṭhaka, a Saviṭṭhaka, a Kulavaḍḍhaka—<br><br>saying, “You’re an Avakaṇṇaka,” “You’re a Javakaṇṇaka,” “You’re a Dhaniṭṭhaka,” “You’re a Saviṭṭhaka,” “You’re a Kulavaḍḍhaka,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—a Buddharakkhita, a Dhammarakkhita, a Saṅgharakkhita—saying, one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—an Avakaṇṇaka, a Javakaṇṇaka, a Dhaniṭṭhaka, a a Gotama,” “You’re a Moggallāna,” “You’re a Kaccāna,” “You’re a Vāsiṭṭha,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—one from the Gotama family, one from the Moggallāna family, one from the Kaccāna family, one from the Vāsiṭṭha family—saying, “You’re a Gotama,” “You’re a Moggallāna,” “You’re a Kaccāna,” “You’re a Vāsiṭṭha,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about occupation</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—a carpenter, a waste remover—saying, “You’re a carpenter,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—a farmer, a trader, a cattle keeper—<br><br>saying, “You’re a carpenter,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—a carpenter, a waste remover—saying, “You’re a farmer,” “You’re a trader,” “You’re a cattle keeper,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—a farmer, a trader, a cattle keeper—saying, “You’re a farmer,” “You’re a trader,” “You’re a cattle keeper,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about profession</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—a reed worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather worker, a barber—saying, “You’re a reed worker,” “You’re a potter,” “You’re a weaver,” “You’re a leather worker,” “You’re a barber,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—an arithmetician, an accountant, a clerk—saying, “You’re a reed worker,” “You’re a potter,” “You’re a weaver,” “You’re a leather worker,” “You’re a barber,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—a reed worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather worker, a barber—saying, “You’re an arithmetician,” “You’re an accountant,” “You’re a clerk,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—an arithmetician, an accountant, a clerk—saying, “You’re an arithmetician,” “You’re an accountant,” “You’re a clerk,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about illnesses</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—a leper, one with abscesses, one with mild leprosy, one with tuberculosis, an epileptic—saying, “You’re a leper,” “You have abscesses,” “You have mild leprosy,” “You have tuberculosis,” “You’re an epileptic,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—a diabetic—saying, “You’re a leper,” “You have abscesses,” “You have mild leprosy,” “You have tuberculosis,” “You’re an epileptic,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—a leper, one with abscesses, one with mild leprosy, one with tuberculosis, an epileptic—saying, “You’re a diabetic,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—a diabetic—saying, “You’re a diabetic,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about physical traits</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—one who is too tall, one who is too short, one who is too dark, one who is too fair—saying, “You’re too tall,” “You’re too short,” “You’re too dark,” “You’re too fair,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—one who is not too tall, one who is not too short, one who is not too dark, one who is not too fair—saying, “You’re too tall,” “You’re too short,” “You’re too dark,” “You’re too fair,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—one who is too tall, one who is too short, one who is too dark, one who is too fair—saying, “You’re not too tall,” “You’re not too short,” “You’re not too dark,” “You’re not too fair,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—one who is not too tall, one who is not too short, one who is not too dark, one who is not too fair—saying, “You’re not too tall,” “You’re not too short,” “You’re not too dark,” “You’re not too fair,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about defilements</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—one full of sensual desire, one full of ill will, one full of confusion—saying, “You’re full of sensual desire,” “You’re full of ill will,” “You’re full of confusion,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—one without sensual desire, one without ill will, one without confusion—saying, “You’re full of sensual desire,” “You’re full of ill will,” “You’re full of confusion,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—one full of sensual desire, one full of ill will, one full of confusion—saying, “You’re without sensual desire,” “You’re without ill will,” “You’re without confusion,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—one without sensual desire, one without ill will, one without confusion—saying, “You’re without sensual desire,” “You’re without ill will,” “You’re without confusion,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Abuse about offenses</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—one who has committed an offense entailing expulsion, one who has committed an offense entailing suspension, one who has committed a serious offense, one who has committed an offense entailing confession, one who has committed an offense entailing acknowledgment, one who has committed an offense of wrong conduct, one who has committed an offense of wrong speech—saying, “You’ve committed an offense entailing expulsion,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing suspension,” “You’ve committed a serious offense,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing confession,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing acknowledgment,” “You’ve committed an offense of wrong conduct,” “You’ve committed an offense of wrong speech,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—a streamenterer—saying, “You’ve committed an offense entailing expulsion,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing suspension,” “You’ve committed a serious offense,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing confession,” “You’ve committed an offense entailing acknowledgment,” “You’ve committed an offense of wrong conduct,” “You’ve committed an offense of wrong speech,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—one who has committed an offense entailing expulsion, one who has committed an offense entailing suspension, one who has committed a serious offense, one who has committed an offense entailing confession, one who has committed an offense entailing acknowledgment, one who has committed an offense of wrong conduct, one who has committed an offense of wrong speech—saying, “You’re a streamenterer,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—a streamenterer—saying, “You’re a streamenterer,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Insulting abuse</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low—a camel, a ram, an ox, a donkey, an animal, one bound for hell—saying, “You’re a camel,” “You’re a ram,” “You’re an ox,” “You’re a donkey,” “You’re an animal,” “You’re bound for hell,” “You’re not going to a good destination,” “You can only expect a bad destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is low to one who is high—one who is wise, one who is competent, one who is intelligent, one who is learned, one who is an expounder of the Teaching—saying, “You’re a camel,” “You’re a ram,” “You’re an ox,” “You’re a donkey,” “You’re an animal,” “You’re bound for hell,” “You’re not going to a good destination,” “You can only expect a bad destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is low—a camel, a ram, an ox, a donkey, an animal, one bound for hell—saying, “You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says what is high to one who is high—one who is wise, one who is competent, one who is intelligent, one who is learned, one who is an expounder of the Teaching—saying, “You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Indirect abuse</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “There are outcasts right here,” “There are bamboo workers right here,” “There are hunters right here,” “There are carriage makers right here,” “There are waste removers right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “There are aristocrats right here,” “There are brahmins right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “There are Avakaṇṇakas right here,” “There are Javakaṇṇakas right here,” “There are Dhaniṭṭhakas right here,” “There are Saviṭṭhakas right here,” “There are Kulavaḍḍhakas right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are Buddharakkhitas right here,” “There are Dhammarakkhitas right here,” “There are Saṅgharakkhitas right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are Kosiyas right here,” “There are Bhāradvājas right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are Gotamas right here,” “There are Moggallānas right here,” “There are Kaccānas right here,” “There are Vāsiṭṭhas right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are carpenters right here,” “There are waste removers right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are farmers right here,” “There are traders right here,” “There are cattle keepers right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are reed workers right here,” “There are potters right here,” “There are weavers right here,” “There are leather workers right here,” “There are barbers right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are arithmeticians right here,” “There are accountants right here,” “There are clerks right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are lepers right here,” “There are some with abscesses right here,” “There are some with mild leprosy right here,” “There are some with tuberculosis right here,” “There are epileptics right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are diabetics right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are some who are too tall right here,” “There are some who are too short right here,” “There are some who are too dark right here,” “There are some who are too fair right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are some who are not too tall right here,” “There are some who are not too short right here,” “There are some who are not too dark right here,” “There are some who are not too fair right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are some who are full of sensual desire right here,” “There are some who are full of ill will right here,” “There are some who are full of confusion right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are some without sensual desire right here,” “There are some without ill will right here,” “There are some without confusion right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are some who have committed an offense entailing expulsion right here … etc. …<br><br>some who have committed an offense of wrong speech right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are streamenterers right here,” …<br><br>says, “There are camels right here,” “There are rams right here,” “There are oxen right here,” “There are donkeys right here,” “There are animals right here,” “There are those bound for hell right here,” “There are those not going to a good destination right here,” “There are those who can only expect a bad destination right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “There are wise ones right here,” “There are competent ones right here,” “There are intelligent ones right here,” “There are learned ones right here,” “There are expounders of the Teaching right here,” “There are those not going to a bad destination right here,” “There are those who can only expect a good destination right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “Perhaps these are outcasts,” “Perhaps these are bamboo workers,” “Perhaps these are hunters,” “Perhaps these are carriage makers,” “Perhaps these are waste removers,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct. …<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “Perhaps these are wise ones,” “Perhaps these are competent ones,” “Perhaps these are intelligent ones,” “Perhaps these are learned ones,” “Perhaps these are expounders of the Teaching,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, says, “We’re not outcasts,” “We’re not bamboo workers,” “We’re not hunters,” “We’re not carriage makers,” “We’re not waste removers,” …<br><br>“We’re not wise ones,” “We’re not competent ones,” “We’re not intelligent ones,” “We’re not learned ones,” “We’re not expounders of the Teaching,” “We’re not going to a bad destination,” “We can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Abuse of one who is not fully ordained</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, says what is low to one who is low …<br><br>says what is low to one who is high …<br><br>says what is high to one who is low …<br><br>says what is high to one who is high—one who is wise, one who is competent, one who is intelligent, one who is learned, one who is an expounder of the Teaching—saying, “You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, says, “There are outcasts right here,” “There are bamboo workers right here,” “There are hunters right here,” “There are carriage makers right here,” “There are waste removers right here,” …<br><br>“There are wise ones right here,” “There are competent ones right here,” “There are intelligent ones right here,” “There are learned ones right here,” “There are expounders of the Teaching right here,” “There are those not going to a bad destination right here,” “There are those who can only expect a good destination right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, says, “Perhaps these are outcasts,” “Perhaps these are bamboo workers,” “Perhaps these are hunters,” “Perhaps these are carriage makers,” “Perhaps these are waste removers,” …<br><br>“Perhaps these are wise ones,” “Perhaps these are competent ones,” “Perhaps these are intelligent ones,” “Perhaps these are learned ones,” “Perhaps these are expounders of the Teaching,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, wishing to revile, wishing to insult, wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, says, “We’re not outcasts,” “We’re not bamboo workers,” “We’re not hunters,” “We’re not carriage makers,” “We’re not waste removers,” …<br><br>“We’re not wise ones,” “We’re not competent ones,” “We’re not intelligent ones,” “We’re not learned ones,” “We’re not expounders of the Teaching,” “We’re not going to a bad destination,” “We can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Not intending to abuse, direct speech</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is low to one who is low—an outcast, a bamboo worker, a hunter, a carriage maker, a waste remover—saying, “You’re an outcast,” “You’re a bamboo worker,” “You’re a hunter,” “You’re a carriage maker,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is low to one who is high—an aristocrat, a brahmin—saying, “You’re an outcast,” “You’re a bamboo worker,” “You’re a hunter,” “You’re a carriage maker,” “You’re a waste remover,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is high to one who is low—an outcast, a bamboo worker, a hunter, a carriage maker, a waste remover—saying, “You’re an aristocrat,” “You’re a brahmin,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is high to one who is high—an aristocrat, a brahmin—saying, “You’re an aristocrat,” “You’re a brahmin,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is low to one who is low …<br><br>says what is low to one who is high …<br><br>says what is high to one who is low …<br><br>says what is high to one who is high—one who is wise, one who is competent, one who is intelligent, one who is learned, one who is an expounder of the Teaching—<br><br>saying, “You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br><b>Not intending to abuse, indirect speech</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “There are outcasts right here,” “There are bamboo workers right here,” “There are hunters right here,” “There are carriage makers right here,” “There are waste removers right here,” …<br><br>“There are wise ones right here,” “There are competent ones right here,” “There are intelligent ones right here,” “There are learned ones right here,” “There are expounders of the Teaching right here,” “There are those not going to a bad destination right here,” “There are those who can only expect a good destination right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “Perhaps these are outcasts,” “Perhaps these are bamboo workers,” “Perhaps these are hunters,” “Perhaps these are carriage makers,” “Perhaps these are waste removers,” …<br><br>“Perhaps these are wise ones,” “Perhaps these are competent ones,” “Perhaps these are intelligent ones,” “Perhaps these are learned ones,” “Perhaps these are expounders of the Teaching,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “We’re not outcasts,” “We’re not bamboo workers,” “We’re not hunters,” “We’re not carriage makers,” “We’re not waste removers,” …<br><br>“We’re not wise ones,” “We’re not competent ones,” “We’re not intelligent ones,” “We’re not learned ones,” “We’re not expounders of the Teaching,” “We’re not going to a bad destination,” “We can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br><b>Not intending to abuse one who is not fully ordained</b><br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says what is low to one who is low …<br><br>says what is low to one who is high …<br><br>says what is high to one who is low …<br><br>says what is high to one who is high—one who is wise, one who is competent, one who is intelligent, one who is learned, one who is an expounder of the Teaching—<br><br>saying, “You’re wise,” “You’re competent,” “You’re intelligent,” “You’re learned,” “You’re an expounder of the Teaching,” “You’re not going to a bad destination,” “You can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “There are outcasts right here,” “There are bamboo workers right here,” “There are hunters right here,” “There are carriage makers right here,” “There are waste removers right here,” …<br><br>“There are wise ones right here,” “There are competent ones right here,” “There are intelligent ones right here,” “There are learned ones right here,” “There are expounders of the Teaching right here,” “There are those not going to a bad destination right here,” “There are those who can only expect a good destination right here,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “Perhaps these are outcasts,” “Perhaps these are bamboo workers,” “Perhaps these are hunters,” “Perhaps these are carriage makers,” “Perhaps these are waste removers,” …<br><br>“Perhaps these are wise ones,” “Perhaps these are competent ones,” “Perhaps these are intelligent ones,” “Perhaps these are learned ones,” “Perhaps these are expounders of the Teaching,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.<br><br>If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, not wishing to humiliate someone who is not fully ordained, but wanting to have fun, says, “We’re not outcasts,” “We’re not bamboo workers,” “We’re not hunters,” “We’re not carriage makers,” “We’re not waste removers,” …<br><br>“We’re not wise ones,” “We’re not competent ones,” “We’re not intelligent ones,” “We’re not learned ones,” “We’re not expounders of the Teaching,” “We’re not going to a bad destination,” “We can only expect a good destination,” then for every statement, he commits an offense of wrong speech.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he is aiming at something beneficial;<br><br>if he is aiming at giving a teaching;<br><br>if he is aiming at giving an instruction;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is deranged;<br><br>if he is overwhelmed by pain;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on abusive speech, the second, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū pesalehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ bhaṇḍantā pesale bhikkhū omasanti—<br><br>jātiyāpi, nāmenapi, gottenapi, kammenapi, sippenapi, ābādhenapi, liṅgenapi, kilesenapi, āpattiyāpi; hīnenapi akkosena khuṁsenti vambhenti.<br><br>Ye te bhikkhū appicchā …pe… te ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma chabbaggiyā bhikkhū pesalehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ bhaṇḍantā pesale bhikkhū omasissanti—<br><br>jātiyāpi, nāmenapi, gottenapi, kammenapi, sippenapi, ābādhenapi, liṅgenapi, kilesenapi, āpattiyāpi; hīnenapi akkosena khuṁsessanti vambhessantī”ti.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū chabbaggiye bhikkhū anekapariyāyena vigarahitvā bhagavato etamatthaṁ ārocesuṁ …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, pesalehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṁ bhaṇḍantā pesale bhikkhū omasatha—jātiyāpi …pe… hīnenapi akkosena khuṁsetha vambhethā”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::10 Musāvāda Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 97	Musāvādasikkhāpadaṁ	Sampajānamusāvāde pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 1	100% Identical.	If a nun lies in full awareness, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Musāvādavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_97.mp3]	325	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Hatthaka the Sakyan was beaten in debate.<br><br>While talking with the monastics of other religions, he would assert things after denying them, and he would deny things after asserting them. He evaded the issues, lied, and made sham appointments.<br><br>The monastics of other religions complained and criticized him, “When Hatthaka talks with us, how can he assert things after denying them, deny things after asserting them, evade the issues, lie, and make sham appointments?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those monastics of other religions.<br><br>They then went to Hatthaka and said,<br><br>“Is it true, Hatthaka, that you’re doing this?”<br><br>“These monastics of other religions should be beaten, whatever it takes!<br><br>They shouldn’t be allowed to win.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“When Hatthaka talks with the monastics of other religions, how can he assert things after denying them, deny things after asserting them, evade the issues, lie, and make sham appointments?”<br><br>After rebuking Hatthaka in many ways, they told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and questioned Hatthaka:<br><br>“Is it true, Hatthaka, that you’re doing this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Lies in full awareness:<br><br>the speech of one who is aiming to deceive—his words, his way of speaking, his breaking into speech, his verbal expression, his eight kinds of ignoble speech: he says that he has seen what he has not seen; he says that he has heard what he has not heard; he says that he has sensed what he has not sensed; he says that he has mentally experienced what he has not mentally experienced; he says that he has not seen what he has seen; he says that he has not heard what he has heard; he says that he has not sensed what he has sensed; he says that he has not mentally experienced what he has mentally experienced.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br><b>Definitions</b><br><br>Not seen:<br><br>not seen with the eye.<br><br>Not heard:<br><br>not heard with the ear.<br><br>Not sensed:<br><br>not smelled with the nose, not tasted with the tongue, not touched with the body.<br><br>Not mentally experienced:<br><br>not mentally experienced with the mind.<br><br>Seen:<br><br>seen with the eye.<br><br>Heard:<br><br>heard with the ear.<br><br>Sensed:<br><br>smelled with the nose, tasted with the tongue, touched with the body.<br><br>Mentally experienced:<br><br>mentally experienced with the mind.<br><br><b>Exposition</b><br><br><b>Falsely claiming to have experienced what he has not experienced: a single sense door</b><br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when three conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied.<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when four conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied; he misrepresents his view of what is true.<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when five conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied; he misrepresents his view of what is true; he misrepresents his belief of what is true.<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when six conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied; he misrepresents his view of what is true; he misrepresents his belief of what is true; he misrepresents his acceptance of what is true.<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when seven conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied; he misrepresents his view of what is true; he misrepresents his belief of what is true; he misrepresents his acceptance of what is true; he misrepresents his sentiment of what is true.<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he says that he has heard what he has not heard …<br><br>saying that he has sensed what he has not sensed …<br><br>saying that he has mentally experienced what he has not mentally experienced, he commits an offense entailing confession when three conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied.<br><br>… when four conditions are fulfilled …<br><br>when five conditions are fulfilled …<br><br>when six conditions are fulfilled …<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has mentally experienced what he has not mentally experienced, he commits an offense entailing confession when seven conditions are fulfilled:<br><br>before he has lied, he knows he is going to lie; while lying, he knows he is lying; after he has lied, he knows he has lied; he misrepresents his view of what is true; he misrepresents his belief of what is true; he misrepresents his acceptance of what is true; he misrepresents his sentiment of what is true.<br><br><b>Falsely claiming to have experienced what he has not experienced: multiple sense doors</b><br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen and heard what he has not seen, he commits an offense entailing confession when three conditions are fulfilled …<br><br>If he lies in full awareness, saying that he has seen and sensed what he has not seen, he commits an There is no offense:<br><br>if he speaks playfully;<br><br>if he speaks too fast;<br><br>(Speaks playfully means:<br><br>speaking quickly.<br><br>Speaks too fast means:<br><br>meaning to say one thing, he says something else.)<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on lying, the first, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena hatthako sakyaputto vādakkhitto hoti.<br><br>So titthiyehi saddhiṁ sallapanto avajānitvā paṭijānāti, paṭijānitvā avajānāti, aññenaññaṁ paṭicarati, sampajānamusā bhāsati, saṅketaṁ katvā visaṁvādeti.<br><br>Titthiyā ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—“kathañhi nāma hatthako sakyaputto amhehi saddhiṁ sallapanto avajānitvā paṭijānissati, paṭijānitvā avajānissati, aññenaññaṁ paṭicarissati, sampajānamusā bhāsissati, saṅketaṁ katvā visaṁvādessatī”ti.<br><br>Assosuṁ kho bhikkhū tesaṁ titthiyānaṁ ujjhāyantānaṁ khiyyantānaṁ vipācentānaṁ.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū yena hatthako sakyaputto tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā hatthakaṁ sakyaputtaṁ etadavocuṁ—<br><br>“saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, āvuso hatthaka, titthiyehi saddhiṁ sallapanto avajānitvā paṭijānāsi, paṭijānitvā avajānāsi, aññenaññaṁ paṭicarasi, sampajānamusā bhāsasi, saṅketaṁ katvā visaṁvādesī”ti?<br><br>“Ete kho, āvuso, titthiyā nāma yena kenaci jetabbā;<br><br>neva tesaṁ jayo dātabbo”ti.<br><br>Ye te bhikkhū appicchā …pe… te ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma hatthako sakyaputto titthiyehi saddhiṁ sallapanto avajānitvā paṭijānissati, paṭijānitvā avajānissati, aññenaññaṁ paṭicarissati, sampajānamusā bhāsissati, saṅketaṁ katvā visaṁvādessatī”ti.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū hatthakaṁ sakyaputtaṁ anekapariyāyena vigarahitvā bhagavato etamatthaṁ ārocesuṁ.<br><br>Atha kho bhagavā etasmiṁ nidāne etasmiṁ pakaraṇe bhikkhusaṅghaṁ sannipātāpetvā hatthakaṁ sakyaputtaṁ visaṁvādesī”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma tvaṁ, moghapurisa, titthiyehi saddhiṁ sallapanto avajānitvā paṭijānissasi, paṭijānitvā If a nun complains or criticizes, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_109.mp3]	338	At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary.<br><br>At that time Venerable Dabba the Mallian was assigning the dwellings and designating the meals,<br><br>and the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka were newly ordained.<br><br>They had little merit, getting inferior dwellings and meals.<br><br>They then complained about Dabba to other monks,<br><br>“Dabba the Mallian assigns dwellings and designates meals based on favoritism.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka complain about Venerable Dabba to other monks?”…<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk complains, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Knowing that the Buddha had prohibited complaining, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka thought of other ways of getting the monks to hear about their grievances.<br><br>They then criticized Dabba the Mallian in the vicinity of other monks,<br><br>“Dabba assigns dwellings and designates meals based on favoritism.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka criticize Venerable Dabba?”…<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Complaining:<br><br>when someone who is fully ordained is the assigner of dwellings or the designator of meals or the distributor of congee or the distributor of fruit or the distributor of fresh foods or the distributor of small requisites, and he has been appointed by the Sangha as such, then if a monk complains about him or criticizes him to one who is fully ordained—desiring to disparage him, desiring to give him a bad reputation, desiring to humiliate him—he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, and he complains or criticizes, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he complains or criticizes, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he complains or criticizes, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he complains or criticizes him to one who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When someone who is fully ordained is the assigner of dwellings or the designator of meals or the distributor of congee or the distributor of fruit or the distributor of fresh foods or the distributor of small requisites, but he has not been appointed by the Sangha as such, then if a monk complains about him or criticizes him to one who is fully ordained or to one who is not fully ordained—desiring to disparage him, desiring to give him a bad reputation, desiring to humiliate him—he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When someone who is not fully ordained is the assigner of dwellings or the designator of meals or the distributor of congee or the distributor of fruit or the distributor of fresh foods or the distributor of small requisites, whether he has been appointed by the Sangha as such or not, then if a monk complains about him or criticizes him to one who is fully ordained or to one who is not fully ordained—desiring to disparage him, desiring to give him a bad reputation, desiring to humiliate him—he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he complains about or criticizes one who regularly acts out of favoritism, ill will, confusion, or fear;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on complaining, the third, is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::11 Bhūtagāma Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 113	Nikkaḍḍhanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī bhikkhuniṁ kupitā anattamanā saṅghikā vihārā nikkaḍḍheyya vā nikkaḍḍhāpeyya vā, pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 17	Uses 'bhikkhunī bhikkhuniṁ',&nbsp;kupitā anattamanā	If a nun, in anger, throws a nun out of a dwelling belonging to the Sangha, or has her thrown out, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_113.mp3]	346	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the monks from the group of seventeen were repairing a large dwelling nearby,<br><br>intending to stay there for the rainy season.<br><br>The monks from the group of six saw this<br><br>and said,<br><br>“These monks from the group of seventeen are repairing a dwelling.<br><br>Let’s throw them out.”<br><br>But some of them said,<br><br>“Let’s wait until they’ve finished repairing it.”<br><br>Soon afterwards the monks from the group of six said to those from the group of seventeen,<br><br>“Leave, this dwelling is ours.”<br><br>“Shouldn’t you have told us beforehand? We would’ve repaired another one.”<br><br>“Doesn’t this dwelling belong to the Sangha?”<br><br>“Yes, it does.”<br><br>“Well then, leave! This dwelling is ours.”<br><br>“The dwelling is large.<br><br>You can stay here and so can we.”<br><br>But they said, “Leave, this dwelling is ours,” and they grabbed them by the necks and threw them out in anger.<br><br>The monks from the group of seventeen cried.<br><br>When other monks asked them why,<br><br>they told them what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six angrily throw other monks out of a dwelling belonging to the Sangha?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>…The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A monk:<br><br>another monk.<br><br>In anger:<br><br>discontent, having hatred, hostile.<br><br>A dwelling belonging to the Sangha:<br><br>given to the Sangha, given up to the Sangha.<br><br>Throws out:<br><br>if he takes hold of him in a room and throws him out to the entryway, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he takes hold of him in the entryway and throws him outside, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Even if he makes him go through many doors with a single effort, he commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has thrown out:<br><br>if he asks another, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he only asks once, then even if the other makes him go through many doors, he commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, and he perceives it as such, and in anger he throws him out, or has him thrown out, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he is unsure of it, and in anger he throws him out, or has him thrown out, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he perceives it as belonging to an individual, and in anger he throws him out, or has him thrown out, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he throws out one of his requisites, or he has it thrown out, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he throws him out, or has him thrown out, from the vicinity of a dwelling, from an assembly hall, from under a roof cover, from the foot of a tree, or from a space out in the open, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he throws out one of his requisites from any of these places, or he has it thrown out, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he throws out one who is not fully ordained, or has them thrown out, from a dwelling, from the vicinity of a dwelling, from an assembly hall, from under a roof cover, from the foot of a tree, or from a space out in the open, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he throws out one of their requisites from any of these places, or has it thrown out, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, but he perceives it as belonging to the Sangha, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, and he perceives it as such, but that individual is not himself, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to himself, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he throws out one who is shameless, or has him thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one of the requisites belonging to that person, or has them thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one who is insane, or has him thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one of the requisites belonging to that person, or has them thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one who is quarrelsome and argumentative, who creates legal issues in the Sangha, or has them thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one of the requisites belonging to that person, or has them thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out a pupil or student who is not conducting himself properly, or has him thrown out;<br><br>if he throws out one of the requisites belonging to such a person, or has them thrown out;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on throwing out, the seventh, is finished. There is no offense:<br><br>if he applies two or three layers;<br><br>if he applies less than two or three layers;<br><br>if it is a shelter;<br><br>if it is a cave;<br><br>if it is a grass hut;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if it is anything apart from a dwelling;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on large dwellings, the ninth, is finished. If a nun pours water that she knows contains living beings onto grass or clay, or has it poured, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>The eleventh subchapter on plants.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_116.mp3]	351	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine,<br><br>the monks there were doing building work. They poured water that they knew contained living beings onto grass and clay, and they had others do the same.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks at Āḷavī pour water that they know contains living beings onto grass and clay, and have others do the same?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>…The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>He knows:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him.<br><br>Pours:<br><br>if he pours it himself, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has poured:<br><br>if he asks another, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he only asks once, then even if the other pours a lot, he commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it contains living beings, and he perceives it as such, and he pours it onto grass or clay, or he has it poured, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it contains living beings, but he is unsure of it, and he pours it onto grass or clay, or he has it poured, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it contains living beings, but he does not perceive it as such, and he pours it onto grass or clay, or he has it poured, there is no offense.<br><br>If it does not contain living beings, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it does not contain living beings, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it does not contain living beings, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is unintentional;<br><br>if he is not mindful;<br><br>if he does not know;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on containing living beings, the tenth, is finished.<br><br>The second subchapter on plants is finished.<br><br>This is the summary:<br><br>“Plant, with evasion, complaining,<br><br>The two with departing;<br><br>Before, throwing out, detachable,<br><br>Door, and containing living beings.”	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā āḷaviyaṁ viharati aggāḷave cetiye.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena āḷavakā bhikkhū navakammaṁ karontā jānaṁ sappāṇakaṁ udakaṁ tiṇampi mattikampi siñcantipi siñcāpentipi.<br><br>Ye te bhikkhū appicchā …pe… te ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma āḷavakā bhikkhū jānaṁ sappāṇakaṁ udakaṁ tiṇampi mattikampi siñcissantipi siñcāpessantipī”ti.<br><br>Atha kho te bhikkhū āḷavake bhikkhū anekapariyāyena vigarahitvā bhagavato etamatthaṁ ārocesuṁ …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, jānaṁ sappāṇakaṁ udakaṁ tiṇampi mattikampi siñcathapi siñcāpethapī”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma tumhe, moghapurisā, jānaṁ sappāṇakaṁ udakaṁ tiṇampi mattikampi siñcissathapi siñcāpessathapi.<br><br>Netaṁ, moghapurisā, appasannānaṁ vā pasādāya …pe…<br><br>evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṁ sikkhāpadaṁ uddiseyyātha—	Yo panāti<br><br>yo yādiso …pe…<br><br>bhikkhūti<br><br>…pe… ayaṁ imasmiṁ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti.<br><br>Jānāti nāma<br><br>sāmaṁ vā jānāti. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::11 Bhūtagāma Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 108	Aññavādakasikkhāpadaṁ	Aññavādake, vihesake pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 12	100% Identical.	If a nun speaks evasively or harasses, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_108.mp3]	337	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Channa was misbehaving. Then, when he was examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha, he spoke evasively,<br><br>“Who has committed an offense? What offense was committed? In regard to what was it committed? How was it committed? Who are you talking about? What are you talking about?”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How can Venerable Channa speak evasively when examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha?”…<br><br>“Is it true, Channa, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …”<br><br>After rebuking him …<br><br>he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Well then, monks, the Sangha should charge Channa with evasive speech.<br><br>And he is to be charged like this.<br><br>A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The monk Channa speaks evasively when examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should charge him with evasive speech.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The monk Channa speaks evasively when examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha.<br><br>The Sangha is charging him with evasive speech.<br><br>Any monk who approves of charging him with evasive speech should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has charged the monk Channa with evasive speech.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>After rebuking Channa in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk speaks evasively, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Later, when Channa was again being examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha, he thought,<br><br>“By speaking evasively I’ll commit an offense,” and he instead harassed the Sangha by remaining silent.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“When he’s examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha, how can Venerable Channa harass the Sangha by remaining silent?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Channa, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …”<br><br>After rebuking him …<br><br>he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Well then, monks, the Sangha should charge Channa with harassment.<br><br>And he is to be charged like this.<br><br>A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The monk Channa, when examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha, harasses the Sangha by remaining silent.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should charge him with harassment.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The monk Channa, when examined about an offense in the midst of the Sangha, harasses the Sangha by remaining silent.<br><br>The Sangha is charging him with harassment.<br><br>Any monk who approves of charging him of harassment should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has charged the monk Channa with harassment.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>After rebuking Channa in many ways, the Buddha spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support …<br><br>“And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>One who speaks evasively:<br><br>when being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, he speaks evasively because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it, saying, “Who has committed an offense? What offense was committed? In regard to what was it committed? How was it committed? Who are you talking about? What are you talking about?”—this is called “one who speaks evasively”.<br><br>One who harasses:<br><br>when being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, he harasses the Sangha by remaining silent because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it—this is called “one who harasses”.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he has not been charged with evasive speech, but he is being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, and he then speaks evasively because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it, saying,<br><br>“Who has committed an offense? What offense was committed? In regard to what was it committed? How was it committed? Who are you talking about? What are you talking about?” then he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he has not been charged with harassment, but he is being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, and he then harasses the Sangha by remaining silent because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it, then he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he has been charged with evasive speech, and he is being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, and he then speaks evasively because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it, saying,<br><br>“Who has committed an offense? What offense was committed? In regard to what was it committed? How was it committed? Who are you talking about? What are you talking about?” then he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he has been charged with harassment, and he is being examined in the midst of the Sangha about an action that was the basis for an offense or about the class of an offense, and he then harasses the Sangha by remaining silent because he does not want to talk about it or reveal it, then he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, and he speaks evasively or he harasses, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he speaks evasively or he harasses, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he speaks evasively or he harasses, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he asks because he does not know;<br><br>if he does not speak because he is sick;<br><br>if he does not speak because he thinks there will be quarrels or disputes in the Sangha;<br><br>if he does not speak because he thinks there will be a fracture or schism in the Sangha;<br><br>if he does not speak because he thinks the legal procedure will be illegitimate, done by an incomplete assembly, or done to one who does not deserve a legal procedure;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on evasive speech, the second, is finished.
