If a nun takes a bed, a bench, a mattress, or a stool belonging to the Sangha and puts it out in the open or has it put out in the open, and she then departs without putting it away, having it put away, or informing anyone, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_110.mp3]	341	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery during winter,<br><br>the monks put furniture out in the open in order to warm themselves in the sun. But when the time for departure was announced, they departed without putting it away, having it put away, or informing anyone.<br><br>The furniture was rained on.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could those monks put furniture out in the open and then depart without putting it away, having it put away, or informing anyone? The furniture was rained on.”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Second sub-story</b><br><br>Soon afterwards, monks who had stayed out in the open brought the furniture back even though it was not the rainy season.<br><br>The Buddha saw this.<br><br>After giving a teaching, he addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, during the eight months outside of the rainy season, I allow you to store furniture under a roof cover or at the foot of a tree or wherever crows or ravens don’t leave droppings.”<br><br><b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>…The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Belonging to the Sangha:<br><br>given to the Sangha, given up to the Sangha.<br><br>A bed:<br><br>there are four kinds of beds:<br><br>one with legs and frame, called <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">masāraka</i>; one with legs and frame, called <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">bundikābaddha</i>; one with crooked legs; one with detachable legs.<br><br>A bench:<br><br>there are four kinds of benches: one with legs and frame, called <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">masāraka</i>; one with legs and frame, called <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">bundikābaddha</i>; one with crooked legs; one with detachable legs.<br><br>A mattress:<br><br>there are five kinds of mattresses: a mattress stuffed with wool, a mattress stuffed with cloth, a mattress stuffed with bark, a mattress stuffed with grass, a mattress stuffed with leaves.<br><br>A stool:<br><br>one made of bark, one made of vetiver grass, one made of reed. It is upholstered and then bound together.<br><br>Puts it:<br><br>puts it oneself.<br><br>Has it put:<br><br>gets another to put it.<br><br>If he gets one who is not fully ordained to put it, it is the responsibility of the monk.<br><br>If he gets one who is fully ordained to put it, it is the responsibility of the one who puts it.<br><br>Departs without putting it away:<br><br>he does not put it away himself.<br><br>Having it put away:<br><br>he does not get another to put it away.<br><br>Or informing anyone:<br><br>if he does not inform a monk, a novice monk, or a monastery worker, then when he goes beyond the distance of a stone’s throw of an average man, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, and he perceives it as such, and he puts it out in the open or has it put out in the open, and he then departs without putting it away or having it put away or informing anyone, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he is unsure of it …<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he perceives it as belonging to an individual, and he puts it out in the open or has it put out in the open, and he then departs without putting it away or having it put away or informing anyone, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a mat underlay, a bedspread, a floor cover, a straw mat, a hide, a foot-wiping cloth, or a plank bench, and he puts it out in the open or has it put out in the open, and he then departs without putting it away or having it put away or informing anyone, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, but he perceives it as belonging to the Sangha, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, and he perceives it as such, but that individual is not himself, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to himself, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if he departs after putting it away;<br><br>if he departs after having it put away;<br><br>if he departs after informing someone;<br><br>if he departs while he is sunning it;<br><br>if the furniture is obstructed;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on furniture, the fourth, is finished. If a nun destroys a plant, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_107.mp3]	336	At one time the Buddha was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.<br><br>At that time the monks of Āḷavī were doing building work, and they cut down trees and had them cut down.<br><br>Then, when a certain monk was cutting down a tree,<br><br>the deity that lived in it said to him,<br><br>“Venerable, don’t cut down our dwelling because you want to build a dwelling for yourself.”<br><br>Not taking any heed, he just cut it down, and he hurt the arm of that deity’s child.<br><br>The deity thought,<br><br>“Why don’t I just kill this monk?”<br><br>But then it reconsidered,<br><br>“It wouldn’t be right to just kill this monk.<br><br>Let me instead tell the Buddha about this matter.”<br><br>And it approached the Buddha and told him what had happened.<br><br>“Well done, deity!<br><br>It’s good that you didn’t kill that monk.<br><br>If you had killed that monk, you would have made much demerit.<br><br>The tree over there is empty. Take that as your dwelling.”<br><br>People complained and criticized the monks,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics cut down trees and have them cut down? They are hurting life with one sense.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can those monks at Āḷavī cut down trees and have them cut down?”…<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>People regard trees as conscious.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Plant:<br><br>there are five kinds of propagation: propagation from roots, propagation from stems, propagation from joints, propagation from cuttings, propagation from seeds.<br><br>Propagation from roots:<br><br>turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, white sweet flag, atis root, black hellebore, vetiver root, nutgrass, or any other plant produced from roots, that grows from roots—this is called “propagation from roots”.<br><br>Propagation from stems:<br><br>the Bodhi tree, the banyan tree, the Indian rock fig, the cluster fig, the Indian cedar, the portia tree, or any other plant produced from stems, that grows from stems—this is called “propagation from stems”.<br><br>Propagation from joints:<br><br>sugarcane, bamboo, reed, or any other plant produced from joints, that grows from joints—this is called “propagation from joints”.<br><br>Propagation from cuttings:<br><br>shrubby basil, rajmahal hemp, Vicks plant, or any other plant produced from cuttings, that grows from cuttings—this is called “propagation from cuttings”.<br><br>Propagation from seeds:<br><br>grains, vegetables, or any other plant produced from seeds, that grows from seeds—this is called “propagation from seeds”.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is capable of propagation, and he perceives that it is, and he cuts it down or has it cut down, or he breaks it or has it broken, or he cooks it or has it cooked, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is capable of propagation, but he is unsure of it, and  he cuts it down or has it cut down, or he breaks it or has it broken, or he cooks it or has it cooked, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is capable of propagation, but he perceives that it is not, and he cuts it down or has it cut down, or he breaks it or has it broken, or he cooks it or has it cooked, there is no offense.<br><br>If it is not capable of propagation, but he perceives that it is, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not capable of propagation, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not capable of propagation, and he perceives that it is not, there is no offense. Pācittiyā	Bhūtagāmavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_114.mp3]	347	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time two monks were staying in a dwelling with an upper story belonging to the Sangha, one staying below and one above.<br><br>The monk above sat down hastily on a bed with detachable legs.<br><br>A leg fell off and hit the monk below on the head.<br><br>He cried out.<br><br>Monks rushed up<br><br>and asked him why,<br><br>and he told them what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How could a monk sit down hastily on a bed with detachable legs on an upper story in a dwelling belonging to the Sangha?”<br><br>After rebuking that monk in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monk, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>…The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A dwelling belonging to the Sangha:<br><br>given to the Sangha, given up to the Sangha.<br><br>An upper story:<br><br>a man of average height does not hit his head.<br><br>A bed with detachable legs:<br><br>it stands after inserting the limbs.<br><br>A bench with detachable legs:<br><br>it stands after inserting the limbs.<br><br>Sits down:<br><br>if he sits down on it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Lies down:<br><br>if he lies down on it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, and he perceives it as such, and he sits down or lies down on a bed or a bench with detachable legs on an upper story, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he is unsure of it …<br><br>If it belongs to the Sangha, but he perceives it as belonging to an individual, and he sits down or lies down on a bed or a bench with detachable legs on an upper story, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it belongs to an individual, but he perceives it as belonging to the perceives it as such, but that individual is not himself, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it belongs to himself, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if there is no upper story;<br><br>if the upper story is so low that one hits the head;<br><br>if the lower story is not in use;<br><br>if the upper story has floorboards;<br><br>if the legs are fastened by bolts;<br><br>if he stands on it to get hold of something or to put something up;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on upper stories, the eighth, is finished. Matches Bu PC 31	Uses 'Agilānāya bhikkhuniyā' instead of 'agilānena bhikkhunā'.&nbsp;Uses 'uttari' instead of 'uttariṃ'.	If a nun who is not sick eats more than one almsmeal at a public guesthouse,<br>she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_117.mp3]	353	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a certain association was preparing an almsmeal at a public guesthouse not far from Sāvatthī.<br><br>Then, after robing up in the morning, the monks from the group of six took their bowls and robes and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Not getting anything, they went to that public guesthouse.<br><br>Because it was a long time since they had been there, people served them respectfully.<br><br>A second and a third day those monks did the same thing.<br><br>Then they thought,<br><br>“What’s the point of returning to the monastery?<br><br>Tomorrow we’ll just have to come back here.”<br><br>So they stayed on and on right there, eating alms at the guesthouse,<br><br>while the monastics of other religions left.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics stay on and on, eating alms at the guesthouse?<br><br>We don’t prepare the almsfood just for them;<br><br>we prepare it for everyone.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six stay on and on, eating alms at a public guesthouse?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk eats more than one almsmeal at a public guesthouse, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards Venerable Sāriputta was traveling through the Kosalan country on his way to Sāvatthī when he came to a public guesthouse.<br><br>Because it was a long time since he had been there, people served him respectfully.<br><br>After he had eaten, Sāriputta became severely ill, and he was unable to leave that guesthouse.<br><br>On the second day, too, those people said to him,<br><br>“Please eat, venerable.”<br><br>But since he knew that<br><br>the Buddha had prohibited eating alms at a public guesthouse after staying on and on, and because he was afraid of wrongdoing, he did not accept.<br><br>As a consequence, he missed his meal.<br><br>When he arrived at Sāvatthī, he told the monks what had happened,<br><br>and they in turn told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick monk to stay on at a public guesthouse and eat alms there.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>he is able to leave that public guesthouse.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>he is unable to leave that public guesthouse.<br><br>Almsmeal at a public guesthouse:<br><br>as much as one needs of any of the five cooked foods, prepared for the general public, in a building, under a roof cover, at the foot of a tree, or out in the open.<br><br>A monk who is not sick may eat there once. If he receives food beyond that with the intention of eating it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful swallowed, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he is not sick, and he perceives himself as not sick, and he eats more than one almsmeal at a public guesthouse, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is not sick, but he is unsure of it, and he eats more than one almsmeal at a public guesthouse, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is not sick, but he perceives himself as sick, and he eats more than one almsmeal at a public guesthouse, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is sick, but he perceives himself as not sick, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is sick, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is sick, and he perceives himself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he is sick;<br><br>if he is not sick and he eats once;<br><br>if he eats while coming or going;<br><br>if he eats after being invited by the owners;<br><br>if the food is prepared specifically for him;<br><br>if there is not as much as he needs;<br><br>if it is anything apart from the five cooked foods;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on almsmeals at public guesthouses, the first, is finished. If a nun eats in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br>These are the appropriate occasions: she is sick; it is the robe-giving season; it is a time of making robes; she is traveling; she is on a boat; it is a big occasion; it is a meal given by a monastic.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_118.mp3]	356	At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary.<br><br>At that time, because of his loss of material support and honor, Devadatta and his followers had to ask families repeatedly to get invited to meals.<br><br>People complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics repeatedly ask families to get invited to meals?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can Devadatta and his followers repeatedly ask families to get invited to meals?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Devadatta, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk eats in a group, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards people invited sick monks to a meal.<br><br>But knowing that the Buddha had prohibited eating in a group and being afraid of wrongdoing, they did not accept.<br><br>They told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick monk to eat in a group.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk eats in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>This is the appropriate occasion: he is sick.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards, during the robe-giving season, people prepared a meal together with robe-cloth and then invited the monks, saying,<br><br>“We wish to offer a meal and then give robe-cloth.”<br><br>But knowing that the Buddha had prohibited eating with a group of people.<br><br>The monks said to those people, “Please go to the shore for a moment while we walk for alms.”<br><br>They replied, “Venerables, please eat right here.”<br><br>But knowing that the Buddha had prohibited eating in a group and being afraid of wrongdoing, they did not accept.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to eat in a group when on board confession.<br><br>These are the appropriate occasions: he is sick; it is the robe-giving season; it is a time of making robes; he is traveling; he is on a boat.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards monks who had completed the rainy-season residence in various regions were coming to Rājagaha to visit the Buddha.<br><br>People saw those monks who had come from various countries and invited them for a meal.<br><br>But knowing that the Buddha had prohibited eating in a group and being afraid of wrongdoing, they did not accept.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to eat in a group on big occasions.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk eats in a group, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>These are the appropriate occasions: he is sick; it is the robe-giving season; it is a time of making robes; he is traveling; he is on a boat; it is a big occasion.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards a relative of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha who had gone forth with the Ājīvaka ascetics went to the king and said, “Great king, I wish to make a meal for the monastics of all religions.”<br><br>“That’s fine, sir, if you first feed the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha.”<br><br>“I’ll do that.”<br><br>And he sent a message to the monks: “Please accept a meal from me tomorrow.”<br><br>But knowing that the Buddha had prohibited eating in a group and being afraid of wrongdoing, they did not accept.<br><br>That Ājīvaka ascetic then went to the Buddha, exchanged pleasantries with him, and said,<br><br>“Good Gotama has gone forth and so have I.<br><br>One who has gone forth should receive alms from another who has gone forth.<br><br>Good Gotama, please accept a meal from me tomorrow together with the Sangha of monks.”<br><br>The Buddha consented by remaining silent.<br><br>The Ājīvaka understood that the Buddha had consented, and he left.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to eat in a group when the meal is given by a monastic.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Eats in a group:<br><br>wherever four monks, after being invited, eat any of the five cooked foods—this is called “eats in a group”.<br><br>Except on an appropriate occasion:<br><br>unless it is an appropriate occasion.<br><br>He is sick:<br><br>even if he has cracked feet, he may eat in a group.<br><br>It is the robe-giving season:<br><br>if he has not participated in the robe-making ceremony, he may eat in a group during the last month of the rainy season. If he has participated in the robe-making ceremony, he may eat in a group during the five month period.<br><br>It is a time of making robes:<br><br>when he is making robes, he may eat in a group.<br><br>He is traveling:<br><br>he may eat in a group if he intends to travel at least six kilometers, while traveling, and after traveling.<br><br>He is on a boat:<br><br>he may eat in a group if he intends to board a boat, while on board, and after disembarking.<br><br>It is a big occasion:<br><br>if two or three monks can get by on walking for alms, but not a group of four, he may eat in a group.<br><br>It is a meal given by a monastic:<br><br>if any kind of wanderer is making the meal, he may eat in a group.<br><br>If he receives something intending to eat it, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful swallowed, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he eats in a group, and he perceives it as such, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he eats in a group, but he is unsure of it, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he eats in a group, but he does not perceive it as such, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he does not eat in a group, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he does not eat in a group, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he does not eat in a group, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is an appropriate occasion;<br><br>if two or three eat together;<br><br>if they eat together after walking for alms;<br><br>if it is a regular meal invitation;<br><br>if it is a meal for which lots are drawn;<br><br>if it is a half-monthly meal;<br><br>if it is on the observance day;<br><br>if it is on the day after the observance day;<br><br>if it is anything apart from the five cooked foods;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on eating in a group, the second, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_118.mp3]	{-group meal} A group meal, except on the proper occasions, is to be confessed. Here the proper occasions are these: a time of illness, a time of giving cloth, a time of making robes, a time of going on a journey, a time of embarking on a boat, an extraordinary occasion, a time when the meal is supplied by contemplatives. These are the proper occasions here. [32]

If a nun goes to a family and is invited to take cookies or crackers, she may accept two or three bowlfuls if she wishes.<br>If she accepts more than that, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br>If she accepts two or three bowlfuls, she should take it away and share it with the nuns. This is the proper procedure.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_119.mp3]	359	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time there was a female lay follower Kāṇamātā who had faith and confidence.<br><br>She had a daughter, Kāṇā, who had been given in marriage to a man in a certain village.<br><br>On one occasion Kāṇā went to her mother’s house on some business.<br><br>Kāṇā’s husband sent her a message: “Please come, Kāṇā, I want you back.”<br><br>Kāṇamātā thought, “It’s shameful to go empty-handed,” and she baked some cookies.<br><br>Just when the cookies were finished, an alms-collecting monk entered Kāṇamātā’s house, and she gave him some.<br><br>After leaving, he told another monk, and he too was given cookies.<br><br>And the same happened a third time.<br><br>At that, all the cookies were gone.<br><br>A second time Kāṇā’s husband sent her the same message, and everything unfolded as before.<br><br>A third time he sent the same message,<br><br>adding, “If Kāṇā doesn’t come, I’ll find another wife.”<br><br>But once again all the cookies were given to monks.<br><br>Kāṇā’s husband found another wife,<br><br>and when Kāṇā heard what had happened, she cried.<br><br>Soon afterwards, after robing up in the morning, the Buddha took his bowl and robe and went to Kāṇamātā’s house where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>Kāṇamātā approached the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>The Buddha asked her why Kāṇā was crying, and she told him what had happened.<br><br>After instructing, inspiring, and gladdening her with a teaching, the Buddha got up from his seat and left.<br><br>Soon afterwards a certain caravan was ready to go south from Rājagaha.<br><br>An alms-collecting monk went up to that caravan to get almsfood,<br><br>and a lay follower gave him flour products.<br><br>After leaving, that monk told another monk, and he too was given flour products.<br><br>And the same happened a third time.<br><br>At that, all his provisions were gone.<br><br>That lay follower said to the other people in the caravan,<br><br>“Sirs, please wait one day. I’ve given my provisions to the monks.<br><br>I need to prepare more.”<br><br>“We can’t wait. The caravan is already on its way.” And they left.<br><br>After preparing provisions, that lay follower followed after the caravan, but he was robbed by thieves.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics receive without moderation?<br><br>This man gave to them, and then because he was following after the caravan he was robbed by thieves.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people<br><br>and they told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Well then, monks, I will lay down a training rule for the following ten reasons:<br><br>for the well-being of the Sangha, for the comfort of the Sangha, for the restraint of bad people, for the ease of good monks, for the restraint of the corruptions relating to the present life, for the restraint of the corruptions relating to future lives, to give rise to confidence in those without it, to increase the confidence of those who have it, for the longevity of the true Teaching, and for supporting the training.<br><br>And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A monk goes to a family:<br><br>a family: there are four kinds of families: the aristocratic family, the brahmin family, the merchant family, the worker family.<br><br>Goes to:<br><br>he has gone there.<br><br>Cookies:<br><br>whatever has been prepared for the purpose of sending away.<br><br>Crackers:<br><br>whatever has been prepared as provisions for a journey.<br><br>Is invited to take:<br><br>“Take as much as you like.”<br><br>If he wishes:<br><br>if he desires.<br><br>He may accept two or three bowlfuls:<br><br>two or three bowlfuls can be accepted.<br><br>If he accepts more than that:<br><br>when he accepts more than that, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he accepts two or three bowlfuls:<br><br>leaving that place and seeing a monk, he should tell him, “I’ve accepted two or three bowlfuls from such-and-such a place; don’t accept anything from there.”<br><br>If he sees a monk, but does not tell him, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the one who is told accepts from there regardless, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>He should take it away and share it with the monks:<br><br>he should take it away when returning from almsround and then share it.<br><br>This is the proper procedure:<br><br>this is the right method.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is more than two or three bowlfuls, and he perceives it as more, and he accepts it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is more than two or three bowlfuls, but he is unsure of it, and he accepts it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is more than two or three bowlfuls, but he perceives it as less, and he accepts it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is less than two or three bowlfuls, but he perceives it as more, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is less than two or three bowlfuls, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is less than two or three bowlfuls, and he perceives it as less, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he accepts two or three bowlfuls;<br><br>if he accepts less than two or three bowlfuls;<br><br>if they give anything that has not been prepared for sending away or as provisions for a journey;<br><br>if they give the leftovers from what was prepared for sending away or as provisions for a journey;<br><br>if they give after the plans to travel have been canceled;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on Kāṇamātā, the fourth, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_119.mp3]	{-Kāṇa’s mother} In case a bhikkhunī arriving at a family residence is invited to take cakes or travellers’ bread, she may accept two or three bowlfuls if she so desires. Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_120.mp3]	360	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove,<br><br>there was a hilltop fair in Rājagaha,<br><br>which the monks from the group of seventeen went to see.<br><br>When people saw the monks, they bathed them, anointed them, fed them cooked food, and gave them fresh food.<br><br>They took that food and brought it back to the monastery. until dawn.<br><br>Fresh food:<br><br>apart from the five cooked foods, the post-midday tonics, the seven-day tonics, and the lifetime tonics—the rest is called “fresh food”.<br><br>Cooked confession.<br><br>If it is the wrong time, but he perceives it as the right time, and he eats fresh or cooked food, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he receives post-midday Matches Bu PC 40	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun eats food that has not been given, except for water and tooth cleaners, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_122.mp3]	362	At one time the Buddha was staying in the hall with the peaked roof in the Great Wood near Vesālī.<br><br>At that time a monk who only used discarded things was staying in a charnel ground.<br><br>He disliked receiving things from people. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::12 Bhojana Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 123	Uyyojanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī bhikkhuniṁ, “ehāyye, gāmaṁ vā nigamaṁ vā piṇḍāya pavisissāmā”ti tassā dāpetvā vā adāpetvā vā uyyojeyya, “gacchāyye, na me tayā saddhiṁ kathā vā nisajjā vā phāsu hoti, ekikāya me kathā vā nisajjā vā phāsu hotī”ti etadeva paccayaṁ karitvā anaññaṁ, pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 42	Uses 'bhikkhunī bhikkhuniṁ', 'ehāyye', 'tassā', 'gacchāyye', 'ekikāya'.	If a nun says to a nun, ‘Come, let’s go to the village or town for alms,’ and then, whether she has had food given to her or not, sends her away, saying, ‘Go away, I’m not comfortable talking or sitting with you, but only if I talk and sit by myself,’ and she does so only for this reason and no other, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_123.mp3]	366	On one occasion when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Upananda the Sakyan said to his brother’s student,<br><br>“Come, let’s go to the village for alms.”<br><br>Then, without getting him any food, he sent him away, saying,<br><br>“Go away! I’m not comfortable talking or sitting with you, but only if I talk and sit by myself.”<br><br>But since the right time for eating was coming to an end, the student was unable to walk for alms. As he returned to the monastery, there was nobody offering food, and so he missed his meal.<br><br>He then went to the monastery and told the monks what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda say to a monk, ‘Come, let’s go to the village for alms,’ and then send him away without getting him any food?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>To a monk:<br><br>to another monk.<br><br>Come … to the village or town:<br><br>a village, also a town, also a city; both a village and a town.<br><br>He has had food given to him:<br><br>he has had congee, a meal, fresh food, or cooked food given to him.<br><br>Not:<br><br>he has not had anything given to him.<br><br>Sends away:<br><br>if, wanting to laugh with a woman, wanting to enjoy himself with her, wanting to sit down in private with her, wanting to misbehave with her, he says, “Go away! I’m not comfortable talking or sitting with you, but only if I talk and sit by myself,” and he sends him away, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the second monk is in the process of going beyond sight or beyond hearing, the first monk commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When the second monk has gone beyond, the first monk commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>He does so only for this reason and no other:<br><br>there is no other reason for sending him away.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the second monk is fully ordained, and the first monk perceives him as such, and he sends him away, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the second monk is fully ordained, but the first monk is unsure of it, and he sends him away, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the second monk is fully ordained, but the first monk does not perceive him as such, and he sends him away, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he puts him down, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he sends away one who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he puts him down, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he sends him away, thinking, “Together we won’t get enough;”<br><br>if he sends him away, thinking, “If he sees these valuable goods, he’ll become greedy;”<br><br>if he sends him away, thinking, “If he sees this woman, he’ll become lustful;”<br><br>if he sends him away, saying, “Take congee or a meal or fresh food or cooked food to the one who is sick or to the one who is left behind or to the one who is guarding the dwellings;”<br><br>if he does not want to misbehave;<br><br>if he sends him away when there is something to be done;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on sending away, the second, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_123.mp3]	{-dismissing} Should any bhikkhunī say to a bhikkhunī, “Come, Venerable, let’s enter the village or town for alms,” and then—whether or not she has had (food) given to her—dismiss her, saying, “Go away, Venerable. Matches Bu PC 43	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun sits down intruding on a lustful couple, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Bhojanavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_124.mp3]	367	On one occasion when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Upananda the Sakyan went to the house of a friend and sat down with his wife in their bedroom.<br><br>The husband approached Upananda, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>He then said to his wife, “Please give him alms.”<br><br>And she did so.<br><br>Soon afterwards he said, “Please leave, sir, the alms have been given.”<br><br>But the woman, knowing that her husband was lustful, said, “Please sit, sir, don’t go.”<br><br>A second time and<br><br>a third time he repeated his request,<br><br>and both times his wife repeated hers.<br><br>He then left the house and complained to the monks,<br><br>“Venerables, Venerable Upananda is seated with my wife in our bedroom.<br><br>When I ask him to leave because we’re busy, he doesn’t want to go.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda sit down intruding on a lustful couple?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A lustful couple:<br><br>both a woman and a man are present. The woman and the man have not both left, and both are not without lust.<br><br>Intruding on:<br><br>enters after.<br><br>Sits down:<br><br>in a large house, if he sits down more than one arm’s reach inside the door frame, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>In a small house, if he sits down beyond the ridge beam, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a bedroom, and he perceives it as such, and he sits down intruding on a lustful couple, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a bedroom, but he is unsure of it, and he sits down intruding on a lustful couple, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a bedroom, but he does not perceive it as such, and he sits down intruding on a lustful couple, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is not a bedroom, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a bedroom, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a bedroom, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if, in a large house, he sits down, but not more one arm’s reach inside the door frame;<br><br>if, in a small house, he sits down, but not beyond the ridge beam;<br><br>if he has a companion monk;<br><br>if both have left;<br><br>if both are without lust;<br><br>if it is not a bedroom;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on lustful, the third, is finished. Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_127.mp3]	373	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove,<br><br>a family that was supporting Venerable Upananda the Sakyan had invited him to a meal,<br><br>and they had invited other monks too.<br><br>But since Upananda was visiting other families before that meal,<br><br>the other monks said to that family,<br><br>“Please give the meal.”<br><br>“Please wait, sirs, until Venerable Upananda arrives.”<br><br>A second time …<br><br>A third time those monks said,<br><br>“Please give the meal before it is too late.”<br><br>“But we prepared the meal because of Venerable Upananda.<br><br>Please wait until he arrives.”<br><br>Then, after visiting those families, Upananda arrived late,<br><br>and those monks did not eat as much as they had intended.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How can Venerable Upananda visit families first when invited to a meal?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training There is no offense:<br><br>if it is an appropriate occasion;<br><br>if he enters after informing an available monk;<br><br>if, when there is no available monk, he enters without informing anyone;<br><br>if the road passes someone else’s house;<br><br>if the road passes the vicinity of someone else’s house;<br><br>if he is going between monasteries;<br><br>if he is going to the dwelling place of nuns;<br><br>if he is going to the dwelling place of the monastics of another religion;<br><br>if he is returning to the monastery;<br><br>if he is going to the house where he has been invited;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on visiting, the sixth, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_127.mp3]	{-visiting} Should any bhikkhunī, being invited for a meal and without taking leave of an available bhikkhunī, go calling on families before or after the meal, except at the proper times, it is to be confessed. Here the proper times are these: the time of giving cloth, the time of making robes. These are the proper times here. [46]

A nun who is not sick may accept an invitation to ask for requisites for four months. If she accepts one beyond that limit, except if it is a further invitation or a permanent invitation, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_128.mp3]	374	"At one time when the Buddha was staying in the Sakyan country in the Banyan Tree Monastery at Kapilavatthu,<br><br>Mahānāma the Sakyan had an for four months.”<br><br>Yet the monks only asked Mahānāma for a small amount of tonics, and so he still had an abundance.<br><br>A second time he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Sir, I wish to invite the Sangha to ask for tonics for a further four months.”<br><br>“Good, good, Mahānāma.<br><br>Please do so.”<br><br>Again the monks were afraid of wrongdoing and did not accept.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to accept a further invitation.”<br><br>Once again the monks only asked Mahānāma for a small amount of tonics, and so he still had an abundance.<br><br>A third time he went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Sir, I wish to invite the Sangha to ask for tonics for life.”<br><br>“Good, good, Mahānāma.<br><br>Please do so.”<br><br>Yet again the monks were afraid of wrongdoing and did not accept.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to accept a permanent invitation.”<br><br>At that time the monks from the group of six were shabbily dressed and improper in appearance.<br><br>Mahānāma criticized them, “Venerables, why are you shabbily dressed and improper in appearance?<br><br>Shouldn’t one who has gone forth be suitably dressed and proper in appearance?”<br><br>The monks from the group of six developed a grudge against Mahānāma.<br><br>Thinking of ways to humiliate him, it occurred to them,<br><br>“Mahānāma has invited the Sangha to ask for tonics. Let’s ask him for ghee.”<br><br>They then went to Mahānāma and said, “We need a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">doṇa</i> measure of ghee.”<br><br>“Please wait until tomorrow.<br><br>People have gone to the cow-pen to get ghee.<br><br>You may come and get it in the morning.”<br><br>A second time<br><br>and a third time the monks from the group of six said the same thing,<br><br>and Mahānāma replied as before.<br><br>They then said, “Why do you give an invitation if you don’t wish to give?”<br><br>Mahānāma complained and criticized them, “How can they not wait for one day when asked?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of Mahānāma,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six not wait for one day when asked by Mahānāma?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you acted like this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you act like this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:"	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A monk who is not sick may accept an invitation to ask for requisites for four months:<br><br>he may accept an invitation to ask for requisites for the sick.<br><br>He may also accept a further invitation:<br><br>he should think, “I’ll ask when I’m sick.”<br><br>He may also accept a permanent invitation:<br><br>he should think, “I’ll ask when I’m sick.”<br><br>If he accepts one beyond that limit:<br><br>there are invitations that have a limit on the tonics, but no limit on the time period;<br><br>there are invitations that have a limit on the time period, but no limit on the tonics;<br><br>there are invitations that have a limit on both the tonics and the time period;<br><br>there are invitations that have neither a limit on the tonics nor on the time period.<br><br>Limit on the tonics:<br><br>the tonics are restricted: “I invite you to ask for these particular tonics.”<br><br>Limit on the time period:<br><br>the time period is restricted: “I invite you to ask during this particular period of time.”<br><br>Limit on both the tonics and the time period:<br><br>both the tonics and the time period are restricted: “I invite you to ask for these particular tonics during this particular period of time.”<br><br>Neither a limit on the tonics nor on the time period:<br><br>neither the tonics nor the time period is restricted.<br><br>When there is a limit on the tonics, if he asks for tonics other than those he has been invited to ask for, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is a limit on the time period, if he asks outside of the period during which he has been invited to ask, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is a limit on both the tonics and on the time period, if he asks for tonics other than those he has been invited to ask for or he asks outside of the period during which he has been invited to ask, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When there is neither a limit on the tonics nor on the time period, there is no offense.<br><br>If he asks for tonics when he has no need for tonics, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he asks for a tonic other than the tonic he needs, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is beyond the limit, and he perceives it as such, and he asks for tonics, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is beyond the limit, but he is unsure of it, and he asks for tonics, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is beyond the limit, but he does not perceive it as such, and he asks for tonics, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is not beyond the limit, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not beyond the limit, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not beyond the limit, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he asks for those tonics for which he was invited to ask;<br><br>if he asks during the time period for which he was invited to ask;<br><br>if he asks by informing, “You have invited me to ask for these tonics, but I need such-and-such a tonic;”<br><br>if he asks by informing, “The time period during which you invited me to ask has passed, but I need tonics;”<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on Mahānāma, the seventh, is finished. Matches Bu PC 48	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun goes to see an army, except if there is a suitable reason, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_129.mp3]	375	On one occasion when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>King Pasenadi of Kosala was marching out with the army,<br><br>and the monks from the group of six went to see it.<br><br>When King Pasenadi saw the monks coming,<br><br>he summoned them and said,<br><br>“Venerables, why have you come here?”<br><br>“We wish to see the great king.”<br><br>“What’s the use of seeing me finding pleasure in battle?<br><br>Shouldn’t you see the Buddha?”<br><br>And people complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics go to see the army?<br><br>It’s our misfortune that we must go out with the army for the sake of our livelihoods and because of our wives and children.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six go to see the army?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk goes to see an army, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards a certain monk had a sick uncle in the army.<br><br>The uncle sent a message to that monk:<br><br>“I’m with the army and I’m sick.<br><br>Please come, venerable.<br><br>I want you to come.”<br><br>Knowing that the Buddha had laid down a rule against going to see an army, that monk thought,<br><br>“I have a sick uncle in the army.<br><br>What should I do now?”<br><br>And he told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to go to the army when there’s a suitable reason.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>An army:<br><br>it has left the inhabited area and is either encamped or marching.<br><br>An army:<br><br>elephants, horses, chariots, infantry.<br><br>An elephant has twelve men; a horse has three men; a chariot has four men; an infantry unit has four men with arrows in hand.<br><br>If he is on his way to see it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Wherever he stands to see it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Every time he goes beyond the range of sight and then sees it again, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Except if there is a suitable reason:<br><br>unless there is a suitable reason.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is an army, and he perceives it as such, and he goes to see it, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an army, but he is unsure of it, and he goes to see it, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an army, but he does not perceive it as such, and he goes to see it, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is on his way to see one division of a fourfold army, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Wherever he stands to see it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Every time he goes beyond the range of sight and then sees it again, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not an army, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not an army, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not an army, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he sees it while standing in a monastery;<br><br>if the army comes to where the monk is standing, sitting, or lying down;<br><br>if he sees it while walking in the opposite direction;<br><br>if he has a suitable reason;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on armies, the eighth, is finished. There is no offense:<br><br>if he stays for two or three nights;<br><br>if he stays for less than two or three nights;<br><br>if he stays for two nights, then leaves before dawn on the third night, and then stays again;<br><br>if he stays because he is sick;<br><br>if he stays because he has to take care of someone who is sick;<br><br>if the army is obstructed by an enemy army;<br><br>if he is obstructed from leaving;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on staying with armies, the ninth, is finished. If a nun drinks this or that kind of alcoholic drink, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_132.mp3]	378	On one occasion when the Buddha was wandering in the country of Ceti on his way to Bhaddavatikā,<br><br>he was seen by a number of cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers.<br><br>They said to him, “Sir, don’t go to Ambatittha.<br><br>There’s a highly venomous dragon with supernormal powers there, in the hermitage of a dreadlocked ascetic.<br><br>Don’t let it harm you.”<br><br>The Buddha was silent.<br><br>They repeated their request a second<br><br>and a third time,<br><br>and the Buddha remained silent.<br><br>The Buddha then continued on to Bhaddavatikā, and he stayed there.<br><br>Just then Venerable Sāgata went to the hermitage of that dreadlocked ascetic and entered his fire hut. After preparing a spread of grass, he sat down, crossed his legs, straightened his body, and established mindfulness in front of him.<br><br>Seeing that Sāgata had entered the fire hut, the dragon was upset and emitted smoke.<br><br>Sāgata, too, emitted smoke.<br><br>The dragon was not able to contain his rage and emitted flames.<br><br>Sāgata entered the fire element and he, too, emitted flames.<br><br>Then, after conquering fire with fire, Sāgata went to Bhaddavatikā.<br><br>After staying at Bhaddavatikā for as long as he liked, the Buddha set out wandering toward Kosambī.<br><br>When he arrived, the lay followers there received him.<br><br>But the lay followers at Kosambī had heard about Sāgata fighting the Ambatittha dragon. And so after receiving the Buddha, they went to see Sāgata. They bowed, stood to one side, and said,<br><br>“Venerable, what can we prepare for you that’s delicious but hard to get?”<br><br>The monks from the group of six replied, “There’s a delicious liquor called Kāpotikā, which is hard for the monks to get. Prepare that.”<br><br>And the lay followers prepared Kāpotikā in house after house. Then, when they saw that Sāgata had entered the town for alms, they said to him, “Drink, venerable, drink the Kāpotikā liquor.”<br><br>Sāgata drank that liquor in house after house, and as he was leaving town, he collapsed at the town gate.<br><br>Just then the Buddha, together with a number of monks, was also leaving town, and he saw Sāgata at the town gate.<br><br>He said, “Monks, pick up Sāgata.”<br><br>Saying, “Yes, sir,” they led him to the monastery, where they put him down with his head toward the Buddha.<br><br>But Sāgata turned around, pointing his feet toward the Buddha.<br><br>The Buddha said, “Previously, monks, wasn’t Sāgata respectful and deferential toward me?”<br><br>“Yes.”<br><br>“But is he now?”<br><br>“Certainly not.”<br><br>“Just recently, didn’t Sāgata fight the Ambatittha dragon?”<br><br>“Yes.”<br><br>“Would he now be able to fight a dragon?”<br><br>“Certainly not.”<br><br>“So, monks, should one drink that which makes one senseless?”<br><br>“Certainly not, sir.”<br><br>“It’s not suitable, monks, it’s not proper for Sāgata, it’s not worthy of a monastic, it’s not allowable, it’s not to be done.<br><br>How could Sāgata drink alcoholic drinks?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>This kind of alcoholic drink:<br><br>alcoholic drinks made from flour, alcoholic drinks made from cookies, alcoholics drink made from rice, those with yeast added, those made from a combination of ingredients.<br><br>That kind of alcoholic drink:<br><br>alcoholic drinks made from flowers, alcoholic drinks made from fruit, alcoholic drinks made from honey, alcoholic drinks made from sugar, those made from a combination of ingredients.<br><br>Drinks:<br><br>if he drinks even what fits on the tip of a blade of grass, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is an alcoholic drink, and he perceives it as such, and he drinks it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an alcoholic drink, but he is unsure of it, and he drinks it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an alcoholic drink, but he perceives it as non-alcoholic, and he drinks it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a non-alcoholic drink, but he perceives it as alcoholic, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a non-alcoholic drink, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a non-alcoholic drink, and he perceives it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he drinks a non-alcoholic drink that has the color, smell, or taste of an alcoholic drink;<br><br>if it is cooked in a bean curry;<br><br>if it is cooked with meat;<br><br>if it is cooked with oil;<br><br>if it is in syrup from emblic myrobalan;<br><br>if he drinks a drink that is normally alcoholic, but which is actually without alcohol;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on drinking alcoholic drinks, the first, is finished. Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_134.mp3]	380	On one occasion when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of seventeen were playing in the than ankle deep, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is playing in a boat in water, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he strikes the water with his hand, with his foot, with a stick, or with a stone, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he plays with water in a vessel, or with congee, milk, buttermilk, dye, urine, or mud in a vessel, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is not playing in water, but he perceives that he is, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is not playing in water, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is not playing in water, and he does not perceive that he is, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he is not aiming to have fun;<br><br>if, when there is something to be done, he enters the water and then immerses himself or emerges on the surface or swims;<br><br>if, while crossing a body of water, he immerses himself or emerges on the surface or swims;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on playing, the third, is finished. will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>Disrespectful:<br><br>there are two kinds of disrespect: disrespect for the person and disrespect for the rule.<br><br>Disrespect for the person:<br><br>if, when corrected by one who is fully ordained about a rule that has been laid down, he thinks, “They’ve been ejected,” “They’ve been reproved,” or “They’ve been censured,” and then, “I won’t do what they say,” and he acts disrespectfully, then he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Disrespect for the rule:<br><br>if, when corrected by one who is fully ordained about a rule that has been laid down, he thinks, “What can be done so that this rule is lost?” “What can be done so that it perishes?”  or “What can be done so that it disappears?” or he does not want to train in that rule, and he acts disrespectfully, then he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, and he perceives them as such, and he acts disrespectfully, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, and he acts disrespectfully, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he does not perceive them as such, and he acts disrespectfully, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If, when corrected about something that has not been laid down, he thinks,<br><br>“This isn’t conducive to self-effacement,” “This isn’t conducive to ascetic practices,” “This isn’t conducive to being inspiring,” “This isn’t conducive to a reduction in things,” or “This isn’t conducive to being energetic,” and he acts disrespectfully, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If, when corrected by one who is not fully ordained, whether or not it has been laid down, he thinks,<br><br>“This isn’t conducive to self-effacement,” “This isn’t conducive to ascetic practices,” “This isn’t conducive to being inspiring,” “This isn’t conducive to a reduction in things,” or “This isn’t conducive to being energetic,” and he acts disrespectfully, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he says, “This is how we were taught and tested by our teachers;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on disrespect, the fourth, is finished. Pācittiyā	Cārittavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_136.mp3]	382	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were scaring the monks from the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A monk:<br><br>another monk.<br><br>Scares:<br><br>if one who is fully ordained, wishing to scare another who is fully ordained, arranges a sight, a sound, a smell, a taste, or a physical contact, then whether the other monk is scared or not, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he tells him about a wilderness inhabited by criminals, predatory animals, or demons, then whether the other monk is scared or not, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, and he perceives him as such, and he scares him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, and he scares him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he does not perceive him as such, and he scares him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If, wishing to scare someone who is not fully ordained, he arranges a sight, a sound, a smell, a taste, or a physical contact,<br><br>then whether the other person is scared or not, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he tells him about a wilderness inhabited by criminals, predatory animals, or demons,<br><br>then whether the other person is scared or not, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he arranges a sight, a sound, a smell, a taste, or a physical contact, or he tells about a wilderness inhabited by criminals, predatory animals, or demons, but not because he wishes to scare anyone;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on scaring, the fifth, is finished. Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_137.mp3]	384	At one time the Buddha was staying in the Bhagga country at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the deer park.<br><br>At that time, during winter, the monks were warming themselves after setting fire to a hollow log.<br><br>Heated by the fire, a black snake came out of the log and attacked the monks.<br><br>The monks ran here and there.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could those monks light a fire to warm themselves?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that monks did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How could those foolish men do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk lights a fire to warm himself, or has one lit, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>At one time a number of monks were sick.<br><br>The monks who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we lit a fire to warm ourselves,<br><br>and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t warm ourselves because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. Because of that we’re not comfortable.”<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick monk to light a fire to warm himself, or to have one lit.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk who is not sick lights a fire to warm himself, or has one lit, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards the monks did not light lamps, small fires, or saunas because they were afraid of wrongdoing.<br><br>They told the Buddha …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to light a fire, or to have one lit, if there’s a suitable reason.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>…The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without a fire.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without a fire.<br><br>To warm himself:<br><br>wanting to heat himself.<br><br>A fire:<br><br>flames are what is meant.<br><br>Lights:<br><br>if he lights it himself, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has one lit:<br><br>if he asks another, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he only asks once, then even if the other lights many fires, he commits one offense entailing confession.<br><br>Except if there is a suitable reason:<br><br>unless there is a suitable reason.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he is not sick, and he does not perceive himself as sick, and he lights a fire to warm himself, or has one lit, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is not sick, but he is unsure of it, and he lights a fire to warm himself, or has one lit, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is not sick, but he perceives himself as sick, and he lights a fire to warm himself, or has one lit, except if there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he puts back a burning piece of wood that has fallen off, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is sick, but he does not perceive himself as sick, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is sick, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is sick, and he perceives himself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he is sick;<br><br>if he warms himself over a fire lit by another;<br><br>if he warms himself over flameless coals;<br><br>if he lights a lamp, a small fire, or a sauna, when there is a suitable reason;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on fire, the sixth, is finished. Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_138.mp3]	387	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove,<br><br>the monks were bathing in the hot springs.<br><br>Just then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha went to the hot springs, intending to wash his hair.<br><br>He waited respectfully for the monks to finish, but they kept on bathing until dark.<br><br>Only then was King Bimbisāra able to wash his hair. And because the town gates had been shut, he had to spend the night outside the city.<br><br>In the morning, with his make-up still on, he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>The Buddha said to him, “Great king, why have you come so early in the morning, with your make-up still on?”<br><br>The king told him what had happened.<br><br>The Buddha then instructed, inspired, and gladdened him with a teaching, after which the king got up from his seat, bowed down, circumambulated the Buddha with his right side toward him, and left.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that monks bathed without moderation, even after seeing the king?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How could those foolish men act in this way?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk bathes at intervals of less than a half-month, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards, because they were afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not bathe when it was hot or when they had a fever, and they went to sleep covered in sweat.<br><br>As a consequence, their robes and beds got dirty.<br><br>They told the Buddha. Because of that we’re not comfortable.”<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick monk to bathe at intervals of less than a half-month.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk bathes at intervals of less than a half-month, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>These are the appropriate occasions: it is the two-and-a-half-month period of summer and the fever season, comprising the last one-and-a-half months of summer and the first month of the rainy season; he is sick.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards the monks were doing building work, but because they were afraid of wrongdoing they did not bathe.<br><br>As a consequence, they went to sleep covered in sweat, and their robes and beds got dirty.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to bathe at intervals of less than a half-month when you’re working.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk bathes at intervals of less than a half-month, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>These are the appropriate occasions: it is the two-and-a-half-month period of summer and the fever season, comprising the last one-and-a-half months of summer and the first month of the rainy season; he is sick; he is working.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards the monks were traveling, but because they were afraid of wrongdoing they did not bathe.<br><br>As a consequence, they went to sleep covered in sweat, and their robes and beds got dirty.<br><br>They told the Buddha. …<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to bathe at intervals of less than a half-month when you’re traveling.<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk bathes at intervals of less than a half-month, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>These are the appropriate occasions: it is the two-and-a-half-month period of summer and the fever season, comprising the last one-and-a-half months of summer and the first month of the rainy season; There is no offense:<br><br>if it is an appropriate occasion;<br><br>if he bathes at intervals of a half-month;<br><br>if he bathes at intervals of more than a half-month;<br><br>if he bathes while crossing a body of water;<br><br>if he is outside the central Ganges plain;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on bathing, the seventh is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_138.mp3]	{-bathing} Should any bhikkhunī bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except at the proper occasions, it is to be confessed. Here the proper occasions are these: the last month and a half of the hot season, the first month of the rains, these two and a half months being a time of heat, a time of fever; (also) a time of illness; a time of work; a time of going on a journey; a time of wind or rain. These are the proper times here. [57]
