Matches Bu PC 58	Uses 'bhikkhuniyā' and 'bhikkhunī', cīvaralābhāya	When a nun gets a new robe, she should apply one of three kinds of stains: blue-green, mud color, or dark brown. If<br>a nun uses a new robe without applying any of the three kinds of stains, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_139.mp3]	390	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a number of monks and wanderers were robbed while traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.<br><br>The king’s men set out from Sāvatthī and caught the thieves and their loot. They then sent a message to the monks:<br><br>“Venerables, please come and pick out your own robes.”<br><br>But the monks did not recognize them.<br><br>The people complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can they not recognize their own robes?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and they told the Buddha.<br><br>He had the Sangha gathered, gave a teaching on what is right and proper, and then addressed the monks:<br><br>“Well then, monks, I will lay down a training rule for the following ten reasons:<br><br>for the well-being of the Sangha, for the comfort of the Sangha, for the restraint of bad people, for the ease of good monks, for the restraint of the corruptions relating to the present life, for the restraint of the corruptions relating to future lives, to give rise to confidence in those without it, to increase the confidence of those who have it,<br><br>for the longevity of the true Teaching, and for supporting the training.<br><br>And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>New:<br><br>a mark has not been made is what is meant.<br><br>A robe:<br><br>one of the six kinds of robes.<br><br>He should apply one of three kinds of stains:<br><br>even if he just applies what fits on the tip of a blade of grass.<br><br>Blue-green:<br><br>there are two kinds of blue-green: the color of copper sulfate and the color of leaves.<br><br>Mud-color:<br><br>watery is what is meant.<br><br>Dark brown:<br><br>whatever is dark brownish.<br><br>If a monk … without applying any of the three kinds of stains:<br><br>if he uses a new robe without first applying one of the three kinds of stains, even just the amount on the tip of a blade of grass, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it has not been applied, and he perceives that it has not, and he uses the robe, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it has not been applied, but he is unsure of it, and he uses the robe, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it has not been applied, but he perceives that it has, and he uses the robe, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it has been applied, but he perceives that it has not, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it has been applied, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it has been applied, and he perceives that it has, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he applies the stain and then uses it;<br><br>if the mark has disappeared;<br><br>if the area where the mark was applied is worn;<br><br>if what had been marked is sewn together with what has not been marked;<br><br>if it is a patch;<br><br>if it is a lengthwise border;<br><br>if it is a crosswise border;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on making stains, the eighth, is finished. Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_140.mp3]	391	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Upananda the Sakyan assigned the ownership of a robe to a monk who was his brother’s student. presence of and assignment in the absence of.<br><br>Assignment in the presence of:<br><br>one should say, “I assign this robe-cloth to you,” or “I assign this robe-cloth to so-and-so.”<br><br>Assignment in the absence of:<br><br>one should say, “I give this robe-cloth to you for the purpose of assigning it.”<br><br>The other should ask, “Who is your friend or There is no offense:<br><br>if the other person gives it or he uses it after taking the other person’s property on trust;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on assigning ownership to another, the ninth, is finished. He cut off their heads and then set them out in a row impaled on stakes.<br><br>The monks asked him,<br><br>“Who killed these crows?”<br><br>“I did.<br><br>I don’t like crows.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How can Venerable Udāyī intentionally kill living beings?” …<br><br>“Is it true, Udāyī, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Intentionally:<br><br>knowing, perceiving, having intended, having decided, he transgresses.<br><br>A living being:<br><br>an animal is what is meant.<br><br>Kills:<br><br>if he cuts off and makes an end of the life faculty, if he destroys its continuity, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a living being, and he perceives it as such, and he kills it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a living being, but he is unsure of it, and he kills it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a living being, but he does not perceive it as such, and he kills it, there is no offense.<br><br>If it is not a living being, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a living being, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a living being, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is unintentional;<br><br>if he is not mindful;<br><br>if he does not know;<br><br>if he is not aiming at death;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on intentionally, the first, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā udāyī issāso hoti, kākā cassa amanāpā honti.<br><br>So kāke vijjhitvā vijjhitvā sīsaṁ chinditvā sūle paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapesi.<br><br>Bhikkhū evamāhaṁsu—<br><br>“kenime, āvuso, kākā jīvitā voropitā”ti?<br><br>“Mayā, āvuso.<br><br>Amanāpā me kākā”ti.<br><br>Ye te bhikkhū appicchā …pe… te ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma āyasmā udāyī sañcicca pāṇaṁ jīvitā voropessatī”ti …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira tvaṁ, udāyi, sañcicca pāṇaṁ jīvitā voropesī”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma tvaṁ, moghapurisa, sañcicca pāṇaṁ jīvitā voropessasi.<br><br>Netaṁ, moghapurisa, appasannānaṁ vā pasādāya …pe…<br><br>evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṁ sikkhāpadaṁ uddiseyyātha—	Yo panāti<br><br>yo yādiso …pe…<br><br>bhikkhūti<br><br>…pe… ayaṁ imasmiṁ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti.<br><br>Sañciccāti<br><br>jānanto sañjānanto cecca abhivitaritvā vītikkamo.<br><br>Pāṇo nāma<br><br>tiracchānagatapāṇo vuccati.<br><br>Jīvitā voropeyyāti<br><br>jīvitindriyaṁ upacchindati uparodheti santatiṁ vikopeti, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Pāṇe pāṇasaññī jīvitā voropeti, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Pāṇe vematiko jīvitā voropeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Pāṇe appāṇasaññī jīvitā voropeti, anāpatti.<br><br>Appāṇe pāṇasaññī, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Appāṇe vematiko, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Appāṇe appāṇasaññī, anāpatti.	Anāpatti—<br><br>asañcicca,<br><br>assatiyā,<br><br>ajānantassa,<br><br>namaraṇādhippāyassa,<br><br>ummattakassa,<br><br>ādikammikassāti.<br><br>Sañciccasikkhāpadaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ paṭhamaṁ.	[sound:ABi_PC_142.mp3]	{-intentionally} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly deprive a living being of life, it is to be confessed. [61]

Matches Bu PC 63	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun reopens a legal issue that she knows has been legitimately settled, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_144.mp3]	395	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the monks from the group of six were reopening a legal issue that they knew had been legitimately settled, saying,<br><br>“The legal procedure hasn’t been done;” “It’s been done badly;” “It should be done again;” “It hasn’t been settled;” “It’s been badly settled;” “It should be settled again.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six reopen a legal issue that they know has been legitimately settled?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you’re doing this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>He knows:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him or the Sangha has told him.<br><br>Legitimately:<br><br>done according to the Teaching, according to the Monastic Law, according to the Teacher’s instruction—this is called “legitimately”.<br><br>A legal issue:<br><br>there are four kinds of legal issues: legal issues arising from disputes, legal issues arising from accusations, legal issues arising from offenses, legal issues arising from business.<br><br>Reopens:<br><br>if he reopens it, saying, “The legal procedure hasn’t been done;” “It’s been done badly;” “It should be done again;” “It hasn’t been settled;” “It’s been badly settled;” “It should be settled again,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, and he reopens it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he reopens it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he reopens it, there is no offense.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he reopens it because he knows that the legal procedure was illegitimate, done by an incomplete assembly, or done against one who did not deserve it;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on reopening, the third, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū jānaṁ yathādhammaṁ nihatādhikaraṇaṁ punakammāya ukkoṭenti—<br><br>“akataṁ kammaṁ dukkaṭaṁ kammaṁ puna kātabbaṁ kammaṁ anihataṁ dunnihataṁ puna nihanitabban”ti.<br><br>Ye te bhikkhū appicchā …pe… te ujjhāyanti khiyyanti vipācenti—<br><br>“kathañhi nāma chabbaggiyā bhikkhū jānaṁ yathādhammaṁ nihatādhikaraṇaṁ punakammāya ukkoṭessantī”ti …pe…<br><br>“saccaṁ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, jānaṁ yathādhammaṁ nihatādhikaraṇaṁ punakammāya ukkoṭethā”ti?<br><br>“Saccaṁ, bhagavā”ti.<br><br>Vigarahi buddho bhagavā …pe…<br><br>kathañhi nāma tumhe, moghapurisā, jānaṁ yathādhammaṁ nihatādhikaraṇaṁ punakammāya ukkoṭessatha.<br><br>Netaṁ, moghapurisā, appasannānaṁ vā pasādāya …pe…<br><br>evañca pana, bhikkhave, imaṁ sikkhāpadaṁ uddiseyyātha—	Yo panāti<br><br>yo yādiso …pe…<br><br>bhikkhūti<br><br>…pe… ayaṁ imasmiṁ atthe adhippeto bhikkhūti.<br><br>Jānāti nāma<br><br>sāmaṁ vā jānāti, aññe vā tassa ārocenti, so vā āroceti.<br><br>Yathādhammaṁ nāma<br><br>dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena kataṁ, etaṁ yathādhammaṁ nāma.<br><br>Adhikaraṇaṁ nāma<br><br>cattāri adhikaraṇāni— vivādādhikaraṇaṁ, anuvādādhikaraṇaṁ, āpattādhikaraṇaṁ, kiccādhikaraṇaṁ.<br><br>Punakammāya ukkoṭeyyāti<br><br>“akataṁ kammaṁ dukkaṭaṁ kammaṁ punakātabbaṁ kammaṁ anihataṁ dunnihataṁ puna nihanitabban”ti ukkoṭeti, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Dhammakamme dhammakammasaññī ukkoṭeti, āpatti pācittiyassa.<br><br>Dhammakamme vematiko ukkoṭeti, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Dhammakamme adhammakammasaññī ukkoṭeti, anāpatti.<br><br>Adhammakamme dhammakammasaññī, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Adhammakamme vematiko, āpatti dukkaṭassa.<br><br>Adhammakamme adhammakammasaññī, anāpatti.	Anāpatti—<br><br>“adhammena vā vaggena vā na kammārahassa vā kammaṁ katan”ti jānanto ukkoṭeti,<br><br>ummattakassa,<br><br>ādikammikassāti.<br><br>Ukkoṭanasikkhāpadaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ tatiyaṁ.	[sound:ABi_PC_144.mp3]	{-agitating} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly agitate for the reviving of an issue that has been rightfully dealt with, it is to be confessed. [63]	
Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::14 Joti Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 145	Theyyasatthasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī jānaṁ theyyasatthena saddhiṁ saṁvidhāya ekaddhānamaggaṁ paṭipajjeyya antamaso gāmantarampi, pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 66	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun knowingly travels by arrangement with a group of thieves, even just to the next inhabited area, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_145.mp3]	396	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a certain group of travelers was about to go south from Rājagaha.<br><br>A monk said to those people,<br><br>“Let me travel with you.”<br><br>“But we’re smuggling goods.”<br><br>“That’s your business.”<br><br>The customs officers heard<br><br>about that group of travelers.<br><br>They then blocked the road,<br><br>caught the group, confiscated the goods, and asked that monk,<br><br>“Venerable, why are you knowingly traveling with a group of thieves?”<br><br>And they detained him.<br><br>After being released, that monk went to Sāvatthī, where he told the monks what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How could a monk knowingly travel by arrangement with a group of thieves?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monk, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Knowingly:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him or the group of travelers has told him.<br><br>A group of thieves:<br><br>thieves who have done their deed or thieves who have not. They are stealing from the king or smuggling.<br><br>With:<br><br>together.<br><br>By arrangement:<br><br>if he makes an arrangement like this: the monk says, “Let’s go,” and they reply, “Yes, let’s go, venerable;” or they say, “Let’s go, venerable,” and the monk replies, “Yes, let’s go;” or the monk says, “Let’s go today,” “Let’s go tomorrow,” or “Let’s go the day after tomorrow,” then he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Even just to the next inhabited area:<br><br>when the inhabited areas are a chicken’s flight apart, then for every next inhabited area he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>When it is an uninhabited area, a wilderness, then for every six kilometers he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a group of traveling thieves, and he perceives it as such, and he travels by arrangement with them, even just to the next inhabited area, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a group of traveling thieves, but he is unsure of it, and he travels by arrangement with them, even just to the next inhabited area, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a group of traveling thieves, but he does not perceive it as such, and he travels by arrangement with them, even just to the next inhabited area, there is no offense.<br><br>If the monk makes an arrangement, but the group does not express its agreement, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a group of traveling thieves, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a group of traveling thieves, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not a group of traveling thieves, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he goes, but not by arrangement;<br><br>if the group has made an arrangement, but he has not expressed his agreement;<br><br>if he goes, but not according to the arrangement;<br><br>if there is an emergency;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on a group of traveling thieves, the sixth, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_145.mp3]	{-caravan of thieves} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly and by arrangement travel together with a caravan of thieves, even for the interval between one village and the next, it is to be confessed. Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_146.mp3]	402	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the monk Ariṭṭha, an ex-vulture-killer, had the following bad and erroneous view:<br><br>“As I understand the Teaching of the Buddha, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>A number of monks heard<br><br>that Ariṭṭha had that view.<br><br>They went to him and asked,<br><br>“Is it true, Ariṭṭha,<br><br>that you have such a view?”<br><br>“Yes, indeed. As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>“No, Ariṭṭha, don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for it’s not good to misrepresent him. The Buddha would never say such a thing.<br><br>The Buddha has given many discourses about the obstacles being obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them.<br><br>The Buddha has said that the enjoyment provided by worldly pleasures is small, whereas the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.<br><br>The Buddha has said that worldly pleasures are similar to a skeleton …<br><br>similar to a piece of meat …<br><br>similar to a grass torch …<br><br>similar to a pit of coals …<br><br>similar to a dream …<br><br>similar to borrowed goods …<br><br>similar to fruits on a tree …<br><br>similar to a knife and chopping block …<br><br>similar to swords and stakes …<br><br>similar to a snake’s head; the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.”<br><br>But even though the monks corrected Ariṭṭha like this, he stubbornly held on to that bad and erroneous view, and continued to insist on it.<br><br>Since they were unable to make him give up that view, they went to the Buddha and told him what had happened.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and questioned Ariṭṭha:<br><br>“Is it true, Ariṭṭha, that you have such a view?”<br><br>“Yes indeed, sir.”<br><br>“Foolish man, who do you think I have taught like this?<br><br>Haven’t I given many discourses about the obstacles being obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them?<br><br>I have said that the enjoyment provided by worldly pleasures is small, whereas the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.<br><br>I have said that worldly pleasures are similar to a skeleton …<br><br>similar to a piece of meat …<br><br>similar to a grass torch …<br><br>similar to a pit of coals …<br><br>similar to a dream …<br><br>similar to borrowed goods …<br><br>similar to fruits on a tree …<br><br>similar to a knife and chopping block …<br><br>similar to swords and stakes …<br><br>similar to a snake’s head; the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.<br><br>And yet, foolish man, by misunderstanding you have misrepresented me, hurt yourself, and made much demerit.<br><br>This will be for your long-lasting harm and suffering.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Says:<br><br>“As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>Him:<br><br>the monk who speaks in that way.<br><br>The monks:<br><br>other monks, those who see it or hear about it. [sound:ABi_PC_146.mp3]	{-“Ariṭṭha”} Should any bhikkhunī say the following: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions,” the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Do not say that, Venerable. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that. In many ways, Venerable, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.” And should the bhikkhunī, thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs are to rebuke her up to three times so as to desist. If while being rebuked up to three times she desists, that is good. If she does not desist, it is to be confessed. [68]<br><br>Part Fourteen: The Fire Chapter

If a nun who is not sick lights a fire to warm herself, or has one lit, except if there is a suitable reason, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>138. If a nun bathes at intervals of less than a half-month, except on an appropriate occasion, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br>These are the appropriate occasions: it is the two-and-a-half-month period of summer and the fever season, comprising the last one-and-a-half months of summer and the first month of the rainy season; she is sick; she is working; she is traveling; there is wind and rain.<br><br>139. When a nun gets a new robe, she should apply one of three kinds of stains: blue-green, mud color, or dark brown. If<br>a nun uses a new robe without applying any of the three kinds of stains, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>140. If a nun herself assigns the ownership of a robe to a monk, a nun, a trainee nun, a novice monk, or a novice nun, and she then uses it without the other first relinquishing it, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>141. If a nun hides a nun’s bowl, robe, sitting mat, needle case, or belt, or she has it hidden, even just for a laugh, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>142. If a nun intentionally kills a living being, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>143. If a nun uses water that she knows contains living beings, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>144. If a nun reopens a legal issue that she knows has been legitimately settled, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>145. If a nun knowingly travels by arrangement with a group of thieves, even just to the next inhabited area, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>146. If a nun says,<br>‘As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them,’<br>then the nuns should correct her like this:<br>‘No, venerable, don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for it’s not good to misrepresent the Buddha. The Buddha would never say such a thing.<br>In many discourses the Buddha has declared the obstacles to be obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them.’<br>If that nun continues as before, the nuns should press her up to three times to make her give up that view.<br>If she then gives it up, all is well.<br>If she does not, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>The fourteenth subchapter on fire.	Pācittiyā	Jotivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_137-146.mp3]	403							[sound:ABi_PC_137-146.mp3]	137. {-fires} Should any bhikkhunī who is not ill, seeking to warm herself, kindle a fire or have one kindled—unless there is a suitable reason—it is to be confessed. [56]<br><br>138. {-bathing} Should any bhikkhunī bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except at the proper occasions, it is to be confessed. Here the proper occasions are these: the last month and a half of the hot season, the first month of the rains, these two and a half months being a time of heat, a time of fever; (also) a time of illness; a time of work; a time of going on a journey; a time of wind or rain. These are the proper times here. [57]<br><br>139. {-discoloring} When a bhikkhunī receives a new robe, any one of three means of discoloring it is to be applied: blue (green), brown, or black. If a bhikkhunī should make use of a new robe without applying any of the three means of discoloring it, it is to be confessed. [58]<br><br>140. {-shared ownership} Should any bhikkhunī, herself having placed robe-cloth under shared ownership (vikappana) with a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, then make use of the robe-cloth without the shared ownership being rescinded, it is to be confessed. [59]<br><br>141. {-hiding} Should any bhikkhunī hide (another) bhikkhunī’s bowl, robe, sitting cloth, needle case, or belt —or have it hidden—even as a joke, it is to be confessed. [60]<br><br>142. {-intentionally} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly deprive a living being of life, it is to be confessed. [61]<br><br>143. {-containing living beings} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly make use of water with living beings in it, it is to be confessed. [62]<br><br>144. {-agitating} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly agitate for the reviving of an issue that has been rightfully dealt with, it is to be confessed. [63]<br><br>145. {-caravan of thieves} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly and by arrangement travel together with a caravan of thieves, even for the interval between one village and the next, it is to be confessed. If a nun lives, does formal meetings, or shares a sleeping place with a nun who she knows is saying such things, who has not made amends according to the rule, and who has not given up that view, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_147.mp3]	404	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the monks from the group of six lived with the monk Ariṭṭha, and they did formal meetings and shared a sleeping place with him. Yet they knew that he was saying such things, that he had not made amends according to the rule, and that he had not given up that view.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six live, do formal meetings, and share a sleeping place with the monk Ariṭṭha, even though they know that he’s saying such things, that he hasn’t made amends according to the rule, and that he hasn’t given up that view?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>He knows:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him or the offender has told him.<br><br>Who is saying such things:<br><br>one who says this: “As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>Who has not made amends according to the rule:<br><br>who has been ejected and not readmitted.<br><br>With a monk who has not given up that view:<br><br>with a monk who has not given up this view.<br><br>Lives with:<br><br>there are two types of living together: material living together and spiritual living together.<br><br>Material living together:<br><br>if he gives or receives material things, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Spiritual living together:<br><br>he recites or has the other recite. If he recites or has the other recite by the line, then for every line he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he recites or has the other recite by the syllable, then for every syllable he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Does formal meetings with:<br><br>if he does the observance-day ceremony, the invitation ceremony, or a legal procedure with one who has been ejected, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Shares a sleeping place with:<br><br>under the same ceiling: if the monk lies down when the one who has been ejected is already lying down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if the monk is already lying down when the one who has been ejected lies down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if they both lie down together, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>every time they get up and then lie down again, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other monk has been ejected, and he perceives him as such, and he lives or does formal meetings or shares a sleeping place with him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the other monk has been ejected, but he is unsure of it, and he lives or does formal meetings or shares a sleeping place with him, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other monk has been ejected, but he does not perceive him as such, and he lives or does formal meetings or shares a sleeping place with him, there is no offense.<br><br>If the other monk has not been ejected, but he perceives him as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other monk has not been ejected, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other monk has not been ejected, and he does not perceive him as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he knows that he has not been ejected;<br><br>if he knows that he has been readmitted after being ejected;<br><br>if he knows that he has given up that view;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on living with one who has been ejected, the ninth, is finished. Also if a novice nun says,<br>‘As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them,’<br>then the nuns should correct her like this:<br>‘No, don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for it’s not good to misrepresent the Buddha. Away with you!’<br>If a nun befriends that novice nun, or she is attended on by her, lives with her, or shares a sleeping place with her, even though she knows that she has been expelled in this way, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_148.mp3]	411	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the novice monastic Kaṇṭaka had the following bad and erroneous view:<br><br>“As I understand the teachings of the Buddha, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>A number of monks heard that the novice monastic Kaṇṭaka had that view.<br><br>They went to see him and asked,<br><br>“Is it true, Kaṇṭaka, that you have such a view?”<br><br>“Yes, indeed. As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>“No, Kaṇṭaka, don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for it’s not good to misrepresent him. The Buddha would never say such a thing.<br><br>The Buddha has given many discourses about the obstacles being obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them.<br><br>The Buddha has said that the enjoyment provided by worldly pleasures is small, whereas the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater. …”<br><br>But even though the monks corrected Kaṇṭaka like this, he stubbornly held on to that bad and erroneous view, and he continued to insist on it.<br><br>Since those monks were unable to make him give up that view, they went to the Buddha and told him what had happened.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and questioned the Kaṇṭaka:<br><br>“Is it true, Kaṇṭaka, that you have such a view?”<br><br>“Yes indeed, venerable sir.”<br><br>“Foolish man, who do you think I have taught like this?<br><br>Haven’t I given many discourses about the obstacles being obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them?<br><br>I have said that the enjoyment provided by worldly pleasures is small, whereas the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.<br><br>I have said that worldly pleasures are similar to a skeleton …<br><br>similar to a snake’s head; the suffering and trouble with them are huge, and so their drawbacks are greater.<br><br>And yet, foolish man, by misunderstanding you have misrepresented me, hurt yourself, and made much demerit.<br><br>This will be for your long-lasting harm and suffering.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence,<br><br>and cause some to lose it.”<br><br>Having rebuked him …<br><br>the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Well then, monks, the Sangha should expel the novice monastic Kaṇṭaka.<br><br>And this is how he should be expelled:<br><br>‘From today, Kaṇṭaka, you may not refer to the Buddha as your teacher.<br><br>And, unlike other novices, you can no longer share a sleeping place with the monks for two or three nights.<br><br>Go! Away with you!’”<br><br>The Sangha then expelled Kaṇṭaka.<br><br>Soon afterwards the monks from the group of six befriended Kaṇṭaka, and they were attended on by him, lived with him, and shared a sleeping place with him. Yet they knew that he had been expelled.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six befriend Kaṇṭaka, and be attended on by him, live with him, and share a sleeping place with him, even though they know that he has been expelled?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A novice monastic:<br><br>a novice monk is what is meant.<br><br>Says:<br><br>“As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them.”<br><br>Him:<br><br>the novice monastic who speaks in that way.<br><br>The monks:<br><br>other monks, those who see it or hear about it. Away with you!”<br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>He knows:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him or the offending novice monastic has told him.<br><br>Expelled in this way:<br><br>expelled like this.<br><br>Novice monastic:<br><br>novice monk is what is meant.<br><br>Befriends:<br><br>if he befriends him, saying, “I’ll give him a bowl,” “I’ll give him a robe,” “I’ll recite to him,” or “I’ll test him,” he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Is attended on by:<br><br>if he accepts bath powder, soap, a tooth cleaner, or water for rinsing the mouth from him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Lives with:<br><br>there are two types of living together:<br><br>material living together and spiritual living together.<br><br>Material living together:<br><br>if he gives or receives material things, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Spiritual living together:<br><br>he recites or has the other recite. If he recites or has the other recite by the line, then for every line he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he recites or has the other recite by the syllable, then for every syllable he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Shares a sleeping place with:<br><br>under the same ceiling: if the monk lies down when the expelled novice monastic is already lying down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if the monk is already lying down when the expelled novice monastic lies down, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>if they both lie down together, he commits an offense entailing confession;<br><br>every time they get up and then lie down again, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the novice monastic has been expelled, and he perceives him as such, and he befriends him or is attended on by him or lives with him or shares a sleeping place with him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If the novice monastic has been expelled, but he is unsure of it, and he befriends him or is attended on by him or lives with him or shares a sleeping place with him, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the novice monastic has been expelled, but he does not perceive him as such, and he befriends him or is attended on by him or lives with him or shares a sleeping place with him, there is no offense.<br><br>If the novice monastic has not been expelled, but he perceives him such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the novice monastic has not been expelled, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the novice monastic has not been expelled, and he does not perceive him as such, there is no offense. [sound:ABi_PC_148.mp3]	{-“Kaṇṭaka”} And if a female novice should say the following: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions,” the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Do not say that, Venerable Novice. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that. In many ways, Venerable, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.” And should that female novice, thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs should admonish her as follows: “From this day forth, Venerable Novice, you are not to claim the Blessed One as your teacher, nor are you even to have the opportunity the other female novices get—that of sharing lodgings two or three nights with the bhikkhunīs. Away with you! Out of our sight!” Should any bhikkhunī knowingly support, receive services from, consort with, or lie down in the same lodging with a novice thus expelled, it is to be confessed. When the Monastic Code is being recited, if a nun says, ‘What’s the point of reciting these minor training rules, when they just lead to anxiety, oppression, and annoyance?’ then in disparaging the training rules, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_150.mp3]	418	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the Buddha gave many talks about the Monastic Law, spoke in praise of the Monastic Law and of learning the Monastic Law, and repeatedly praised Venerable Upāli.<br><br>When the monks heard this, they thought,<br><br>“Well then, let’s learn the Monastic Law from Venerable Upāli.” And many monks, both senior and junior, as well as those of middle standing, learned the Monastic Law from Upāli.<br><br>The monks from the group of six<br><br>considered this and thought,<br><br>“If these monks become well-versed in the Monastic Law, they’ll boss us around as they like.<br><br>So let’s disparage the Monastic Law.”<br><br>They went to the other monks and said,<br><br>“What’s the point of reciting these minor training rules, when they just lead to anxiety, oppression, and annoyance?”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six disparage the Monastic Law?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>When the Monastic Code is being recited:<br><br>when reciting it, when having it recited, or when practicing it.<br><br>Says:<br><br>“What’s the point of reciting these minor training rules, when they just lead to anxiety, oppression, and annoyance?”<br><br>If he disparages the Monastic Law to one who is fully ordained, saying, “Those who learn this will be anxious,” “They will feel oppressed,” “They will be annoyed;” “Those who don’t learn this won’t be anxious,” “They won’t feel oppressed,” “They won’t be annoyed;” “It’s better left unrecited,” “It’s better left unlearned,” “It’s better left unstudied,” “It’s better left unmastered;” “May the Monastic Law disappear, or may these monks remain ignorant,” then he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he disparages the Monastic Law to one who is fully ordained, and he perceives them as fully ordained, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he disparages the Monastic Law to one who is fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he disparages the Monastic Law to one who is fully ordained, but he does not perceive them as fully ordained, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he disparages some other rule, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he disparages the Monastic Law or some other rule to one who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is to one who is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is to one who is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is to one who is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if, not desiring to disparage, he says, “Listen, learn discourses or verses or philosophy, and later you can learn the Monastic Law;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on annoyance, the second, is finished. Matches Bu PC 73	Uses 'bhikkhunī', 'ayye', 'bhikkhuniṁ aññā bhikkhuniyo', 'imāya bhikkhuniyā',&nbsp;bhiyyo not bhiyyoti, 'tassā bhikkhuniyā', 'āpannā', 'uttari ca assā', not uttariñcassa,&nbsp;aṭṭhiṁ katvā not aṭṭhikatvā.&nbsp;	During the half-monthly recitation of the Monastic Code, a nun might say,<br>‘Just now did I find out that this rule too has come down in the Monastic Code, is included in the Monastic Code, and comes up for recitation every half-month.’<br>If other nuns know that that nun has previously sat through at least two or three recitations of the Monastic Code, then that nun<br>is not let off because of ignorance, and she is to be dealt with according to the rule. Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_151.mp3]	425	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were misbehaving. They said to each other, “Let’s make the other monks think that we committed these offenses because we didn’t know the rules.” Then, during the recitation of the Monastic Code, they said,<br><br>“Only now did we find out that this rule too is included in the Monastic Code and comes up for recitation every half-month.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six say this during the recitation of the Monastic Code?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you said this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you say this during the recitation of the Monastic Code?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Half-monthly:<br><br>on every observance day.<br><br>During the recitation of the Monastic Code:<br><br>during the reciting.<br><br>Might say:<br><br>after misbehaving, he thinks,<br><br>“Let them think that I committed these offenses because I didn’t know the rules.” If, during the recitation of the Monastic Code, he then says,<br><br>“Only now did I find out that this rule too has come down in the Monastic Code, is included in the Monastic Code, and comes up for recitation every half-month,” then he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If other monks know that the monk who wants to deceive has previously sat through at least two or three recitations of the Monastic Code, then that monk is not let off because of ignorance, and he is to be dealt with according to the rule. Further, he should be charged with deception.<br><br>“And, monks, he is to be charged like this.<br><br>A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>Monk so-and-so did not pay proper attention during the recitation of the Monastic Code.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should charge him with deception.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>Monk so-and-so did not pay proper attention during the recitation of the Monastic Code.<br><br>The Sangha charges him with deception.<br><br>Any monk who approves of charging him with deception should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t approve should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has charged monk so-and-so with deception.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>If he deceives, but he has not been charged with deception, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he deceives, and he has been charged with deception, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as legitimate, and he deceives, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he deceives, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he deceives, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he has not heard it in full;<br><br>if he has heard it fewer than two or three times in full;<br><br>if he does not want to deceive;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on deception, the third, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_151.mp3]	{-deception} Should any bhikkhunī, when the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, say: “Just now have I heard that this case, too, is handed down in the Pātimokkha, is included in the Pātimokkha, and comes up for recitation every half-month”; and if other bhikkhunīs should know: “That bhikkhunī has already sat through two or three recitations of the Pātimokkha, if not more,” the bhikkhunī is not exempted for being ignorant. Whatever the offence she has committed, she is to be dealt with in accordance with the rule; and in addition, her deception is to be exposed: “It is no gain for you, Venerable, it is ill-done, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not pay proper attention and take it to heart.” Here the deception is to be confessed. [73]

Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_155.mp3]	429	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six intentionally made the monks from the group of seventeen anxious. Pācittiyā	Diṭṭhivaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_156.mp3]	432	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were arguing with the good …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>On monks:<br><br>on other monks.<br><br>Who are arguing and disputing:<br><br>who are engaged in a legal issue.<br><br>Eavesdrops:<br><br>if he is on his way to eavesdrop, thinking, “After hearing what they say, I’ll accuse them,” “… I’ll remind them,” “… I’ll counter accuse them,” “… I’ll counter remind them,” “… I’ll humiliate them,” he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Wherever he stands to listen, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is walking behind someone, and he speeds up with the intention to eavesdrop, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Wherever he stands to listen, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he is walking in front of someone, and he slows down with the intention to eavesdrop, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>Wherever he stands to eavesdrop, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he goes to where a monk who is speaking privately is standing, sitting, or lying down, he should clear his throat or make his presence known. If he does not clear his throat or make his presence known, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>He does so only for this reason and no other:<br><br>there is no other reason for eavesdropping.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is one who is fully ordained, and he perceives him as such, and he eavesdrops on him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is one who is fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, and he eavesdrops on him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is one who is fully ordained, but he does not perceive him as such, and he eavesdrops on him, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he eavesdrops on one who is not fully ordained, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is one who is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is one who is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is one who is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he goes, thinking, “After hearing what they say, I’ll hold back,” “… I’ll abstain,” “… I’ll resolve it,” “… I’ll free myself;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on eavesdropping, the eighth, is finished. If a nun lives, does formal meetings, or shares a sleeping place with a nun who she knows is saying such things, who has not made amends according to the rule, and who has not given up that view, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>148. Also if a novice nun says,<br>‘As I understand the Buddha’s Teaching, the things he calls obstacles are unable to obstruct one who indulges in them,’<br>then the nuns should correct her like this:<br>‘No, don’t misrepresent the Buddha, for it’s not good to misrepresent the Buddha. The Buddha would never say such a thing.<br>In many discourses the Buddha has declared the obstacles to be obstructive and how they obstruct one who indulges in them.’<br>If that novice nun continues as before, she should be told:<br>‘From today on you may not refer to the Buddha as your teacher.<br>And, unlike other novices, you can no longer share a sleeping place with the nuns for two or three nights.<br>Go! Away with you!’<br>If a nun befriends that novice nun, or she is attended on by her, lives with her, or shares a sleeping place with her, even though she knows that she has been expelled in this way, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>149. If a nun, when legitimately corrected by the nuns, says, ‘I won’t practice this training rule until I’ve questioned a nun who is an expert on the Monastic Law,’ she commits an offense entailing confession.<br>A nun who is training should understand, should question, should enquire. This is the proper procedure.<br><br>150. When the Monastic Code is being recited, if a nun says, ‘What’s the point of reciting these minor training rules, when they just lead to anxiety, oppression, and annoyance?’ then in disparaging the training rules, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>151. During the half-monthly recitation of the Monastic Code, a nun might say,<br>‘Just now did I find out that this rule too has come down in the Monastic Code, is included in the Monastic Code, and comes up for recitation every half-month.’<br>If other nuns know that that nun has previously sat through at least two or three recitations of the Monastic Code, then that nun<br>is not let off because of ignorance, and she is to be dealt with according to the rule. Further, she should be charged with deception:<br>‘It’s a loss for you that you don’t pay proper attention during the recitation of the Monastic Code.’<br>And for the act of deception, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>152. If a nun hits a nun in anger, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>153. If a nun raises a hand in anger against a nun, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>154. If a nun groundlessly charges a nun with an offense entailing suspension, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>155. If a nun intentionally makes a nun anxious, thinking, ‘In this way she will be ill at ease at least for a moment,’ and she does so only for this reason and no other, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>156. If a nun eavesdrops on nuns who are arguing and disputing, thinking, ‘I’ll hear what they say,’ and she does so only for this reason and no other, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>The fifteenth subchapter on view. [69]<br><br>148. {-“Kaṇṭaka”} And if a female novice should say the following: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions,” the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Do not say that, Venerable Novice. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that. In many ways, Venerable, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.” And should that female novice, thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs should admonish her as follows: “From this day forth, Venerable Novice, you are not to claim the Blessed One as your teacher, nor are you even to have the opportunity the other female novices get—that of sharing lodgings two or three nights with the bhikkhunīs. Away with you! Out of our sight!” Should any bhikkhunī knowingly support, receive services from, consort with, or lie down in the same lodging with a novice thus expelled, it is to be confessed. [70]<br><br>149. {-righteously} Should any bhikkhunī, admonished by the bhikkhunīs in accordance with a rule, say: “Venerables, I will not train myself under this training rule until I have put questions about it to another bhikkhunī, experienced and learned in the discipline,” it is to be confessed. Bhikkhunīs, (a training rule) is to be understood, is to be asked about, is to be pondered. This is the proper course here. [71]<br><br>150. {-confusion} Should any bhikkhunī, when the Pātimokkha is being repeated, say: “Why are these lesser and minor training rules repeated when they lead only to anxiety, bother, and confusion?” the criticism of the training rules is to be confessed. [72]<br><br>151. {-deception} Should any bhikkhunī, when the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, say: “Just now have I heard that this case, too, is handed down in the Pātimokkha, is included in the Pātimokkha, and comes up for recitation every half-month”; and if other bhikkhunīs should know: “That bhikkhunī has already sat through two or three recitations of the Pātimokkha, if not more,” the bhikkhunī is not exempted for being ignorant. Whatever the offence she has committed, she is to be dealt with in accordance with the rule; and in addition, her deception is to be exposed: “It is no gain for you, Venerable, it is ill-done, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not pay proper attention and take it to heart.” Here the deception is to be confessed. [73]<br><br>152. {-a blow} Should any bhikkhunī, angered and displeased, give a blow to a bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed. [74]<br><br>153. {-raised hand} Should any bhikkhunī, angered and displeased, raise her hand against a bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed. [75]<br><br>154. {-unfounded} Should any bhikkhunī charge a bhikkhunī with an unfounded saṅghādisesa (offence), it is to be confessed. [76]<br><br>155. {-deliberately} Should any bhikkhunī purposefully provoke anxiety in a bhikkhunī (thinking): “This way, even for just a moment, she will have no peace”—if doing it for just this reason and no other—it is to be confessed. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::16 Dhammika Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 157	Kammappaṭibāhanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī dhammikānaṁ kammānaṁ chandaṁ datvā pacchā khīyanadhammaṁ āpajjeyya, pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu PC 79	Uses 'bhikkhunī'. Uses 'khīyanadhammaṁ' instead of 'khiyyanadhammaṃ'.	If a nun gives her consent to legitimate legal procedures, and then criticizes them afterwards, she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Dhammikavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_157.mp3]	434	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were misbehaving, but when a legal procedure was being done against any one of them, they would object.<br><br>On one occasion the Sangha had gathered on some business.<br><br>The monks from the group of six were busy making robes and so they gave their consent to one among them.<br><br>When the monks saw that only one monk from the group of six had come, they did a legal procedure against him.<br><br>When he returned to the monks from the group of six,<br><br>they asked him,<br><br>“What did the Sangha do?”<br><br>“It did a legal procedure against me.”<br><br>“We didn’t give our consent for that.<br><br>If we had known that a procedure would be done against you, we wouldn’t have given our consent.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six give their consent to legitimate legal procedures and then criticize them afterwards?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>A legitimate legal procedure:<br><br>a legal procedure consisting of getting permission, a legal procedure consisting of one motion, a legal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement, a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements; done according to the Teaching, according to the Monastic Law, according to the Teacher’s instruction. This is called a “legitimate legal procedure”.<br><br>If he gives his consent, and then criticizes the procedure, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, and he criticizes it after giving his consent, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he criticizes it after giving his consent, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he criticizes it after giving his consent, there is no offense.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he criticizes it because he knows that the legal procedure was illegitimate, done by an incomplete assembly, or done against one who did not deserve it;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on obstructing a legal procedure, the ninth, is finished. Pācittiyā	Dhammikavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_158.mp3]	435	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the Sangha had gathered on some business.<br><br>The monks motion.<br><br>That monk from the group of six thought,<br><br>“This is just how they do legal procedures against us one by one, but against who will you do this one?” and without giving his consent, he got up from his seat and left.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“When the Sangha is in the middle of a discussion, how could that monk get up from his seat and leave without giving his consent?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monk, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>When the Sangha is in the middle of a discussion:<br><br>when the topic has been announced but the discussion has not yet been concluded, or when the motion has been put forward, or when the announcement is still under way.<br><br>Gets up from his seat and leaves without first giving his consent:<br><br>if he leaves, thinking, “How may this legal procedure be disturbed?” or “How may this legal procedure be done by an incomplete assembly?” or “How may this legal procedure not be done?” then he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he is in the process of going beyond arm’s reach of the gathering, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he has gone beyond arm’s reach, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, and he gets up from his seat and leaves without first giving his consent, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, and he gets up from his seat and leaves without first giving his consent, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is a legitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as illegitimate, and he gets up from his seat and leaves without first giving his consent, there is no offense.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he perceives it as legitimate, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is an illegitimate legal procedure, and he perceives it as such, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he leaves because he thinks there will be quarrels or disputes in the Sangha;<br><br>if he leaves because he thinks there will be a fracture or schism in the Sangha;<br><br>if he leaves because he thinks the legal procedure will be illegitimate, done by an incomplete assembly, or done against one who does not deserve it;<br><br>if he leaves because he is sick;<br><br>if he leaves because he has to take care of someone who is sick;<br><br>if he leaves because he needs to relieve himself;<br><br>if he leaves with the intention to return, and not because he wants to invalidate the legal procedure;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on leaving without giving consent, the tenth, is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::6.Pācittiyā::16 Dhammika Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI PC 161	Ratanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī ratanaṁ vā ratanasammataṁ vā aññatra ajjhārāmā vā ajjhāvasathā vā uggaṇheyya vā uggaṇhāpeyya vā, pācittiyaṁ. <br>Ratanaṁ vā pana bhikkhuniyā ratanasammataṁ vā ajjhārāme vā ajjhāvasathe vā uggahetvā vā uggahāpetvā vā nikkhipitabbaṁ, “yassa bhavissati, so harissatī”ti, ayaṁ tattha sāmīci.		Matches Bu PC 84	Uses 'bhikkhunī' and 'bhikkhuniyā'.	If a nun picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or she has it picked up, except within a monastery or inside a lodging, she commits an offense entailing confession.<br>If she picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or she has it picked up, within a monastery or inside a lodging, she should put it aside with the thought, ‘Whoever owns it will come and get it.’ This is the proper procedure.	Pācittiyā	Dhammikavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_161.mp3]	440	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a monk was bathing in the river Aciravatī, when a brahmin, too, came there to bathe. He deposited a bag with five hundred coins on the ground, bathed, forgot about the bag, and left.<br><br>The monk thought, “This is the bag belonging to that brahmin; it wouldn’t be nice if it got lost,” and he picked it up.<br><br>Soon the brahmin remembered. He hurried back and asked that monk, “Sir, did you see my bag?”<br><br>Saying, “I did indeed,” he gave it to him.<br><br>The brahmin thought, “How can I avoid giving a reward to this monk?”<br><br>And he said, “I didn’t have five hundred coins, I had a thousand!” And he seized hold of that monk.<br><br>After being released, that monk went to the monastery and told the monks what had happened.<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How could a monk pick up precious things?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monk, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or he has it picked up, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>Soon afterwards there was a celebration in Sāvatthī. People were going to the park all dressed up,<br><br>as did Visākhā Migāramātā.<br><br>As she was leaving her village, she thought, “What will I do when I get to the park? Why don’t I pay a visit to the Buddha!”<br><br>She then removed all her ornaments, bound them in a bundle with her upper robe, and gave it to her slave girl, saying, “Listen, look after this bundle.”<br><br>Visākhā then went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>And the Buddha instructed, inspired, and gladdened her with a teaching, after which she got up from her seat, bowed down, circumambulated him with her right side toward him, and left.<br><br>And the slave girl left too, forgetting the bundle.<br><br>The monks saw it and told the Buddha. “Well then, monks, pick it up and put it aside.”<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Within a monastery, monks, you should pick up precious things or what’s regarded as precious, or have it picked up, and then put it aside with the thought, ‘Whoever owns it will come and get it.’<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:<br><br>‘If a monk picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or he has it picked up, except within a monastery, he commits an offense entailing confession.’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the monks.<br><br>At that time the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had a whole village working for him in the country of Kāsi,<br><br>and he had told an apprentice there that if the monks arrive he should make them a meal.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of monks were wandering in the country of Kāsi, when they came to that village.<br><br>When that man saw them coming, he approached them, bowed, and said, “Venerables, please accept a meal from Anāthapiṇḍika tomorrow.”<br><br>The monks accepted by remaining silent.<br><br>The following morning, after having various kinds of fine foods prepared, he had the monks informed that it was time for the meal. He removed a ring from his finger and then offered the food to the monks, saying,<br><br>“Venerables, please leave after you’ve eaten. I have to go to work.” And he left, forgetting his ring.<br><br>The monks saw it and said, “If we just go, this ring will be lost,” and so they stayed right there.<br><br>When that man returned from work, he saw the monks and said to them, “Why are you still here?”<br><br>And the monks told him what had happened.<br><br>Those monks then went to Sāvatthī where they told the monks,<br><br>who in turn told the Buddha.<br><br>After giving a teaching, the Buddha addressed the monks:<br><br>“Within a monastery, monks, or inside a lodging, you should pick up precious things or what’s regarded as precious, or have it picked up, and then put it aside with the thought,<br><br>‘Whoever owns it will come and get it.’<br><br>And so, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Something precious:<br><br>a pearl, a gem, a beryl, mother-of-pearl, quartz, a coral, silver, gold, a ruby, a cat’s eye.<br><br>Something regarded as precious:<br><br>whatever people regard as valuable or useful—this is called “regarded as precious”.<br><br>Except within a monastery or inside a lodging:<br><br>apart from within a monastery or inside a lodging.<br><br>Within a monastery:<br><br>if the monastery is enclosed, then within the enclosure. If the monastery is unenclosed, then in the vicinity.<br><br>Inside a lodging:<br><br>if the lodging is enclosed, then within the enclosure. If the lodging is unenclosed, then in the vicinity.<br><br>Picks up:<br><br>if he takes hold of it himself, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>Has picked up:<br><br>if he gets someone else to take hold of it, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or he has it picked up, within a monastery or inside a lodging, he should put it aside:<br><br>after taking note of its appearance or distinguishing marks, he should put it aside, and then make an announcement: “Whoever has lost anything should come.”<br><br>If anyone comes, they should be told, “Please describe it.”<br><br>If they rightly describe its appearance or distinguishing marks, it should be given to them. If they do not, they should be told, “Keep looking.”<br><br>If that monk is leaving that monastery, he should first place that item into the hands of suitable monks there.<br><br>If there are no suitable monks, he should place it into the hands of suitable householders there.<br><br>This is the proper procedure:<br><br>this is the right method.	There is no offense:<br><br>if he picks up something precious or something regarded as precious, or he has it picked up, within a monastery or inside a lodging, and then puts it aside with the thought, “Whoever owns it will come and get it;”<br><br>if he takes something regarded as precious on trust or he borrows it or he perceives it as discarded;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on precious things, the second, is finished. [sound:ABi_PC_161.mp3]	{-valuables} Should any bhikkhunī pick up or have (someone) pick up a valuable or what is considered a valuable, except within a monastery or within a dwelling, it is to be confessed. But when a bhikkhunī has picked up or had (someone) pick up a valuable or what is considered a valuable (left) in a monastery or in a dwelling, she is to keep it, (thinking,) “Whoever it belongs to will (come and) fetch it.” This is the proper course here. Matches Bu PC 86	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun has a needle case made from bone, ivory, or horn, it is to be destroyed, and she commits an offense entailing confession.	Pācittiyā	Dhammikavaggo	[sound:Bi_PC_162.mp3]	441	At one time the Buddha was staying in the Sakyan country in the Banyan Tree Monastery at Kapilavatthu.<br><br>At that time an ivory-worker had invited the monks<br><br>who needed needle cases to ask for one.<br><br>And the monks asked for many needle cases.<br><br>Those who had small needle cases asked for large ones,<br><br>and those who had large needle cases asked for small ones.<br><br>The ivory-worker was so busy making needle cases for the monks that he was unable to make goods for sale. He could not make a living for himself, and his wives and children suffered.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics not have any sense of moderation and ask for many needle cases?<br><br>This ivory-worker is so busy making needle cases for them that he’s unable to make goods for sale. He can’t make a living for himself, and his wives and children are suffering.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can those monks not have a sense of moderation and ask for many needle cases?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that there are monks who do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can those foolish men do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Bone:<br><br>any kind of bone.<br><br>Ivory:<br><br>elephant tooth is what is meant.<br><br>Horn:<br><br>any kind of horn.<br><br>Has made:<br><br>if he makes one or has one made, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets it, it is to be destroyed, and he is then to confess an offense entailing confession.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he finishes what he began himself, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he has others finish what he began himself, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he finishes himself what was begun by others, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he has others finish what was begun by others, he commits an offense entailing confession.<br><br>If he makes one or has one made for the benefit of someone else, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he gets one that was made by someone else and then uses it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is a toggle;<br><br>if it is a fire kindler;<br><br>if it is a buckle;<br><br>if it is an ointment box;<br><br>if it is an ointment stick;<br><br>if it is an adz handle;<br><br>if it is a water wiper;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on needle cases, the fourth, is finished.
