[See Bhikkhus’ Saṅghādisesa 1]<br><br>6. {-standing close} Should any bhikkhunī, when a bhikkhu is eating, attend on him with water or a fan, it is to be confessed.<br><br>7. {-raw grain} Should any bhikkhunī, having asked for raw grain or having had it asked for, having roasted it or having had it roasted, having pounded it or having had it pounded, having cooked it or having had it cooked, then eat it, it is to be confessed.<br><br>8. {-1st about tossing excrement} Should any bhikkhunī toss or get someone else to toss excrement or urine or trash or leftovers over a wall or a fence, it is to be confessed.<br><br>9. {-2nd about tossing excrement} Should any bhikkhunī toss or get someone else to toss excrement or urine or trash or leftovers on living crops, it is to be confessed.<br><br>10. {-singing and dancing} Should any bhikkhunī go to see dancing or singing or instrument-playing, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.2.6]<br><br>Part One: The Garlic Chapter<br><br>11. {-dark of the night} Should any bhikkhunī stand or converse with a man, one on one, in the darkness of the night without a light, it is to be confessed.<br><br>12. {-a screened place} Should any bhikkhunī stand or converse with a man, one on one, in a concealed place, it is to be confessed.<br><br>13. {-talking together in an open place} Should any bhikkhunī stand or converse with a man, one on one, in the open air, it is to be confessed.<br><br>14. {-dismissing a companion} Should any bhikkhunī— along a road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads—stand or converse with a man one on one, or whisper in his ear, or dismiss the bhikkhunī who is her companion, it is to be confessed.<br><br>15. {-departing without permission} Should any bhikkhunī, having gone to family residences before the meal (before noon), having sat down on a seat, depart without taking the owner’s leave, it is to be confessed.<br><br>16. {-sitting down without permission} Should any bhikkhunī, having gone to family residences after the meal (between noon and sunset), sit or lie down on a seat without asking the owner’s permission, it is to be confessed.<br><br>17. {-spreading without permission} Should any bhikkhunī, having gone to family residences in the wrong time (between sunset and dawn), having spread out bedding or having had it spread out, sit or lie down (there) without asking the owner’s permission, it is to be confessed.<br><br>18. {-maligning another} Should any bhikkhunī, because of a misapprehension, because of a misunderstanding, malign another (bhikkhunī), it is to be confessed.<br><br>19. {-cursing another} Should any bhikkhunī curse herself or another (bhikkhunī) with regard to hell or monastic life, it is to be confessed.<br><br>20. {-weeping} Should any bhikkhunī weep, beating and beating herself, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Two: The Darkness Chapter<br><br>21. {-naked} Should any bhikkhunī bathe naked, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.VIII.28.1]<br><br>22. {-bathing cloth} When a bhikkhunī is making a bathing cloth, it is to be made to the standard measurement. Here the standard is this: four spans— using the Sugata span—in length, two spans in width. In excess of that, it is to be cut down and confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 91]<br><br>23. {-unsewing a robe} Should any bhikkhunī, having unsewn (another) bhikkhunī’s robe or having had it unsewn, and then later—when there are no obstructions—neither sew it nor make an effort to have it sewn within four or five days, it is to be confessed.<br><br>24. {-outer robe period} Should any bhikkhunī exceed her five-day outer robe period, it is to be confessed.<br><br>25. {-robe to be given back} Should any bhikkhunī wear a robe that should be given back (one that she has borrowed from another bhikkhunī without asking her permission), it is to be confessed.<br><br>26. {-robes of a group} Should any bhikkhunī put an obstruction in the way of a group’s receiving robe-cloth, it is to be confessed.<br><br>27. {-blocking} Should any bhikkhunī block a robe-cloth distribution that is in accordance with the rule, it is to be confessed.<br><br>28. {-giving robes} Should any bhikkhunī give a contemplative robe (a robe that has been marked so as to be allowable for a bhikkhu or bhikkhunī) to a householder, a male wanderer, or female wanderer, it is to be confessed.<br><br>29. {-letting the season pass} Should any bhikkhunī let the robe-season (the period for receiving kaṭhina donations) pass on the basis of a weak expectation for cloth, it is to be confessed.<br><br>30. {-removal of kaṭhina} Should any bhikkhunī block or prohibit the removal of the kaṭhina privileges in accordance with the rule, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Three: The Naked Chapter<br><br>31. {-sharing one bed} Should two bhikkhunīs share a single bed, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.19.2]<br><br>32. {-sharing one blanket} Should two bhikkhunīs share a single blanket or sleeping mat, it is to be confessed.<br><br>33. {-causing annoyance} Should any bhikkhunī intentionally cause annoyance to (another) bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed.<br><br>34. {-not attending} Should any bhikkhunī not attend to her ailing student nor make an effort to have her attended to, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.VIII.12.2]<br><br>35. {-evicting} Should any bhikkhunī, having given living space to another bhikkhunī, then, angry and displeased, evict her or have her evicted, it is to be confessed.<br><br>36. {-living entangled} Should any bhikkhunī live entangled with a householder or a householder’s son, the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Venerable, don’t live entangled with a householder or a householder’s son. Live alone, Venerable. The Saṅgha recommends isolation for the venerable.” And should that bhikkhunī, thus admonished, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs are to rebuke her up to three times so as to desist. If while being rebuked up to three times by the bhikkhunīs she desists, that is good. If she does not desist, it is to be confessed.<br><br>37. {-within a territory} Should any bhikkhunī, without joining a caravan of merchants, set out within the local king’s territory on a journey considered dubious and risky, it is to be confessed.<br><br>38. {-outside a territory} Should any bhikkhunī, without joining a caravan of merchants, set out outside the local king’s territory on a journey considered dubious and risky, it is to be confessed.<br><br>39. {-during the rains} Should any bhikkhunī set out on a journey during the rains retreat, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.III.3.2]<br><br>40. {-not going on a journey} Should any bhikkhunī, having completed the rains retreat, not depart on a journey of at least five or six leagues, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Four: The Sharing Chapter<br><br>41. {-a king’s house} Should any bhikkhunī go to see a royal pleasure house or a picture gallery (any building decorated for amusement) or a park or a pleasure grove or a lotus pond, it is to be confessed.<br><br>42. {-using a high chair} Should any bhikkhunī make use of a high chair or a couch stuffed with hair, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.VI.8.1]<br><br>43. {-spinning yarn} Should any bhikkhunī spin yarn (thread), it is to be confessed.<br><br>44. {-lay person’s chores} Should any bhikkhunī do a chore for a lay person, it is to be confessed.<br><br>45. {-legal issues} Should any bhikkhunī when told by another bhikkhunī, “Come, Venerable. Help settle this issue,” and having answered, “Very well” then, when there are no obstructions, neither settle it nor make an effort to have it settled, it is to be confessed.<br><br>46. {-giving food} Should any bhikkhunī give, with her own hand, staple or non-staple food to a householder, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is to be confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 41]<br><br>47. {-menstrual cloth} Should any bhikkhunī use a menstrual cloth without having forfeited it (after her previous period), it is to be confessed.<br><br>48. {-dwellings} Should any bhikkhunī depart on a journey without having forfeited her dwelling space, it is to be confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 15]<br><br>49. {-study lowly arts} Should any bhikkhunī study lowly arts (literally, bestial knowledge), it is to be confessed.<br><br>50. {-teaching lowly arts} Should any bhikkhunī teach lowly arts, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.33.2]<br><br>Part Five: The Picture Gallery Chapter<br><br>51. {-entering a monastery} Should any bhikkhunī, without asking permission, knowingly enter a monastery containing a bhikkhu, it is to be confessed. [See Bk’ Pāc. 23]<br><br>52. {-insulting a bhikkhu} Should any bhikkhunī revile or insult a bhikkhu, it is to be confessed.<br><br>53. {-insult group} Should any bhikkhunī, in a fit of temper, revile a group (of bhikkhunīs), it is to be confessed.<br><br>54. {-being invited} Should any bhikkhunī, having eaten and turned down an offer (of further food), chew or consume staple or non-staple food (elsewhere), it is to be confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 35]<br><br>55. {-being stingy with families} Should any bhikkhunī be stingy with regard to families (of supporters), it is to be confessed.<br><br>56. {-residence with no bhikkhu} Should any bhikkhunī spend the rains retreat in a dwelling where there are no bhikkhus (nearby), it is to be confessed.<br><br>57. {-not inviting} Should any bhikkhunī, having completed the rains retreat, not invite (criticism) from both Communities with regard to three matters—what they have seen, heard, or suspected (her of doing)—it is to be confessed.<br><br>58. {-ovāda} Should any bhikkhunī not go for the ovāda or for the (meetings which define) communion (the uposatha and pavāraṇā), it is to be confessed.<br><br>59. {-requesting the ovāda} Every half-month a bhikkhunī should request two things from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha: the asking of the date of the uposatha and the approaching for the ovāda. In excess of that (half-month), it is to be confessed.<br><br>60. {-lower part of body} Should any bhikkhunī, without having informed a Saṅgha or a group (of bhikkhunīs), alone with a man have a boil or scar that has appeared on the lower part of her body (between the navel and the knees) burst or cut open or cleaned or smeared with a salve or bandaged or unbandaged, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Six: The Monastery Chapter<br><br>61. {-pregnant women} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a pregnant woman, it is to be confessed.<br><br>62. {-nursing} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a woman who is still nursing, it is to be confessed.<br><br>63. {-1st on probationers} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a probationer who has not trained for two years in the six precepts, it is to be confessed.<br><br>64. {-2nd on probationers} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a probationer who has trained for two years in the six precepts but who has not received authorization from the Saṅgha, it is to be confessed.<br><br>65. {-1st on married} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a married woman less than twelve years old, it is to be confessed.<br><br>66. {-2nd on married} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a married woman fully twelve years old but who has not trained for two years in the six precepts, it is to be confessed.<br><br>67. {-3rd on married} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a married woman fully twelve years old who has trained for two years in the six precepts but who has not received authorization from the Saṅgha, it is to be confessed.<br><br>68. {-1st on one living with} Should any bhikkhunī, having ordained her student, neither assist her (in her training) nor have her assisted for (the next) two years, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.VIII.12.2-11]<br><br>69. {-not attending to preceptor} Should any bhikkhunī not attend to her preceptor for two years, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.VIII.11.2-18]<br><br>70. {-2nd on one living with} Should any bhikkhunī, having ordained her student, neither take her away nor have her taken away for at least five or six leagues, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Seven: The Pregnant Woman Chapter<br><br>71. {-1st about a maiden} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a maiden less than twenty years old, it is to be confessed. [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 65]<br><br>72. {-2nd maiden} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a maiden fully twenty years old but who has not trained for two years in the six precepts, it is to be confessed.<br><br>73. {-3rd maiden} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a maiden fully twenty years old who has trained for two years in the six precepts but who has not received authorization from the Saṅgha, it is to be confessed.<br><br>74. {-less than twelve years} Should any bhikkhunī give ordination when she has less than twelve years (seniority), it is to be confessed. [See Mv.I.31.5]<br><br>75. {-fully twelve years} Should any bhikkhunī, even if she has fully twelve years (seniority) give ordination when she has not been authorized by the Saṅgha (of bhikkhunīs), it is to be confessed.<br><br>76. {-critical nature} Should any bhikkhunī—having been told, “Enough, Venerable, of your giving ordination for the time being,” and having answered, “Very well”— later complain, it is to be confessed.<br><br>77. {-1st about not ordaining a probationer} Should any bhikkhunī having said to a probationer, “If you give me a robe, I will ordain you,” then, when there are no obstructions, neither ordain her nor make an effort to have another ordain her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>78. {-2nd about not ordaining a probationer} Should any bhikkhunī having said to a probationer: “If you attend to me for two years, I will ordain you,” then, when there are no obstructions, neither ordain her nor make an effort to have another ordain her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>79. {-cause of grief} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a probationer who is entangled with men, entangled with youths, temperamental, a cause of grief, it is to be confessed.<br><br>80. {-without permission} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a probationer without getting permission from her parents or her husband, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.I.54.6]<br><br>81. {-expired} Should any bhikkhunī ordain a probationer by an expired giving of proxy consent, it is to be confessed.<br><br>82. {-each year} Should any bhikkhunī ordain in consecutive years, it is to be confessed.<br><br>83. {-one year} Should any bhikkhunī ordain twice in one year, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.I.52.1]<br><br>Part Eight: The Maiden Chapter<br><br>84. {-sunshade and footwear} Should any bhikkhunī, not being ill, use a sunshade and leather footwear (outside a monastery), it is to be confessed. [Cv.V.23.3; Mv.V.4.3, 5.2]<br><br>85. {-vehicles} Should any bhikkhunī, not being ill, ride in a vehicle, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.V.10.2]<br><br>86. {-hip ornaments} Should any bhikkhunī wear a hip ornament, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.2.1]<br><br>87. {-women’s ornaments} Should any bhikkhunī wear a women’s ornament, it is to be confessed. [See Cv.V.2.1]<br><br>88. {-perfume and scents} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) bathe with perfumes and scents, it is to be confessed. [See Mv.VI.9.2 and Cv.V.2.5]<br><br>89. {-scented} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) bathe with scented sesame powder, it is to be confessed.<br><br>90. {-rubbed by a bhikkhunī} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) have another bhikkhunī rub or massage her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>91. {-rubbed by a probationer} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) have a probationer rub or massage her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>92. {-rubbed by a female novice} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) have a female novice rub or massage her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>93. {-rubbed by a woman householder} Should any bhikkhunī (not being ill) have a woman householder rub or massage her, it is to be confessed.<br><br>94. {-not asking} Should any bhikkhunī sit down in front of a bhikkhu without asking permission, it is to be confessed.<br><br>95. {-asking questions} Should any bhikkhunī ask a question (about the Suttas, Vinaya, or Abhidhamma) of a bhikkhu who has not given leave, it is to be confessed.<br><br>96. {-without a vest} Should any bhikkhunī enter a village without her vest, it is to be confessed.<br><br>Part Nine: The Sunshade and Leather Footwear Chapter<br><br>97. {-false speech} A deliberate lie is to be confessed. [1]<br><br>98. {-abusive speech} An insult is to be confessed. [2]<br><br>99. {-slander} Malicious tale-bearing among bhikkhunīs is to be confessed. [3]<br><br>100. {-Dhamma line by line} Should any bhikkhunī have an unordained person recite Dhamma line by line (with her), it is to be confessed. [4]<br><br>101. {-1st on a sleeping place together with} Should any bhikkhunī lie down in the same sleeping place as an unordained woman for more than two or three consecutive nights, it is to be confessed. [5]<br><br>102. {-2nd on a sleeping place together with} Should any bhikkhunī lie down in the same sleeping place as a man, it is to be confessed. [6]<br><br>103. {-teaching Dhamma} Should any bhikkhunī teach more than five or six sentences of Dhamma to a man, unless a knowledgeable woman is present, it is to be confessed. [7]<br><br>104. {-factual reporting} Should any bhikkhunī report (her own) factual superior human state to an unordained person, it is to be confessed. [8]<br><br>105. {-reporting gross offence} Should any bhikkhunī report (another) bhikkhunī’s gross offence to an unordained person—unless authorized by the bhikkhunīs—it is to be confessed. [9]<br><br>106. {-digging soil} Should any bhikkhunī dig soil or have it dug, it is to be confessed. [10]<br><br>Part Ten: The Lie Chapter<br><br>107. {-vegetation} The damaging of a living plant is to be confessed. [11]<br><br>108. {-evading} Evasive speech and uncooperativeness are to be confessed. [12]<br><br>109. {-maligning} Maligning or complaining (about a community official) is to be confessed. [13]<br><br>110. {-1st on lodgings} Should any bhikkhunī set a bed, bench, mattress, or stool belonging to the Saṅgha out in the open—or have it set out—and then on departing neither put it away nor have it put away, or should she go without taking leave, it is to be confessed. [14]<br><br>111. {2nd on lodgings} Should any bhikkhunī, having set out bedding in a lodging belonging to the Saṅgha—or having had it set out—and then on departing neither put it away nor have it put away, or should she go without taking leave, it is to be confessed. [15]<br><br>112. {-intruding} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly lie down in a lodging belonging to the Saṅgha so as to intrude on a bhikkhunī who arrived there first, (thinking), “Whoever feels crowded will go away”—doing it for this reason and no other—it is to be confessed. [16]<br><br>113. {-evicting} Should any bhikkhunī, angry and dis- pleased, evict a bhikkhunī from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, or have her evicted, it is to be confessed. [17]<br><br>114. {-hut with a loft} Should any bhikkhunī sit or lie down on a bed or bench with detachable legs on an (unplanked) loft in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, it is to be confessed. [18]<br><br>115. {-large dwelling} When a bhikkhunī is building a large dwelling, she may apply two or three layers of facing to plaster the area around the window frame and reinforce the area around the door frame the width of the door opening, while standing where there are no crops to speak of. Should she apply more than that, even if standing where there are no crops to speak of, it is to be confessed. [19]<br><br>116. {-containing living beings} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly pour water containing living beings—or have it poured—on grass or on clay, it is to be confessed. [20]<br><br>Part Eleven: The Living Plant Chapter<br><br>117. {-public alms center} A bhikkhunī who is not ill may eat one meal at a public alms center. Should she eat more than that, it is to be confessed. [31]<br><br>118. {-group meal} A group meal, except on the proper occasions, is to be confessed. Here the proper occasions are these: a time of illness, a time of giving cloth, a time of making robes, a time of going on a journey, a time of embarking on a boat, an extraordinary occasion, a time when the meal is supplied by contemplatives. These are the proper occasions here. [32]<br><br>119. {-Kāṇa’s mother} In case a bhikkhunī arriving at a family residence is invited to take cakes or travellers’ bread, she may accept two or three bowlfuls if she so desires. If she should accept more than that, it is to be confessed. Having accepted the two or three bowlfuls and having taken them from there, she is to share them among the bhikkhunīs. This is the proper course here. [34]<br><br>120. {-eating at the wrong time} Should any bhikkhunī chew or consume staple or non-staple food at the wrong time, it is to be confessed. [37]<br><br>121. {-storing up} Should any bhikkhunī chew or consume stored-up staple or non-staple food, it is to be confessed. [38]<br><br>122. {-tooth sticks} Should any bhikkhunī take into her mouth an edible that has not been given—except for water and tooth-cleaning sticks—it is to be confessed. [40]<br><br>123. {-dismissing} Should any bhikkhunī say to a bhikkhunī, “Come, Venerable, let’s enter the village or town for alms,” and then—whether or not she has had (food) given to her—dismiss her, saying, “Go away, Venerable. I don’t like sitting or talking with you. I prefer sitting or talking (with someone) alone”; if doing it for that reason and no other, it is to be confessed. [42]<br><br>124. {-having a meal} Should a bhikkhunī sit intruding on a family “with its meal,” it is to be confessed. [43]<br><br>125. {-being private and secluded} Should any bhikkhunī sit in private on a secluded seat with a man, it is to be confessed. [44]<br><br>126. {-sitting in private} Should any bhikkhunī sit in private, alone with a man, it is to be confessed. [45]<br><br>Part Twelve: The Food Chapter<br><br>127. {-visiting} Should any bhikkhunī, being invited for a meal and without taking leave of an available bhikkhunī, go calling on families before or after the meal, except at the proper times, it is to be confessed. Here the proper times are these: the time of giving cloth, the time of making robes. These are the proper times here. [46]<br><br>128. {-“Mahānāma”} A bhikkhunī who is not ill may accept (and make use of) a four-month invitation to ask for requisites. If she should accept (and make use of) it for longer than that—unless the invitation is renewed or is permanent—it is to be confessed. [47]<br><br>129. {-army on active duty} Should any bhikkhunī go to see an army on active duty, unless there is a suitable reason, it is to be confessed. [48]<br><br>130. {-staying with an army} There being some reason or another for a bhikkhunī to go to an army, she may stay two or three (consecutive) nights with the army. If she should stay longer than that, it is to be confessed. [49]<br><br>131. {-battlefield} If a bhikkhunī staying two or three nights with an army should go to a battlefield, a roll call, the troops in battle formation, or to see a review of the (battle) units, it is to be confessed. [50]<br><br>132. {-drinking alcohol} The drinking of alcohol or fermented liquor is to be confessed. [51]<br><br>133. {-tickling with the fingers} Tickling with the fingers is to be confessed. [52]<br><br>134. {-playing} The act of playing in the water is to be confessed. [53]<br><br>135. {-disrespect} Disrespect is to be confessed. [54]<br><br>136. {-frightening} Should any bhikkhunī try to frighten another bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed. [55]<br><br>Part Thirteen: The Go-calling Chapter<br><br>137. {-fires} Should any bhikkhunī who is not ill, seeking to warm herself, kindle a fire or have one kindled—unless there is a suitable reason—it is to be confessed. [56]<br><br>138. {-bathing} Should any bhikkhunī bathe at intervals of less than half a month, except at the proper occasions, it is to be confessed. Here the proper occasions are these: the last month and a half of the hot season, the first month of the rains, these two and a half months being a time of heat, a time of fever; (also) a time of illness; a time of work; a time of going on a journey; a time of wind or rain. These are the proper times here. [57]<br><br>139. {-discoloring} When a bhikkhunī receives a new robe, any one of three means of discoloring it is to be applied: blue (green), brown, or black. If a bhikkhunī should make use of a new robe without applying any of the three means of discoloring it, it is to be confessed. [58]<br><br>140. {-shared ownership} Should any bhikkhunī, herself having placed robe-cloth under shared ownership (vikappana) with a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female probationer, a male novice, or a female novice, then make use of the robe-cloth without the shared ownership being rescinded, it is to be confessed. [59]<br><br>141. {-hiding} Should any bhikkhunī hide (another) bhikkhunī’s bowl, robe, sitting cloth, needle case, or belt —or have it hidden—even as a joke, it is to be confessed. [60]<br><br>142. {-intentionally} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly deprive a living being of life, it is to be confessed. [61]<br><br>143. {-containing living beings} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly make use of water with living beings in it, it is to be confessed. [62]<br><br>144. {-agitating} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly agitate for the reviving of an issue that has been rightfully dealt with, it is to be confessed. [63]<br><br>145. {-caravan of thieves} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly and by arrangement travel together with a caravan of thieves, even for the interval between one village and the next, it is to be confessed. [66]<br><br>146. {-“Ariṭṭha”} Should any bhikkhunī say the following: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions,” the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Do not say that, Venerable. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that. In many ways, Venerable, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.” And should the bhikkhunī, thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs are to rebuke her up to three times so as to desist. If while being rebuked up to three times she desists, that is good. If she does not desist, it is to be confessed. [68]<br><br>Part Fourteen: The Fire Chapter<br><br>147. {-living with one suspended} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly consort, join in communion, or lie down in the same lodging with a bhikkhunī professing such a view who has not acted in compliance with the rule, who has not abandoned that view, it is to be confessed. [69]<br><br>148. {-“Kaṇṭaka”} And if a female novice should say the following: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those acts the Blessed One says are obstructive, when indulged in are not genuine obstructions,” the bhikkhunīs should admonish her thus: “Do not say that, Venerable Novice. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say anything like that. In many ways, Venerable, the Blessed One has described obstructive acts, and when indulged in they are genuine obstructions.” And should that female novice, thus admonished by the bhikkhunīs, persist as before, the bhikkhunīs should admonish her as follows: “From this day forth, Venerable Novice, you are not to claim the Blessed One as your teacher, nor are you even to have the opportunity the other female novices get—that of sharing lodgings two or three nights with the bhikkhunīs. Away with you! Out of our sight!” Should any bhikkhunī knowingly support, receive services from, consort with, or lie down in the same lodging with a novice thus expelled, it is to be confessed. [70]<br><br>149. {-righteously} Should any bhikkhunī, admonished by the bhikkhunīs in accordance with a rule, say: “Venerables, I will not train myself under this training rule until I have put questions about it to another bhikkhunī, experienced and learned in the discipline,” it is to be confessed. Bhikkhunīs, (a training rule) is to be understood, is to be asked about, is to be pondered. This is the proper course here. [71]<br><br>150. {-confusion} Should any bhikkhunī, when the Pātimokkha is being repeated, say: “Why are these lesser and minor training rules repeated when they lead only to anxiety, bother, and confusion?” the criticism of the training rules is to be confessed. [72]<br><br>151. {-deception} Should any bhikkhunī, when the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, say: “Just now have I heard that this case, too, is handed down in the Pātimokkha, is included in the Pātimokkha, and comes up for recitation every half-month”; and if other bhikkhunīs should know: “That bhikkhunī has already sat through two or three recitations of the Pātimokkha, if not more,” the bhikkhunī is not exempted for being ignorant. Whatever the offence she has committed, she is to be dealt with in accordance with the rule; and in addition, her deception is to be exposed: “It is no gain for you, Venerable, it is ill-done, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not pay proper attention and take it to heart.” Here the deception is to be confessed. [73]<br><br>152. {-a blow} Should any bhikkhunī, angered and displeased, give a blow to a bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed. [74]<br><br>153. {-raised hand} Should any bhikkhunī, angered and displeased, raise her hand against a bhikkhunī, it is to be confessed. [75]<br><br>154. {-unfounded} Should any bhikkhunī charge a bhikkhunī with an unfounded saṅghādisesa (offence), it is to be confessed. [76]<br><br>155. {-deliberately} Should any bhikkhunī purposefully provoke anxiety in a bhikkhunī (thinking): “This way, even for just a moment, she will have no peace”—if doing it for just this reason and no other—it is to be confessed. [77] 73 Sikkhamānāya, bhikkhave, bhikkhuniyā aññātabbaṁ paripucchitabbaṁ paripañhitabbaṁ, ayaṁ tattha sāmīci.<br><br>156. {-eavesdropping} Should any bhikkhunī stand eavesdropping on bhikkhunīs when they are arguing, quarreling, and disputing (thinking): “I will overhear what they say”—if doing it for just this reason and no other—it is to be confessed. [78]<br><br>Part Fifteen: The View Chapter<br><br>157. {-objecting to a formal act} Should any bhikkhunī, having given consent (by proxy) to a formal act carried out in accordance with the rule, later complain (about the act), it is to be confessed. [79]<br><br>158. {-going without giving consent} Should any bhikkhunī, when deliberation is being carried on in the Saṅgha, get up from her seat and leave without having given consent, it is to be confessed. [80]<br><br>159. {-worn thin} Should any bhikkhunī, (acting as part of) a Saṅgha in concord, give robe-cloth (to an individual bhikkhunī) and later complain, “The bhikkhunīs apportion the Saṅgha’s gains according to friendship,” it is to be confessed. [81]<br><br>160. {-allocation} Should any bhikkhunī knowingly divert to an individual gains that had been allocated for the Saṅgha, it is to be confessed. [82]<br><br>161. {-valuables} Should any bhikkhunī pick up or have (someone) pick up a valuable or what is considered a valuable, except within a monastery or within a dwelling, it is to be confessed. But when a bhikkhunī has picked up or had (someone) pick up a valuable or what is considered a valuable (left) in a monastery or in a dwelling, she is to keep it, (thinking,) “Whoever it belongs to will (come and) fetch it.” This is the proper course here. [84]<br><br>162. {-needle cases} Should any bhikkhunī have a needle case made of bone, ivory, or horn, it is to be broken and confessed. [86]<br><br>163. {-beds and benches} When a bhikkhunī is making a new bed or bench, it is to have legs (at most) eight fingerbreadths long, using Sugata fingerbreadths, not counting the lower edge of the frame. In excess of that it is to be cut down and confessed. [87]<br><br>164. {-upholstered with cotton} Should any bhikkhunī have a bed or bench upholstered with cotton, it (the upholstery) is to be torn off and confessed. [88]<br><br>165. {-skin-eruption cloth} When a bhikkhunī is making a skin-eruption cloth, it is to be made to the measurement. Here the standard is this: four Sugata spans in length, two spans in width. If in excess, it is to be cut down and confessed. [90]<br><br>166. {-“Nanda”} Should any bhikkhunī have a robe made the size of the Sugata robe or larger, it is to be cut down and confessed. Here, the size of the Sugata robe is this: nine spans — using the Sugata span — in length, six spans in width. This is the size of the Sugata’s Sugata robe. [92]<br><br>Part Sixteen: The In-accordance-with-the-Rule Chapter<br><br>Recited, Venerables, are the hundred and sixty-six matters entailing confession. Herein I ask the venerables: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? For the third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The venerables are pure in this; therefore they are silent. So I remember it.<br><br>The section on confession is finished.

If a nun who is not sick asks for ghee and then eats it, she must acknowledge it: ‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’	Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_1.FULL.mp3]	456	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns from the group of six were eating ghee that they had asked for.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns eat ghee that they have asked for?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six eat ghee that they have asked for?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that those nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:<br><br>‘If a nun asks for ghee and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br><br>“I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.”’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the nuns.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of nuns were sick.<br><br>The nuns who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we ate ghee that we had asked for, and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t ask because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. And because of that we’re not comfortable.” …<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to eat ghee that she has asked for.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without ghee.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without ghee.<br><br>Ghee:<br><br>ghee from cows, ghee from goats, ghee from buffaloes, or ghee from whatever animal whose meat is allowable.<br><br>If she is not sick and she asks for herself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she eats ghee that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she eats ghee that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she eats ghee that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The first training rule on acknowledgment is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhuniyo sappiṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjanti.<br><br>Manussā ujjhāyanti [sound:ABi_PD_1.FULL.mp3]	{The precept about -asking for ghee} Should any bhikkhunī, not being ill, ask for ghee and consume it, she is to acknowledge it: “Venerable, I have committed a blameworthy, unsuitable act that ought to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.” [See Bhikkhus’ Pācittiya 39]	
Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::7.Pāṭidesanīyā	BI VIN PAT BI PD 2	Telaviññāpanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā telaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.		Bhikkhu Pācittiya 39	navanītaṁ missing, follow the pāṭidesanīya instead of Pācittiya, also simpler.	If a nun who is not sick asks for oil and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’	Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_2.mp3]	457	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns from the group of six were eating oil that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating honey that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating syrup that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating fish that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating meat that they had asked for.<br><br>… were drinking milk that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating curd that they had asked for.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns eat curd that they have asked for?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six eat curd that they have asked for?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that those nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:<br><br>‘If a nun asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br><br>“I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.”’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the nuns.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of nuns were sick.<br><br>The nuns who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we ate curd that we had asked for, and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t ask because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. And because of that we’re not comfortable.” …<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to eat curd that she has asked for.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without curd.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without curd.<br><br>Oil:<br><br>sesame oil, mustard seed oil, honey tree oil, castor oil, oil from tallow.<br><br>Honey:<br><br>honey from bees.<br><br>Syrup:<br><br>from sugar cane.<br><br>Fish:<br><br>what lives in water is what is meant.<br><br>Meat:<br><br>the meat of those animals whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Milk:<br><br>milk from cows, milk from goats, milk from buffaloes, or milk from whatever animal whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Curd:<br><br>curd from those same animals.<br><br>If she is not sick and she asks for herself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eighth training rule entailing acknowledgment is finished.<br><br>“Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing acknowledgment in the Nuns’ Analysis is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::7.Pāṭidesanīyā	BI VIN PAT BI PD 4	Phāṇitaviññāpanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā phāṇitaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.		Bhikkhu Pācittiya 39	navanītaṁ missing, follow the pāṭidesanīya instead of Pācittiya, also simpler.	If a nun who is not sick asks for syrup and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’	Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_4.mp3]	459	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns from the group of six were eating oil that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating honey that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating syrup that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating fish that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating meat that they had asked for.<br><br>… were drinking milk that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating curd that they had asked for.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns eat curd that they have asked for?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six eat curd that they have asked for?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that those nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:<br><br>‘If a nun asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br><br>“I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.”’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the nuns.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of nuns were sick.<br><br>The nuns who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we ate curd that we had asked for, and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t ask because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. And because of that we’re not comfortable.” …<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to eat curd that she has asked for.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without curd.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without curd.<br><br>Oil:<br><br>sesame oil, mustard seed oil, honey tree oil, castor oil, oil from tallow.<br><br>Honey:<br><br>honey from bees.<br><br>Syrup:<br><br>from sugar cane.<br><br>Fish:<br><br>what lives in water is what is meant.<br><br>Meat:<br><br>the meat of those animals whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Milk:<br><br>milk from cows, milk from goats, milk from buffaloes, or milk from whatever animal whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Curd:<br><br>curd from those same animals.<br><br>If she is not sick and she asks for herself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eighth training rule entailing acknowledgment is finished.<br><br>“Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing acknowledgment in the Nuns’ Analysis is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::7.Pāṭidesanīyā	BI VIN PAT BI PD 6	Maṁsaviññāpanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā maṁsaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.		Bhikkhu Pācittiya 39	navanītaṁ missing, follow the pāṭidesanīya instead of Pācittiya, also simpler.	If a nun who is not sick asks for meat and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’	Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_6.mp3]	461	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns from the group of six were eating oil that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating honey that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating syrup that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating fish that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating meat that they had asked for.<br><br>… were drinking milk that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating curd that they had asked for.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns eat curd that they have asked for?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six eat curd that they have asked for?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that those nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:<br><br>‘If a nun asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br><br>“I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.”’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the nuns.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of nuns were sick.<br><br>The nuns who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we ate curd that we had asked for, and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t ask because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. And because of that we’re not comfortable.” …<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to eat curd that she has asked for.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without curd.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without curd.<br><br>Oil:<br><br>sesame oil, mustard seed oil, honey tree oil, castor oil, oil from tallow.<br><br>Honey:<br><br>honey from bees.<br><br>Syrup:<br><br>from sugar cane.<br><br>Fish:<br><br>what lives in water is what is meant.<br><br>Meat:<br><br>the meat of those animals whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Milk:<br><br>milk from cows, milk from goats, milk from buffaloes, or milk from whatever animal whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Curd:<br><br>curd from those same animals.<br><br>If she is not sick and she asks for herself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eighth training rule entailing acknowledgment is finished.<br><br>“Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing acknowledgment in the Nuns’ Analysis is finished. offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eighth training rule entailing acknowledgment is finished.<br><br>“Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing acknowledgment in the Nuns’ Analysis is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::7.Pāṭidesanīyā	BI VIN PAT BI PD 8	Dadhiviññāpanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā dadhiṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: <br>“gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.		Bhikkhu Pācittiya 39	navanītaṁ missing, follow the pāṭidesanīya instead of Pācittiya, also simpler.	If a nun who is not sick asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’	Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_8.FULL.mp3]	463	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>the nuns from the group of six were eating oil that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating honey that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating syrup that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating fish that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating meat that they had asked for.<br><br>… were drinking milk that they had asked for.<br><br>… were eating curd that they had asked for.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can nuns eat curd that they have asked for?<br><br>Who doesn’t like nice food? Who doesn’t prefer tasty food?”<br><br>The nuns heard the complaints of those people.<br><br>The nuns of few desires complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six eat curd that they have asked for?” …<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that those nuns do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, Sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can the nuns from the group of six do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:<br><br>‘If a nun asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br><br>“I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.”’”<br><br>In this way the Buddha laid down this training rule for the nuns.<br><br>Soon afterwards a number of nuns were sick.<br><br>The nuns who were looking after them asked,<br><br>“I hope you’re bearing up? I hope you’re getting better?”<br><br>“Previously we ate curd that we had asked for, and then we were comfortable.<br><br>But now that the Buddha has prohibited this, we don’t ask because we’re afraid of wrongdoing. And because of that we’re not comfortable.” …<br><br>They told the Buddha. Soon afterwards the Buddha had the Sangha gathered and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow a sick nun to eat curd that she has asked for.<br><br>And so, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Nun:<br><br>… The nun who has been given the full ordination in unanimity by both Sanghas through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of nun is meant in this case.<br><br>Who is not sick:<br><br>who is comfortable without curd.<br><br>Who is sick:<br><br>who is not comfortable without curd.<br><br>Oil:<br><br>sesame oil, mustard seed oil, honey tree oil, castor oil, oil from tallow.<br><br>Honey:<br><br>honey from bees.<br><br>Syrup:<br><br>from sugar cane.<br><br>Fish:<br><br>what lives in water is what is meant.<br><br>Meat:<br><br>the meat of those animals whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Milk:<br><br>milk from cows, milk from goats, milk from buffaloes, or milk from whatever animal whose meat is allowable.<br><br>Curd:<br><br>curd from those same animals.<br><br>If she is not sick and she asks for herself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When she receives it with the intention of eating it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>For every mouthful, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If she is not sick, and she does not perceive herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she is unsure of it, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is not sick, but she perceives herself as sick, and she eats curd that she has asked for, she commits an offense entailing acknowledgment.<br><br>If she is sick, but she does not perceive herself as sick, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, but she is unsure of it, she commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If she is sick, and she perceives herself as sick, there is no offense.	There is no offense:<br><br>if she is sick;<br><br>if she asked for it when she was sick, but eats it when she is no longer sick;<br><br>if she eats the leftovers from one who is sick;<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of her own property;<br><br>if she is insane;<br><br>if she is the first offender.<br><br>The eighth training rule entailing acknowledgment is finished.<br><br>“Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing acknowledgment in the Nuns’ Analysis is finished. Pāṭidesanīyā		[sound:Bi_PD_CONCL.mp3]	464							[sound:ABi_PD_CONCL.mp3]	Recited, Venerables, are the eight matters to be acknowledged. Herein I ask the venerables: Are you pure in this? Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::7.Pāṭidesanīyā	BI VIN PAT BI PD		Ime kho panāyyāyo aṭṭha pāṭidesanīyā dhammā uddesaṁ āgacchanti.<br><br>1. Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā sappiṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.<br><br>2. Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā telaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.<br><br>3. Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā madhuṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.<br><br>4. Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā phāṇitaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.<br><br>5. Yā pana bhikkhunī agilānā macchaṁ viññāpetvā bhuñjeyya, paṭidesetabbaṁ tāya bhikkhuniyā: “gārayhaṁ, ayye, dhammaṁ āpajjiṁ asappāyaṁ pāṭidesanīyaṁ, taṁ paṭidesemī”ti.<br><br>6. Venerables, these eight rules on acknowledgment come up for recitation.<br><br>1. If a nun who is not sick asks for ghee and then eats it, she must acknowledge it: ‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>2. If a nun who is not sick asks for oil and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>3. If a nun who is not sick asks for honey and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>4. If a nun who is not sick asks for syrup and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>5. If a nun who is not sick asks for fish and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>6. If a nun who is not sick asks for meat and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>7. If a nun who is not sick asks for milk and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I’ve done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>8. If a nun who is not sick asks for curd and then eats it, she must acknowledge it:<br>‘I have done a blameworthy and unsuitable thing that is to be acknowledged. I acknowledge it.’<br><br>Venerables, the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited.<br>In regard to this I ask you, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>A second time I ask, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>A third time I ask, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I will remember it thus.<br><br>The eight offenses entailing acknowledgment are finished. Venerables, these rules of training come up for recitation.<br><br>1. ‘I will wear my sarong evenly all around,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>2. ‘I will wear my upper robe evenly all around,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>3. ‘I will be well-covered while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>4. ‘I will be well-covered while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>5. ‘I will be well-restrained while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>6. ‘I will be well-restrained while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>7. ‘I will lower my eyes while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>8. ‘I will lower my eyes while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>9. ‘I will not lift my robe while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>10. ‘I will not lift my robe while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>The first subchapter on evenly all around.<br><br>11. ‘I will not laugh loudly while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>12. ‘I will not laugh loudly while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>13. ‘I will not be noisy while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>14. ‘I will not be noisy while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>15. ‘I will not sway my body while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>16. ‘I will not sway my body while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>17. ‘I will not swing my arms while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>18. train.<br><br>20. ‘I will not sway my head while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>The second subchapter on laughing loudly.<br><br>21. ‘I will not put my hands on my hips while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>22. ‘I will not put my hands on my hips while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>23. ‘I will not cover my head while walking in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>24. ‘I will not cover my head while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>25. ‘I will not move about while squatting on my heels in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>26. ‘I will not clasp my knees while sitting in inhabited areas,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>27. ‘I will receive almsfood respectfully,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>28. ‘I will receive almsfood with attention on the almsbowl,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>29. ‘I subchapter on hands on hips.<br><br>31. ‘I will eat almsfood respectfully,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>32. ‘I will eat almsfood with attention on the almsbowl,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>33. ‘I will eat almsfood in order,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>34. ‘I will eat almsfood with the right proportion of bean curry,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>35. ‘I will not eat almsfood after making a heap,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>36. ‘I will not cover my curries with rice because I want more,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>37. ‘When not sick, I will not request bean curry or rice for myself and then eat it,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>38. ‘I will not look at another’s almsbowl finding fault,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>39. ‘I will not make mouthfuls that are too large,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>40. ‘I will make rounded mouthfuls,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>The fourth subchapter on respectfully.<br><br>41. ‘I will not open my mouth without bringing a mouthful to it,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>42. ‘I will not put my whole hand in my mouth while eating,’ this is how not make a chomping sound while eating,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>The fifth subchapter on mouthfuls.<br><br>51. ‘I will not slurp while eating,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>52. ‘I will not lick my hand while eating,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>53. ‘I will not lick my almsbowl while eating,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>54. ‘I will not lick my lips while to the path to anyone walking on the path who is not sick,’ this is how you should train.<br><br>73. ‘When not sick, I will not defecate or urinate while standing,’ this is how you should Venerables, these seven principles for the settling of legal issues come up for recitation.&nbsp;<br>For the settling and resolving of legal issues whenever they arise there is:<br><br>Resolution face-to-face to be applied.<br>Resolution through recollection to be granted.<br>Resolution because of past insanity to be granted.<br>Acting according to what has been admitted.<br>Majority decision.<br>Further penalty.<br>Covering over as if with grass.<br><br>Venerables, the seven principles for the settling of legal issues have been recited.<br>In regard to this I ask you, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>A second time I ask, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>A third time I ask, ‘Are you pure in this?’<br>You are pure in this and therefore silent. I will remember it thus.<br><br>The seven principles for the settling of legal issues are finished.<br><br>Venerables, the introduction has been recited;<br>the eight rules on expulsion have been recited;<br>the seventeen rules on suspension have been recited;<br>the thirty rules on relinquishment and confession have been recited;<br>the one hundred and sixty-six rules on confession have been recited;<br>the eight rules on acknowledgment have been recited;<br>the rules of training have been recited;<br>the seven principles for the settling of legal issues have been recited.<br><br>This much has come down and is included in the Monastic Code of the Buddha and comes up for recitation every half-month.<br>In regard to this everyone should train in unity, in concord, without dispute.”<br><br>The fourth recitation, in detail, is finished.<br><br>The Monastic Code for nuns is finished.<br><br>Excellent! Adhikaraṇasamathā		[sound:Bi_AS-FINAL.mp3]	547							[sound:ABi_AS-FINAL.mp3]	Now, Venerables, these seven matters for the settlement of issues come up for recitation.<br>For the settling and pacification of issues that have arisen: <br><br>1. A verdict in the presence of may be given. <br>2. A verdict of mindfulness may be given. <br>3. A verdict of past insanity may be given. <br>4. Acting in accordance with what is admitted. <br>5. Acting in accordance with the majority. <br>6. Acting in accordance with the accused's further misconduct. <br>7. Covering over as with grass.<br><br>Recited, Venerables, are the seven matters of the settlement of issues. Herein I ask the venerables: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask: Are you pure in this? A third time I ask: Are you pure in this? The venerables are pure in this; therefore they are silent. So I remember it.<br><br>The settlement of issues is finished.<br><br>Recited, Venerables, is the introduction, <br>recited are the eight matters entailing defeat, <br>recited are the seventeen matters entailing initial and subsequent [meetings] of the Saṅgha, <br>recited are the thirty matters entailing confession with forfeiture, <br>recited are the one hundred and sixty-six matters entailing confession, <br>recited are the eight matters to be acknowledged, <br>recited are the rules for training, <br>recited are the seven matters for the settlement of issues.<br><br>So much, comes down in the sutta of the Blessed One, contained in the sutta, comes up for recitation every half month. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::3 Jātarūpa Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 25	Bhesajjasikkhāpadaṁ	Yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṁ bhikkhunīnaṁ paṭisāyanīyāni bhesajjāni, seyyathidaṁ: sappi navanītaṁ telaṁ madhu phāṇitaṁ, tāni paṭiggahetvā sattāhaparamaṁ sannidhikārakaṁ paribhuñjitabbāni. <br>Taṁ atikkāmentiyā, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu NP 23	Uses 'bhikkhunīnaṁ', atikkāmentiyā	After being received, the tonics allowable for sick nuns—that is, ghee, butter, oil, honey, and syrup—should be used from storage for at most seven days.<br>If one uses them longer than that, one commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_25.mp3]	190	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Pilindavaccha was clearing a slope near Rājagaha, intending to build a shelter.<br><br>Just then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha went to Pilindavaccha, bowed, sat down, and said, “Venerable, what are you having made?”<br><br>“I’m clearing a slope, great king. I want to build a shelter.”<br><br>“Do you need a monastery worker?”<br><br>“The Buddha hasn’t allowed monastery workers.”<br><br>“Well then, sir, please ask the Buddha and tell me the outcome.”<br><br>“Yes, great king.”<br><br>Pilindavaccha then instructed, inspired, and gladdened King Bimbisāra with a teaching,<br><br>after which the king got up from his seat, bowed down, circumambulated Pilindavaccha with his right side toward him, and left.<br><br>Soon afterwards Pilindavaccha sent a message to the Buddha:<br><br>“Sir, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha wishes to provide a monastery worker.<br><br>What should I tell him?”<br><br>The Buddha then gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow monastery workers.”<br><br>Once again King Bimbisāra went to Pilindavaccha, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Sir, has the Buddha allowed monastery workers?”<br><br>“Yes, great king.”<br><br>“Well then, I’ll provide you with a monastery worker.”<br><br>But after making this promise, he forgot, and only remembered after a long time. He then addressed the official in charge of all practical affairs: “Listen, has the monastery worker I promised been provided?”<br><br>“No, sir, he hasn’t.”<br><br>“How long has it been since we made that promise?”<br><br>The official counted the days and said, “It’s been five hundred days.”<br><br>“Well then, provide him with five hundred monastery workers.”<br><br>“Yes.”<br><br>The official provided Pilindavaccha with those monastery workers and a separate village was established.<br><br>They called it “The Monastery Workers’ Village” and “Pilinda Village”.<br><br>And Pilindavaccha began associating with the families in that village.<br><br>After robing up one morning, he took his bowl and robe and went to Pilinda Village for alms.<br><br>At that time they were holding a celebration in that village and the children were dressed up with ornaments and garlands.<br><br>As Pilindavaccha was walking on continuous almsround, he came to the house of a certain monastery worker where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>Just then the daughter of that house had seen the other children dressed up in ornaments and garlands. She cried, saying, “Give me a garland! Give me ornaments!”<br><br>Pilindavaccha asked her mother why the girl was crying.<br><br>She told him, adding, “Poor people like us can’t afford garlands and ornaments.”<br><br>Pilindavaccha took a pad of grass and said to the mother, “Here, place this on the girl’s head.”<br><br>She did, and it turned into a beautiful golden garland.<br><br>Even the royal compound had nothing like it.<br><br>People told King Bimbisāra, “In the house of such-and-such a monastery worker there’s a beautiful golden garland.<br><br>Even in your court, sir, there’s nothing like it.<br><br>So how did those poor people get it?<br><br>They must have stolen it.”<br><br>King Bimbisāra had that family imprisoned.<br><br>Once again Pilindavaccha robed up in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to Pilinda Village for alms.<br><br>As he was walking on continuous almsround, he came to the house of that monastery worker. He then asked the neighbors what had happened to that family.<br><br>“The king has jailed them, venerable, because of that golden garland.”<br><br>Pilindavaccha then went to King Bimbisāra’s house and sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>King Bimbisāra approached Pilindavaccha, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>Pilindavaccha said, “Great king, why have you jailed the family of that monastery worker?”<br><br>“Sir, in the house of that monastery worker there was a beautiful golden garland.<br><br>Even the royal compound has nothing like it.<br><br>So how did those poor people get it?<br><br>They must have stolen it.”<br><br>Pilindavaccha then focused his mind on turning King Bimbisāra’s stilt house into gold.<br><br>As a result, the whole house became gold.<br><br>He said, “Great king, how did you get so much gold?”<br><br>“Understood, sir! It’s your supernormal power.”<br><br>He then released that family.<br><br>People said, “They say Venerable Pilindavaccha has performed a superhuman feat, a wonder of supernormal power, for the king and his court!”<br><br>Being delighted and gaining confidence in Pilindavaccha, they brought him the five tonics: ghee, butter, oil, honey, and syrup.<br><br>Ordinarily, too, Pilindavaccha was getting the five tonics.<br><br>Since he was getting so much, he gave it away to his followers,<br><br>who ended up with an abundance of tonics.<br><br>After filling up basins and waterpots and setting these aside, they filled their water filters and bags and hung these in the windows.<br><br>But the tonics were dripping, and the dwellings became infested with rats.<br><br>When people walking about the dwellings saw this, they complained and criticized them,<br><br>“These Sakyan monastics are hoarding things indoors, just like King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can these monks choose to live with such abundance?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that there are monks who live like this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can those foolish men live like this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>The
