conduct.<br><br>If it is less than seven days, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is less than seven days and he perceives it as less, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if within seven days they have been determined, given away, lost, destroyed, burned, stolen, or taken on trust;<br><br>if, without any desire for them, he gives them up to a person who is not fully ordained, and he then obtains them again and then uses them;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on tonics, the third, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā pilindavaccho rājagahe pabbhāraṁ sodhāpeti leṇaṁ kattukāmo.<br><br>Atha kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro yenāyasmā pilindavaccho tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ etadavoca—“kiṁ, bhante, thero kārāpetī”ti?<br><br>“Pabbhāraṁ, mahārāja, sodhāpemi leṇaṁ kattukāmo”ti.<br><br>“Attho, bhante, ayyassa ārāmikenā”ti?<br><br>“Na kho, mahārāja, bhagavatā ārāmiko anuññāto”ti.<br><br>“Tena hi, bhante, bhagavantaṁ paṭipucchitvā mama āroceyyāthā”ti.<br><br>“Evaṁ, mahārājā”ti kho āyasmā pilindavaccho rañño māgadhassa seniyassa bimbisārassa paccassosi.<br><br>Atha kho āyasmā pilindavaccho rājānaṁ māgadhaṁ seniyaṁ bimbisāraṁ dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṁsesi.<br><br>Atha kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro āyasmatā pilindavacchena dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṁsito uṭṭhāyāsanā āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṁ katvā pakkāmi.<br><br>Atha kho āyasmā pilindavaccho bhagavato santike dūtaṁ pāhesi—<br><br>“rājā, bhante, māgadho seniyo bimbisāro ārāmikaṁ dātukāmo.<br><br>Kathaṁ nu kho, bhante, mayā paṭipajjitabban”ti?<br><br>Atha kho bhagavā etasmiṁ nidāne etasmiṁ pakaraṇe dhammiṁ kathaṁ katvā bhikkhū āmantesi—<br><br>“anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ārāmikan”ti.<br><br>Dutiyampi kho rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro yenāyasmā pilindavaccho tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ pilindavacchaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Matches Bu NP 25	Uses 'bhikkhuniyā' instead of 'bhikkhussa',&nbsp;kupitā anattamanā	If a nun herself gives a robe to a nun, but then, in anger, takes it back or has it taken back, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_26.mp3]	191	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>Venerable Upananda the Sakyan said to his brother’s student,<br><br>“Come, let’s go wandering the country.”<br><br>“I can’t, venerable,<br><br>my robes are worn out.”<br><br>“I’ll give you a robe.”<br><br>And he gave him a robe.<br><br>Soon afterwards that monk heard<br><br>that the Buddha was about to go wandering the country.<br><br>He thought,<br><br>“Now I’ll go wandering with the Buddha instead.”<br><br>Then, when Upananda said,<br><br>“Let’s go,”<br><br>he replied, “I’m not going with you, but with the Buddha.”<br><br>“Well, that robe I gave you is going with me,”<br><br>and he just took it back in anger.<br><br>That monk told other monks what had happened.<br><br>And the monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda give away a robe and then take it back in anger?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>To a monk:<br><br>to another monk.<br><br>Himself:<br><br>he himself has given it.<br><br>A robe:<br><br>one of the six kinds of robe-cloth, but not smaller than what can be assigned to another.<br><br>In anger:<br><br>discontent, having hatred, hostile.<br><br>Takes back:<br><br>if he takes it back himself, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>Has taken back:<br><br>if he asks another, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If he only asks once, then even if the other takes back many, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The robe-cloth should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-vb-np1#3.2.5"">Bu NP 1:3.2.5</a>–3.2.29, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, this robe-cloth, which I took back after giving it to a monk, is to be relinquished. I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this robe-cloth back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If the other person is fully ordained and he perceives them as such, and after giving them robe-cloth, he takes it back in anger or has it taken back, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, and after giving them robe-cloth, he takes it back in anger or has it taken back, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If the other person is fully ordained, but he does not perceive them as such, and after giving them robe-cloth, he takes it back in anger or has it taken back, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If, after giving them another requisite, he takes it back in anger or has it taken back, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If, after giving robe-cloth or another requisite to a person who is not fully ordained, he takes it back in anger or has it taken back, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he perceives them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If the other person is not fully ordained, and he does not perceive them as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct."	There is no offense:<br><br>if the other person gives it back;<br><br>if he takes it on trust from them;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on taking back a robe, the fifth, is finished. [sound:ABi_NP_26.mp3]	{-snatching robes} Should any bhikkhunī, having herself given a robe-cloth to a bhikkhunī, and then being angered and displeased, snatch it back or have it snatched back, it is to be forfeited and confessed. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::3 Jātarūpa Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 23	Kayavikkayasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī nānappakārakaṁ kayavikkayaṁ samāpajjeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu NP 20	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun engages in various kinds of barter, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_23.mp3]	184	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time Venerable Upananda the Sakyan had become skilled at making robes.<br><br>He made an upper robe of old cloth, well-dyed and beautifully made, and he wore it.<br><br>Just then a certain wanderer who was wearing an expensive robe went up to Upananda and said,<br><br>“Your upper robe is beautiful.<br><br>Please give it to me in exchange for my robe.”<br><br>“Are you sure?”<br><br>“I am.”<br><br>Saying, “Alright, then,” he gave it.<br><br>The wanderer put on the upper robe and went to the wanderers’ monastery.<br><br>The wanderers said to him,<br><br>“This upper robe of yours is beautiful.<br><br>Where did you get it?”<br><br>“I traded it for my robe.”<br><br>“But how long will it last?<br><br>Your other robe was better.”<br><br>The wanderer realized they were right,<br><br>and so he returned to Upananda and said,<br><br>“Here’s your upper robe. Please give me back mine.”<br><br>“But didn’t I ask you if you were sure?<br><br>I won’t give it back.”<br><br>Then that wanderer complained and criticized him,<br><br>“Even householders give back to each other when they regret a trade.<br><br>How, then, can a monastic not do the same?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of that wanderer,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda barter with a wanderer?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned Upananda:<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Various kinds:<br><br>robes, almsfood, a dwelling, or medicinal supplies; even a bit of bath powder, a tooth cleaner, or a piece of string.<br><br>Engages in barter:<br><br>if he misbehaves, saying, “Give that for this,” “Bring that for this,” “Trade that with this,” “Exchange that for this,” he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>When it has been bartered—his own goods are in the hands of the other and the other’s goods are in his own hands—it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The goods should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, they should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-vb-np1#3.2.5"">Bu NP 1:3.2.5</a>–3.2.29, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, I have engaged in various kinds of barter.<br><br>This is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is bartering, and he perceives it as such, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is bartering, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is bartering, but he does not perceive it as such, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not bartering, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not bartering, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not bartering, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if he asks about the value;<br><br>if he tells an attendant;<br><br>if he says, “I have this and I have need of such-and-such;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on bartering, the tenth, is finished.<br><br>The second subchapter on silk is finished.<br><br>This is the summary:<br><br>“Silk, entirely, two parts,<br><br>Six years, sitting mat;<br><br>And two on wool, should take,<br><br>Two on various kinds.”	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā upanando sakyaputto paṭṭo hoti cīvarakammaṁ kātuṁ.<br><br>So paṭapilotikānaṁ saṅghāṭiṁ karitvā surattaṁ suparikammakataṁ katvā pārupi.<br><br>Atha kho aññataro paribbājako mahagghaṁ paṭaṁ pārupitvā yenāyasmā upanando sakyaputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ upanandaṁ sakyaputtaṁ etadavoca—<br><br>“sundarā kho tyāyaṁ, āvuso, saṅghāṭi;<br><br>dehi me paṭenā”ti.<br><br>“Jānāhi, āvuso”ti.<br><br>“Āmāvuso, jānāmī”ti.<br><br>“Handāvuso”ti, adāsi.<br><br>Atha kho so paribbājako taṁ saṅghāṭiṁ pārupitvā paribbājakārāmaṁ agamāsi.<br><br>Paribbājakā taṁ paribbājakaṁ etadavocuṁ—<br><br>“sundarā kho tyāyaṁ, āvuso, saṅghāṭi;<br><br>kuto tayā laddhā”ti?<br><br>“Tena me, āvuso, paṭena parivattitā”ti.<br><br>“Katihipi tyāyaṁ, āvuso, saṅghāṭi bhavissati,<br><br>soyeva te paṭo varo”ti.<br><br>Atha kho so paribbājako—“saccaṁ kho paribbājakā āhaṁsu—‘katihipi myāyaṁ saṅghāṭi bhavissati. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::3 Jātarūpa Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 24	Ūnapañcabandhanasikkhāpadaṁ	Yā pana bhikkhunī ūnapañcabandhanena pattena aññaṁ navaṁ pattaṁ cetāpeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. <br>Tāya bhikkhuniyā so patto bhikkhuniparisāya nissajjitabbo, <br>yo ca tassā bhikkhuniparisāya pattapariyanto, so tassā bhikkhuniyā padātabbo: <br>“ayaṁ te bhikkhuni patto yāvabhedanāya dhāretabbo”ti, ayaṁ tattha sāmīci.		Matches Bu NP 22	Uses Yā pana bhikkhunī, Tāya bhikkhuniyā,&nbsp;&nbsp;'bhikkhuniparisāya' instead of 'bhikkhuparisāya', tassā&nbsp;	If a nun exchanges an almsbowl with fewer than five mends for a new almsbowl, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br>That nun should relinquish that almsbowl to a gathering of nuns.<br>She should then be given the last almsbowl belonging to that gathering:<br>‘Nun, this bowl is yours. Keep it until it breaks.’ This is the proper procedure.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_24.mp3]	187	At one time the Buddha was staying in the Sakyan country in the Banyan Tree Monastery at Kapilavatthu.<br><br>At that time a potter had invited the monks, saying,<br><br>“If any of you needs an almsbowl, I’ll provide it.”<br><br>But the monks had no sense of moderation, and they asked for many bowls.<br><br>Those who had small bowls asked for large ones,<br><br>and those who had large bowls asked for small ones.<br><br>The potter was so busy making bowls for the monks that he was unable to make goods for sale.<br><br>He could not make a living for himself, and his wives and children suffered.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics have no sense of moderation and ask for many bowls?<br><br>This potter is so busy making bowls for them that he is unable to make goods for sale.<br><br>He is unable to make a living for himself, and his wives and children are suffering.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can those monks have no sense of moderation and ask for many bowls?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that there are monks who do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“How can those foolish men do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>After rebuking them, he gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, a monk should not ask for an almsbowl. If he does, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.”<br><br>Soon afterwards the bowl of a certain monk broke.<br><br>Knowing that the Buddha had prohibited asking for a bowl and being afraid of wrongdoing, he did not ask for a new one.<br><br>As a consequence, he collected almsfood with his hands.<br><br>People complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics collect almsfood with their hands, just like the monastics of other religions?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people<br><br>and they told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to ask for a new almsbowl if your bowl has been lost or is broken.”<br><br>When they heard about the Buddha’s allowance, the monks from the group of six asked for many bowls even when their existing bowls only had a minor chip or scratch.<br><br>Once again that potter was so busy making bowls for the monks that he was unable to make goods for sale.<br><br>He could not make a living for himself, and his wives and children suffered.<br><br>And people complained and criticized them as before.<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six ask for many bowls even when their existing bowls only has a minor chip or scratch?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>An almsbowl with fewer than five mends:<br><br>it has no mends, one mend, two mends, three mends, or four mends.<br><br>An almsbowl with a mend that does not count:<br><br>one that does not have a fracture of 3.5 cm.<br><br>An almsbowl with a mend that counts:<br><br>one that does have a fracture of 3.5 cm.<br><br>New almsbowl:<br><br>asked for is what is meant.<br><br>Exchanges:<br><br>if he asks, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets the bowl, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha.<br><br>All determined bowls should be brought together.<br><br>One should not determine an inferior bowl, thinking,<br><br>“I’ll get a valuable one.”<br><br>If one determines an inferior bowl, thinking, “I’ll get a valuable one,” one commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>After approaching the Sangha, that monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder and pay respect at the feet of the senior monks. He should then squat on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say:<br><br>‘Venerables, this almsbowl, which I got in exchange for a bowl that had fewer than five mends, is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’”<br><br>After relinquishing it, he should confess the offense.<br><br>The confession should be received by a competent and capable monk.<br><br>A monk who has five qualities should be appointed as the distributor of almsbowls:<br><br>one who is not biased by favoritism, ill will, confusion, or fear, and who knows what has and has not been distributed.<br><br>“And, monks, this is how he should be appointed.<br><br>First the monk should be asked,<br><br>and then a competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of almsbowls.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The Sangha appoints monk so-and-so as the distributor of almsbowls.<br><br>Any monk who agrees to appointing monk so-and-so as the distributor of almsbowls should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t agree should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has appointed monk so-and-so as the distributor of almsbowls.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent.<br><br>I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>The appointed monk should give away that relinquished bowl.<br><br>He should tell the most senior monk,<br><br>“Sir, would you like this bowl?”<br><br>If the most senior monk takes it, his old bowl should be offered to the next monk.<br><br>He should not not take that bowl out of sympathy. If he does, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>It is not to be offered to anyone who does not have bowl.<br><br>In this manner it should be offered all the way to the most junior monk in the Sangha.<br><br>He should then be given the last almsbowl belonging to that gathering: “Monk, this bowl is yours. Keep it until it breaks”:<br><br>That monk is not to store that bowl in an unsuitable place, use it in an unsuitable way, or give it away, thinking, “How may this bowl be lost, destroyed, or broken?”<br><br>If he stores it in an unsuitable place, uses it in an unsuitable way, or gives it away, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>This is the proper procedure:<br><br>this is the right method.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If he exchanges a bowl without mends for a bowl without mends, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges a [sound:ABi_NP_24.mp3]	{-less than five mends} Should a bhikkhunī with an alms bowl having less than five mends exchange it for another new bowl, it is to be forfeited and confessed. The bowl is to be forfeited by the bhikkhunī to the assembly of bhikkhunīs. That assembly of bhikkhunīs’ final bowl should be presented to the bhikkhunī (saying): “This, bhikkhuni, is your bowl. It is to be kept until broken.” This is the proper procedure here. [22]

Yā pana bhikkhunī jānaṁ saṅghikaṁ lābhaṁ pariṇataṁ attano pariṇāmeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ. <br><br>Jātarūparajatavaggo&nbsp;tatiyo.	Matches Bu NP 30	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun diverts to herself material support that she knows was intended for the Sangha, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>The third subchapter on gold and silver.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_30.mp3]	202	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>an association had prepared a meal together with robe-cloth for the Sangha,<br><br>intending to offer the robe-cloth after giving the meal.<br><br>But the monks from the group of six went to that association<br><br>and said,<br><br>“Please give this robe-cloth to us.”<br><br>“Venerables, we can’t do that.<br><br>We’ve prepared our annual alms-offering together with robe-cloth for the Sangha.”<br><br>“The Sangha has many donors and supporters.<br><br>But since we’re staying here, we look to you for support.<br><br>If you don’t give to us, who will?<br><br>So give us the robe-cloth.”<br><br>Being pressured by the monks from the group of six, that association gave the prepared robe-cloth to them and served the food to the Sangha.<br><br>The monks who knew that a meal together with robe-cloth had been prepared for the Sangha, but who did not know that the robe-cloth had been given to the monks from the group of six, said,<br><br>“Please offer the robe-cloth.”<br><br>“There isn’t any.<br><br>The monks from the group of six have diverted to themselves the robe-cloth we had prepared.”<br><br>The monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six divert to themselves things they knew were intended for the Sangha?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>He knows:<br><br>he knows by himself or others have told him or the donor has told him.<br><br>For the Sangha:<br><br>given to the Sangha, given up to the Sangha.<br><br>Material support:<br><br>robe-cloth, almsfood, a dwelling, and medicinal supplies; even a bit of bath powder, a tooth cleaner, or a piece of string.<br><br>Intended:<br><br>they have said, “We’ll give,” “We’ll prepare.”<br><br>If he diverts it to himself, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets it, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>It should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-vb-np1#3.2.5"">Bu NP 1:3.2.5</a>–3.2.29, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, this thing, which I diverted to myself knowing that it was intended for the Sangha, is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it was intended for the Sangha and he perceives it as such, and he diverts it to himself, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it was intended for the Sangha, but he is unsure of it, and he diverts it to himself, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was intended for the Sangha, but he does not perceive it as such, and he diverts it to himself, there is no offense.<br><br>If it was intended for one Sangha and he diverts it to another Sangha or to a shrine, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was intended for one shrine and he diverts it to another shrine or to a sangha or to an individual, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was intended for an individual and he diverts it to another individual or to a sangha or to a shrine, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was not intended for the Sangha, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was not intended for the Sangha, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it was not intended for the Sangha and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if being asked, “Where may we give?” he says, “Give where your gift will be useful;” “Give where it goes toward repairs;” “Give where it will last for a long time;” “Give where you feel inspired;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on what was intended, the tenth, is finished.<br><br>The third subchapter on almsbowls is finished.<br><br>This is the summary:<br><br>“Two on bowls, and tonics,<br><br>Rainy season, the fifth on a gift;<br><br>Oneself, having woven, haste,<br><br>Risky, and with the Sangha.”<br><br>“Venerables, the thirty rules on relinquishment and confession have been recited.<br><br>In regard to this I ask you,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A second time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>A third time I ask,<br><br>‘Are you pure in this?’<br><br>You are pure in this and therefore silent.<br><br>I’ll remember it thus.”<br><br>The chapter on offenses entailing relinquishment is finished.<br><br>The canonical text beginning with offenses entailing expulsion is finished. Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_27.mp3]	192	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove,<br><br>the monks from the group of six were making robes and they asked for a large amount of thread.<br><br>But when their robes were finished, there was much thread left over.<br><br>They said,<br><br>“Well, let’s ask for even more thread and get weavers to weave us robe-cloth.”<br><br>Yet even when that robe-cloth had been woven, there was much thread left over.<br><br>A second time they asked for more thread and had weavers weave them robe-cloth.<br><br>Once again there was much thread left over.<br><br>A third time they asked for more thread and had weavers weave them robe-cloth.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could the Sakyan monastics ask for thread and then get weavers to weave them robe-cloth?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How could the monks from the group of six ask for thread and then get weavers to weave them robe-cloth?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::3 Jātarūpa Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 29	Accekacīvarasikkhāpadaṁ	Dasāhānāgataṁ kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamaṁ bhikkhuniyā paneva accekacīvaraṁ uppajjeyya, accekaṁ maññamānāya bhikkhuniyā paṭiggahetabbaṁ, paṭiggahetvā yāva cīvarakālasamayaṁ nikkhipitabbaṁ. <br>Tato ce uttari nikkhipeyya, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu NP 28	Uses 'bhikkhuniyā', maññamānāya Uses 'uttari' instead of 'uttariṃ'.	When there are ten days left to the Kattika full moon that ends the first rainy-season residence and a haste-cloth is given to a nun, she may receive it if she regards it as urgent. She may then store it until the end of the robe season.<br>If she stores it beyond that, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_29.mp3]	201	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a government official who was about to set out on a journey sent a message to the monks, saying,<br><br>“Come, venerables, I wish to give robe-cloth to those who have completed the rainy-season residence.”<br><br>The monks thought,<br><br>“The Buddha has allowed such robes only for those who have completed the rains residence,”<br><br>and being afraid of wrongdoing they did not go.<br><br>That government official complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could they not come when I send a message?<br><br>I’m about to set out with the army.<br><br>It’s hard to know whether I’ll live or die.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of that government official,<br><br>and they told the Buddha.<br><br>Soon afterwards the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:<br><br>“Monks, I allow you to receive a haste-cloth, and then store it.”<br><br>When they heard about this,<br><br>monks received haste-cloths and stored them beyond the robe season,<br><br>keeping them in bundles on a bamboo robe rack.<br><br>While walking about the dwellings, Venerable Ānanda saw that cloth, and he asked the monks,<br><br>“Whose cloth is this?”<br><br>“It’s our haste-cloth.”<br><br>“But how long have you stored it?”<br><br>They told him.<br><br>Ānanda then complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How could these monks receive haste-cloth and then store it beyond the robe season?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, Ānanda told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned the monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that there are monks who do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Monks, how could those foolish men do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>There are ten days left:<br><br>the invitation ceremony is ten days in the future.<br><br>The Kattika full moon that ends the first rainy-season residence:<br><br>the Kattika full moon of the invitation ceremony is what is meant.<br><br>Haste-cloth:<br><br>when someone intends to set out with the army, when someone intends to set out on a journey, when someone is sick, when someone is pregnant, when someone without faith acquires faith, when someone without confidence acquires confidence—if that person sends a message to the monks, saying, “Come, venerables, I wish to give a robe to those who have completed the rainy-season residence,” this is called “haste-cloth”.<br><br>He may receive it if he regards it as urgent. He may then store it until the end of the robe season:<br><br>establishing the perception of it as a haste-cloth, he may store it.<br><br>The robe season:<br><br>for one who has not participated in the robe-making ceremony, it is the last month of the rainy season;<br><br>for one who has participated in the robe-making ceremony, it is the five month period.<br><br>If he stores it beyond that:<br><br>for one who has not participated in the robe-making ceremony, if he stores it beyond the last day of the rainy season, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>For one who has participated in the robe-making ceremony, if he stores it beyond the day on which the robe season ends, the cloth becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The cloth should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>(To be expanded as in <a href=""https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bu-vb-np1#3.2.5"">Bu NP 1:3.2.5</a>–3.2.29, with appropriate substitutions.)<br><br>‘Venerables, this haste-cloth, which I have stored beyond the robe season, is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’ …<br><br>the Sangha should give …<br><br>you should give …<br><br>‘I give this cloth back to you.’”<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is haste-cloth and he perceives it as such, and he stores it beyond the robe season, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is haste-cloth, but he is unsure of it, and he stores it beyond the robe season, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is haste-cloth, but he does not perceive it as such, and he stores it beyond the robe season, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it has not been determined, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been assigned to another, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been given away, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been lost, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been destroyed, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been burned, but he perceives that it has …<br><br>If it has not been stolen, but he perceives that it has, and he stores it beyond the robe season, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he uses a cloth that should be relinquished without first relinquishing it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not haste-cloth, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not haste-cloth, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not haste-cloth and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if within the robe season the haste-cloth has been determined, assigned to another, given away, lost, destroyed, burned, stolen, or taken on trust;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on haste-cloth, the eighth, is finished. Matches Bu NP 19	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun engages in various kinds of trades involving money, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_22.mp3]	183	At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery.<br><br>At that time the monks from the group of six engaged in various kinds of trades involving money.<br><br>People complained and criticized them,<br><br>“How can the Sakyan monastics engage in trades that involve money? They’re just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of those people,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized those monks,<br><br>“How can the monks from the group of six do this?”<br><br>After rebuking those monks in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned those monks:<br><br>“Is it true, monks, that you do this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked them …<br><br>“Foolish men, how can you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Various kinds:<br><br>what is shaped, what is not shaped, and what is both shaped and not shaped.<br><br>What is shaped:<br><br>what is meant for the head, what is meant for the neck, what is meant for the hands, what is meant for the feet, what is meant for the waist.<br><br>What is not shaped:<br><br>what is shaped in a lump is what is meant.<br><br>What is both shaped and not shaped:<br><br>both of them.<br><br>Money:<br><br>a golden <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i> coin, a copper <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin, a wooden <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin, a resin <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin—whatever is used in commerce.<br><br>Engages:<br><br>If he exchanges what is shaped with what is shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is not shaped with what is shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is both shaped and not shaped with what is shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is shaped with what is not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is not shaped with what is not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is both shaped and not shaped with what is not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is shaped with what is both shaped and not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is not shaped with what is both shaped and not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If he exchanges what is both shaped and not shaped with what is both shaped and not shaped, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>After approaching the Sangha, that monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder and pay respect at the feet of the senior monks. He should then squat on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say,<br><br>‘Venerables, I have engaged in various kinds of trades involving money.<br><br>This is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’”<br><br>After relinquishing it, he is to confess the offense.<br><br>The confession should be received by a competent and capable monk.<br><br>If a monastery worker or a lay follower is available, you should tell him,<br><br>“Look into this.”<br><br>If he says,<br><br>“What can I get you with this?”<br><br>one should not say,<br><br>“Get this or that;”<br><br>one should point out what is allowable:<br><br>ghee, oil, honey, or syrup.<br><br>If he makes a purchase and brings back what is allowable, everyone may enjoy it except the one who did the exchange involving money.<br><br>If this is what happens, all is well.<br><br>If not, he should be told,<br><br>“Discard this.”<br><br>If he discards it, all is well.<br><br>If he does not, a monk who has five qualities should be appointed as the money discarder:<br><br>one who is not biased by desire, ill will, confusion, or fear, and who knows what has and has not been discarded.<br><br>“And, monks, this is how he should be appointed.<br><br>First the monk should be asked<br><br>and then a competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should appoint monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The Sangha appoints monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>Any monk who agrees to appointing monk so-and-so as the money discarder should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t agree should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has appointed monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent.<br><br>I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>The appointed monk should throw it away without taking note of where.<br><br>If he takes note of where he throws it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is money, and he perceives it as such, and he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is money, but he is unsure of it, and he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is money, but he does not perceive it as such, and he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not money, but he perceives it as such, and he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not money, but he is unsure of it, and he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not money, and he does not perceive it as such, but he exchanges it for money, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not money, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not money, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not money, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on trades involving money, the ninth, is finished. Pali Bhikkhunī Patimokkha Memorizing for Bhikkhunī::5.Nissaggiya pācittiyā::3 Jātarūpa Vagga	BI VIN PAT BI NP 28	Mahāpesakārasikkhāpadaṁ	Bhikkhuniṁ paneva uddissa aññātako gahapati vā gahapatānī vā tantavāyehi cīvaraṁ vāyāpeyya, tatra cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā tantavāye upasaṅkamitvā cīvare vikappaṁ āpajjeyya: “idaṁ kho āvuso cīvaraṁ maṁ uddissa viyyati, āyatañca karotha, vitthatañca appitañca suvītañca suppavāyitañca suvilekhitañca suvitacchitañca karotha, appeva nāma mayampi āyasmantānaṁ kiñcimattaṁ anupadajjeyyāmā”ti, evañca sā bhikkhunī vatvā kiñcimattaṁ anupadajjeyya antamaso piṇḍapātamattampi, nissaggiyaṁ pācittiyaṁ.		Matches Bu NP 27	Uses 'bhikkhuniṁ',&nbsp;cesā bhikkhunī pubbe appavāritā,&nbsp;sā bhikkhunī	If a male or female householder is having robe-cloth woven by weavers for an unrelated nun and, without first being invited, that nun goes to those weavers and specifies the kind of robe-cloth she wants, saying, ‘This robe-cloth that you are weaving for me, make it long and wide; make it closely woven, well-woven, well-stretched, well-scraped, and well-combed, and perhaps I will even give you a small gift,’ then, in saying that and afterwards giving them a small gift, even a bit of almsfood, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_28.mp3]	198	At one time when the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery,<br><br>a man who was going away said to his wife, “Please weigh some thread, take it to the weavers, get them to weave robe-cloth, and put the robe-cloth aside.<br><br>When I return, I’ll give it to Venerable Upananda.”<br><br>An alms-collecting monk heard that man speaking those words.<br><br>He then went to Upananda the Sakyan and said, “Upananda, you have much merit.<br><br>In such-and-such a place I heard a man, as he was going away, tell his wife to get robe-cloth woven so that he could give it to you when he returned.”<br><br>“He’s my supporter.”<br><br>And the weaver was Upananda’s supporter too.<br><br>Upananda then went to that weaver and said,<br><br>“This robe-cloth that you’re weaving for me, make it long and wide. And make it closely woven, well-woven, well-stretched, well-scraped, and well-combed.”<br><br>“Venerable, they’ve already weighed the thread and given it to me,<br><br>telling me to weave the robe-cloth with that.<br><br>I won’t be able to make it long, wide, or closely woven.<br><br>But I’m able to make it well-woven, well-stretched, well-scraped, and well-combed.”<br><br>“Just make it long, wide, and closely woven.<br><br>There’ll be enough thread.”<br><br>Then, when all the thread had been used up, that weaver went to that woman and said, “Ma’am, I need more thread.”<br><br>“But didn’t I tell you to weave the robe-cloth with that thread?”<br><br>“You did.<br><br>But Venerable Upananda told me to make it long, wide, and closely woven.<br><br>And he said there would be enough thread.”<br><br>That woman then gave him as much thread again as she had done the first time.<br><br>When Upananda heard that the husband had returned from his travels, he went to his house and sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>That man approached him, bowed, and sat down.<br><br>He then said to his wife, “Has the robe-cloth been woven?”<br><br>“Yes, it has.”<br><br>“Please bring it. I’ll give it to Venerable Upananda.”<br><br>She then got the robe-cloth, gave it to her husband, and told him what had happened.<br><br>After giving the robe-cloth to Upananda, he complained and criticized him,<br><br>“These Sakyan monastics have great desires; they’re not content.<br><br>It’s no easy matter to give them robe-cloth.<br><br>How could Venerable Upananda go to the weavers and say what kind of robe-cloth he wanted without first being invited by me?”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of that man,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized Upananda,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda go to a householder’s weavers and say what kind of robe-cloth he wants without first being invited?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned Upananda:<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>“Is he a relative of yours?”<br><br>“No, sir.”<br><br>“Foolish man, people who are unrelated don’t know what’s appropriate and inappropriate, what’s good and bad, in dealing with each other.<br><br>And still you did this.<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>For a monk:<br><br>for the benefit of a monk; making a monk the object of consideration, one wants to give to him.<br><br>Unrelated:<br><br>anyone who is not a descendant of one’s male ancestors going back eight generations, either on the mother’s side or on the father’s side.<br><br>A male householder:<br><br>any man who lives at home.<br><br>A female householder:<br><br>any woman who lives at home.<br><br>By weavers:<br><br>by those who weave.<br><br>Robe-cloth:<br><br>one of the six kinds of robe-cloth, but not smaller than what can be assigned to another.<br><br>Is having woven:<br><br>is causing to weave.<br><br>If that monk:<br><br>the monk the robe-cloth is being woven for.<br><br>Without first being invited:<br><br>without it first being said, “Venerable, what kind of robe-cloth do you need? What kind of robe-cloth should I get woven for you?”<br><br>Goes to those weavers:<br><br>having gone to their house, having gone up to them wherever.<br><br>Specifies the kind of robe-cloth he wants:<br><br>“This robe-cloth that you are weaving for me, make it long and wide;<br><br>make it closely woven, well-woven, well-stretched, well-scraped, and well-combed;<br><br>and perhaps I will tooth cleaner, a piece of string, and even if he gives a teaching.<br><br>If the weaver makes it long or wide or closely woven because of the monk’s statement, then for the effort there is an act of wrong conduct.<br><br>When he gets the robe-cloth, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>The robe-cloth should be relinquished to a sangha, a group, or an individual.<br><br>“And, monks, it perceives them as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if it is from relatives;<br><br>if it is from those who have given an invitation;<br><br>if it is for the benefit of someone else;<br><br>if it is by means of his own property;<br><br>if someone wants to have expensive robe-cloth woven, but he has them weave inexpensive robe-cloth instead;<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The long training rule on weavers, the seventh, is finished. [sound:ABi_NP_28.mp3]	{-greater about weavers} In case a man or woman householder unrelated to a bhikkhunī has weavers weave robe-cloth for her, and if the bhikkhunī without previous invitation should approach the weavers and make stipulations for the cloth, saying: “This cloth, friends, is to be woven for me. Make it long, broad, tightly woven, well woven, well spread, well scraped, well smoothed, and perhaps I may gave you a little something.” And should the bhikkhunī, having said that, give them a little something, even a bit of alms food, it (the cloth) is to be forfeited and confessed. Matches Bu NP 18	Uses 'bhikkhunī'.	If a nun takes, has someone else take, or consents to gold, silver, or money being deposited for her, she commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.	Nissaggiya pācittiyā	Jātarūpavaggo	[sound:Bi_NP_21.mp3]	182	"At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary.<br><br>At that time Venerable Upananda was associating with a family from which he received a regular meal.<br><br>Whenever that family obtained food, they put aside a portion for Upananda.<br><br>And that’s what they did when one evening they obtained some meat.<br><br>The following morning their son got up early and cried, “Give me meat!”<br><br>The man said to his wife, “Give him the venerable’s portion.<br><br>We’ll buy something else for the venerable.”<br><br>On the same morning Upananda robed up, took his bowl and robe, and went to that family where he sat down on the prepared seat.<br><br>The man of the house approached Upananda, bowed, sat down, and said,<br><br>“Yesterday evening, venerable, we obtained some meat, and we put aside a portion for you.<br><br>But then in the morning our son got up early and cried, ‘Give me meat!’ and we gave him your portion.<br><br>What can we get you for a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i>?”<br><br>“Are you giving up a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i> coin for me?”<br><br>“Yes.”<br><br>“Then just give me that <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i>.”<br><br>After giving a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i> to Upananda, that man complained and criticized him, “The Sakyan monastics accept money just as we do.”<br><br>The monks heard the complaints of that man,<br><br>and the monks of few desires complained and criticized him,<br><br>“How could Venerable Upananda receive money?”<br><br>After rebuking him in many ways, they told the Buddha. Soon afterwards he had the Sangha gathered and questioned Upananda:<br><br>“Is it true, Upananda, that you did this?”<br><br>“It’s true, sir.”<br><br>The Buddha rebuked him …<br><br>“Foolish man, how could you do this?<br><br>This will affect people’s confidence …” …<br><br>“And, monks, this training rule should be recited like this:"	"<b>Definitions</b><br><br>A:<br><br>whoever …<br><br>Monk:<br><br>… The monk who has been given the full ordination by a unanimous Sangha through a legal procedure consisting of one motion and three announcements that is irreversible and fit to stand—this sort of monk is meant in this case.<br><br>Gold:<br><br>that which has the color of the Teacher is what is meant.<br><br>Silver:<br><br>a <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">kahāpaṇa</i> coin, a copper <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin, a wooden <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin, a resin <i lang=""pi"" translate=""no"">māsaka</i> coin—whatever is used in commerce.<br><br>Takes:<br><br>if he takes hold of it himself, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>Has someone else take:<br><br>if he has another take hold of it, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>Consents to … being deposited for him:<br><br>if someone says, “This is for you,” and he consents to it being deposited for him, it becomes subject to relinquishment.<br><br>It should be relinquished in the midst of the Sangha.<br><br>“And, monks, it should be relinquished like this.<br><br>After approaching the Sangha, that monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder and pay respect at the feet of the senior monks. He should then squat on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say:<br><br>‘Venerables, I have received money.<br><br>It is to be relinquished.<br><br>I relinquish it to the Sangha.’”<br><br>After relinquishing it, he is to confess the offense.<br><br>The confession should be received by a competent and capable monk.<br><br>If a monastery worker or a lay follower is available, you should tell him,<br><br>“Look into this.”<br><br>If he says,<br><br>“What can I get you with this?”<br><br>one should not say,<br><br>“Get this or that;”<br><br>one should point out what is allowable:<br><br>ghee, oil, honey, or syrup.<br><br>If he makes a purchase and brings back what is allowable, everyone may enjoy it except the one who received the money.<br><br>If this is what happens, all is well.<br><br>If not, he should be told,<br><br>“Discard it.”<br><br>If he discards it, all is well.<br><br>If he does not, a monk who has five qualities should be appointed as the money discarder:<br><br>one who is not biased by desire, ill will, confusion, or fear, and who knows what has and has not been discarded.<br><br>“And, monks, this is how he should be appointed.<br><br>First the monk should be asked<br><br>and then a competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:<br><br>‘Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>If the Sangha is ready, it should appoint monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>This is the motion.<br><br>Please, venerables, I ask the Sangha to listen.<br><br>The Sangha appoints monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>Any monk who agrees to appointing monk so-and-so as the money discarder should remain silent.<br><br>Any monk who doesn’t agree should speak up.<br><br>The Sangha has appointed monk so-and-so as the money discarder.<br><br>The Sangha approves and is therefore silent.<br><br>I’ll remember it thus.’”<br><br>The appointed monk should throw it away without taking note of where.<br><br>If he takes note of where he throws it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br><b>Permutations</b><br><br>If it is money, and he perceives it as such, and he receives it, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is money, but he is unsure of it, and he receives it, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is money, but he does not perceive it as such, and he receives it, he commits an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.<br><br>If it is not money, but he perceives it as such, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not money, but he is unsure of it, he commits an offense of wrong conduct.<br><br>If it is not money, and he does not perceive it as such, there is no offense."	There is no offense:<br><br>if, within a monastery or a lodging, he takes it or has someone take it, and he then puts it aside with the thought,<br><br>“Whoever owns it will come and get it;”<br><br>if he is insane;<br><br>if he is the first offender.<br><br>The training rule on money, the eighth, is finished.	Tena samayena buddho bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā upanando sakyaputto aññatarassa kulassa kulūpako hoti niccabhattiko.<br><br>Yaṁ tasmiṁ kule uppajjati khādanīyaṁ vā bhojanīyaṁ vā tato āyasmato upanandassa sakyaputtassa paṭiviso ṭhapiyyati.<br><br>Tena kho pana samayena sāyaṁ tasmiṁ kule maṁsaṁ uppannaṁ hoti.<br><br>Tassa kulassa dārako rattiyā paccūsasamayaṁ paccuṭṭhāya rodati—“maṁsaṁ me dethā”ti.<br><br>Atha kho so puriso pajāpatiṁ etadavoca—“ayyassa paṭivisaṁ dārakassa dehi.<br><br>Aññaṁ cetāpetvā ayyassa dassāmā”ti.<br><br>Atha kho āyasmā upanando sakyaputto pubbaṇhasamayaṁ nivāsetvā pattacīvaraṁ ādāya yena taṁ kulaṁ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi.<br><br>Atha kho so puriso yenāyasmā upanando sakyaputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṁ upanandaṁ sakyaputtaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi.
